items.prompt: Why did Dilnoza feel she should look for a new job?
items.answer: Nobody at her firm took her ideas seriously
items.passage:
Dilnoza Karimova had rehearsed her answers for nearly two weeks before the interview at Silk Route Logistics, a freight company in Samarkand that employs about three hundred people. She had been working as a dispatcher for a smaller firm since 2018, and although she enjoyed the job, she felt that nobody there would ever take her ideas seriously. When the advertisement for a regional operations coordinator appeared in March, she applied the same evening, half expecting never to hear back.

To her surprise, the company phoned her within four days and invited her to an interview on Thursday the seventeenth, at half past ten. She had assumed the panel would consist of a single manager, so she was a little unsettled to find three people waiting: the operations director, Mr. Yusupov, a younger human resources officer called Natalia, and an engineer who said very little throughout. The interview was scheduled to last forty-five minutes, but it ran for almost an hour and a half.

The first question was the one she had feared most: why did she want to leave a stable job? Instead of criticising her employer, as many candidates do, Dilnoza explained that she wished to take on more responsibility. Mr. Yusupov nodded, but then pressed her. He asked her to describe a situation in which a delivery had gone badly wrong. She told them about a shipment of medical supplies that had been delayed at the border for two days because of a paperwork error. Rather than blaming the customs officer, she admitted that her own team had filled in the form hastily. What impressed the panel, Natalia later told her, was not the mistake itself but the fact that Dilnoza had introduced a double-checking system afterwards, which reduced similar errors by roughly half.

Not everything went smoothly, however. When the engineer finally spoke, he asked how she would handle a driver who refused to work on weekends. Dilnoza hesitated, then answered that she would simply order him to come in. The room fell silent, and she realised at once that this had sounded rigid. She tried to repair the damage by adding that she would first listen to his reasons, but she was not sure it was enough. Looking back, she thinks that moment taught her more than all her preparation, because it showed her that honesty about uncertainty is better than a confident but careless answer.

At the end, she was asked about salary. She had read that candidates should never name the first figure, yet Mr. Yusupov asked directly, so she suggested a range of eight to nine million soums a month. He did not react. A week later she received an email offering her the post at eight and a half million, with a probation period of three months. She accepted, though she negotiated an extra five days of annual leave. She starts on the first of June, and she says she is nervous but not regretful.
options: Nobody at her firm took her ideas seriously
Her firm was about to close
items.explain: She felt that nobody would ever take her ideas seriously.

items.prompt: Where does Aziz do most of his work at home?
items.answer: In a room that used to be a storeroom
items.passage:
Aziz Normatov has worked for a software company in Berlin since January of last year, yet he has never once set foot in its office. He lives in Bukhara, in a house he shares with his parents and his younger sister, and he does his job from a small room on the second floor that used to be a storeroom. When he first accepted the offer, he imagined that remote work would be a kind of freedom: no commuting, no rigid timetable, and the chance to earn a European salary while living in the city he loves. Eighteen months later, his opinion is considerably more mixed.

The most obvious difficulty is the time difference. Berlin is three hours behind Bukhara in winter and four in summer, which means that the team's daily meeting, held at ten o'clock German time, begins at one or two in the afternoon for him. At first he considered this a minor inconvenience, but he soon discovered that most of the spontaneous discussions happen in the morning in Germany, when he is still asleep or having breakfast. By the time he logs on, decisions have often already been made, and he has to read through hundreds of chat messages to catch up. His manager, a patient woman called Katrin, has tried to improve the situation by recording every meeting and writing short summaries, but Aziz admits that it is not the same as being in the room.

A second problem, less expected, was loneliness. Although he is rarely physically alone, since his family is always around, he felt cut off from the casual conversations that make an office tolerable. Nobody asked him how his weekend had been, and nobody noticed when he was having a bad day. After about six months he began to feel unmotivated, and his productivity dropped noticeably. He did not tell anyone, partly because he feared that his employer would conclude that remote work did not suit him.

The solution came from an unlikely source. A friend invited him to a coworking space in the old part of the city, where freelancers, a few architects and a group of university students rent desks by the day. Aziz now goes there three days a week and works from home on the other two. He pays around forty dollars a month, which he considers money well spent. Surrounded by people who are doing entirely different jobs, he finds it easier to concentrate, and the short conversations over tea have restored his sense of belonging.

Interestingly, Aziz is not convinced that remote work is better than office work in general. He thinks it suits experienced employees who already know their company, but he would not recommend it to someone in their first job, who needs to learn by watching colleagues. Next spring, the company will fly the whole team to Berlin for a week-long gathering. Aziz is excited to finally meet his colleagues, though he has already warned them that he is much quieter in person than in writing.
options: In a room that used to be a storeroom
items.explain: He works from a small room that used to be a storeroom.

items.prompt: What does the word Tezkor mean?
items.passage:
Madina Rashidova still keeps the wooden sign of her first company on a shelf above her desk. It reads Tezkor, which means quick in Uzbek, and it was meant to hang outside the office of what she hoped would become the biggest food delivery service in Central Asia. Instead, it now serves as a reminder of the most expensive lesson of her life.

In the spring of 2019, Madina and two university friends, Otabek and Sevara, launched Tezkor from a rented apartment in Tashkent. The idea was simple: customers ordered meals through an app, and couriers on motorbikes brought them within thirty minutes. Within the first year, fifty restaurants had signed up, and around fifteen couriers were working for them. A group of investors, impressed by how quickly the number of orders was growing, gave the founders one hundred and twenty thousand dollars. Madina remembers the evening they received the money as the happiest of her working life, and also, looking back, as the moment when their judgement began to fail.

Rather than perfecting the service in the capital, the founders decided to open in Samarkand and Namangan at the same time. Their reasoning was that competitors were about to arrive, and that whoever reached the regions first would win. It was a reasonable argument, but it ignored a practical problem: in smaller cities there were fewer customers per kilometre, so each delivery cost more than the company could charge. The more orders Tezkor received outside Tashkent, the more money it lost. Madina insists that the numbers were visible in the spreadsheets, but nobody wanted to look at them. Growth had become more important than profit.

The situation became critical in the autumn of 2020, when a larger rival introduced free delivery for three months. Tezkor could not match the offer. Within six weeks, nearly half of its customers had disappeared, and two of the three investors refused to provide more money. The founders tried to cut costs, but dismissing couriers damaged the service further, and the remaining customers complained about late meals. In February of the following year, they closed the company. Eleven people lost their jobs, and Madina spent months paying back what she owed to restaurants.

What surprises people is that she does not describe the failure as a disaster. She works today as an operations consultant for small shops, and she says that her clients trust her precisely because she has made every possible mistake. If she could advise her younger self, she would say that speed is useful only after the basics are working. She has also learned never to hire friends without a clear agreement on who decides what; her friendship with Otabek, once close, has never fully recovered. She still hopes to start another business one day, but this time she will wait until she has at least a year of profit.
items.explain: It means quick in Uzbek.

items.prompt: According to Feruza, which hour of the night is the most dangerous?
items.answer: Between three and four in the morning
items.passage:
Feruza Qodirova has been a nurse on the night shift at a district hospital outside Fergana for eleven years, and she can tell you precisely which hour of the night is the most dangerous. It is not midnight, as most people assume, but somewhere between three and four in the morning, when the body's temperature falls, patients grow weaker, and even experienced staff find it hard to stay alert. She works from eight in the evening until eight in the morning, four nights in a row, followed by four days off, and she admits that the rhythm has shaped her whole life.

Her ward, which has thirty-two beds, is staffed at night by only three nurses and one doctor who is often asleep in the duty room unless he is urgently needed. This means that Feruza makes many decisions herself. Last winter, for example, an elderly patient called Mr. Hakimov began to breathe with difficulty at about half past three. She noticed that his lips were slightly blue, checked his oxygen level, and called the doctor without waiting for the next scheduled round. Because she acted quickly, he was moved to intensive care within fifteen minutes and recovered. Feruza does not consider this heroic; she says it was simply what the training had prepared her to do. What bothers her is that nobody outside the hospital sees these moments.

The price of the job is considerable. Her sleep is never quite normal, even on days off, and she has suffered from headaches for years. She has learned to eat a proper meal at midnight rather than relying on tea and biscuits, to keep the bedroom completely dark during the day, and to avoid coffee after two in the morning. Her husband, a bus driver who works regular hours, sees her mostly at the weekend, and her daughter, who is nine, has grown used to doing homework alone. Feruza feels guilty about this, although her husband insists that the family is proud of her.

There are, however, compensations. Night staff are paid about thirty percent more than their day colleagues, and the atmosphere is calmer, without the crowds of visitors and the constant noise of the morning. Patients often talk more freely at night; fear and loneliness make them honest, and Feruza has heard stories that she will never forget. She remembers an old teacher who recited poetry to her at four in the morning because he could not sleep.

Her plan is to continue for another four or five years, then move to a day position training younger nurses. Whether the hospital will allow this is uncertain, since few nurses are willing to do nights. Her daughter already dreams of studying medicine, a plan that Feruza supports with mixed feelings, because she knows exactly what the profession demands from a family.
options: Between three and four in the morning
Between eight and nine in the evening
items.explain: Not midnight, as most people assume.

items.prompt: For how long had Bakhtiyor worked as an accountant?
items.passage:
At the age of forty, Bakhtiyor Aliyev did something that his friends described as either brave or foolish, depending on how generously they felt towards him. After seventeen years as an accountant at a large Tashkent bank, he resigned, enrolled in a teacher-training course and, two years later, stood for the first time in front of a class of thirty-one nine-year-olds. He had not been dismissed, and he was not in debt. He simply woke up one morning and realised that he could not imagine doing the same work for another twenty-five years.

The decision had been developing slowly. For several years Bakhtiyor had volunteered on Saturdays at a community centre, helping children with their mathematics. He noticed that he looked forward to those mornings far more than to any day at the bank, and that he lost track of time while he was explaining fractions. Still, he hesitated. His salary was high, his position was secure, and his wife, Zulfiya, had recently begun to expect a more comfortable life. When he finally told her, she was silent for a long while, then asked only one question: whether he was certain this was not a temporary mood. He had thought about it for eighteen months, so he could answer honestly.

The practical consequences were severe. A teacher's salary was roughly forty percent lower than what he had earned, so the family postponed the purchase of a new car and gave up their annual holiday by the sea. Zulfiya went back to full-time work to compensate. The training itself was also demanding. Most of his fellow students were in their early twenties, and some of them treated him with a mixture of respect and amusement, as if he were somebody's uncle who had wandered into the wrong building. A lecturer even suggested, quite openly, that schools preferred younger candidates. Bakhtiyor admits that this comment hurt, but it also made him more determined.

Interestingly, the skills he had acquired in banking turned out to be useful. He is exceptionally organised, he is not afraid of parents who complain, and he understands numbers in a way that many of his colleagues do not. Within his first year, the headteacher asked him to manage the school's budget as well, for a small additional payment. On the other hand, he found classroom management unexpectedly hard. Children do not respond to logic in the way that adults do, and he spent the first term making mistakes he now finds embarrassing.

Today, three years after the change, he does not regret it for a moment, though he is careful not to advise others to follow his example. Each person's circumstances differ, he says, and he was fortunate to have a partner who shared the risk. What he does recommend is testing a new career on a small scale first, as he did with his Saturday lessons, before giving up the old one.
items.explain: After seventeen years at the bank he resigned.

items.prompt: For how long had Priya and Jamshid shared a desk area?
items.passage:
The disagreement between Priya Nair and Jamshid Tursunov began with a simple email, and it took almost three months to repair. Both worked in the research department of a market analysis company in London, where they had shared a desk area for four years and, until that autumn, had considered themselves friends. Priya was the older of the two, with more experience, but Jamshid had joined the team through a graduate scheme and was widely regarded as the rising star.

The trouble started when the department produced a major report on consumer spending, which took five weeks to complete. Priya wrote most of the analysis, thirty pages in all, while Jamshid designed the charts and wrote the thirteen-page summary at the front. When the director presented the report to a client, he thanked Jamshid by name for what he called the main insights, and mentioned Priya only as a contributor. Priya sat in the meeting without saying a word, but she was furious. That evening she sent a long email to the entire team, explaining exactly who had done what. It was accurate, but it was also sharp in tone, and it implied that Jamshid had taken credit deliberately.

Jamshid was deeply hurt. He had not chosen the director's words, and he had not even known how the presentation would be introduced. Instead of discussing the matter privately, he replied to the whole team with a defensive message, listing his own long hours. By the next morning, colleagues had begun to take sides. Some thought Priya had been right to speak up, while others felt that she had humiliated a younger colleague in public. Work slowed down, meetings became awkward, and two clients noticed that the team no longer communicated smoothly.

After about a fortnight, the head of human resources, a calm woman named Helen Brooks, suggested a mediation session. Neither of them was keen, but both agreed. Helen did not try to decide who was right. She asked each of them to describe what they had felt, without interrupting, and then asked what they needed in order to work together again. Priya admitted that her email had been written in anger and that she should have spoken to the director directly. Jamshid acknowledged that he should have apologised for the confusion instead of defending himself. By the end of the hour, they had agreed on two practical rules: every future report would list its authors with their specific contributions, and any complaint would be raised in person before it was put in writing.

Looking back, Priya says that the conflict was never really about credit. It was about feeling invisible after fifteen years in the same field. Jamshid says that he learned how easily a careless sentence from someone in authority can damage a team. They are not close friends again, but they work well together, and the department now holds a short review meeting after every project.
items.explain: They had shared a desk area for four years.

items.prompt: According to Kamola, what is the main difference between employment and freelancing?
items.answer: An employee is paid for time, a freelancer for results
items.passage:
When Kamola Ismoilova left her translation agency job three years ago, she calculated that freelancing would pay her about twice as much for the same hours. She was right about the arithmetic, and wrong about almost everything else. Her first month brought in more than she had ever earned in one go, but the second brought almost nothing, and by the third she was working fourteen hours a day to compensate. Only then did she understand the principal difference between employment and freelancing: an employee is paid for time, while a freelancer is paid, if she is lucky, for results.

The most painful lesson concerned late payments. A foreign client, a publishing house in Vienna, owed her around nine hundred euros for a book translation and kept promising to send it next week. Kamola was too polite to insist, and the delay lasted almost four months. She survived only because her sister lent her money, and she has not forgotten the humiliation of having to ask. Since then, she has changed her method completely. She now asks for thirty percent in advance, sends an invoice on the day she delivers, and adds a clear penalty for payments that arrive more than a fortnight late. Some clients complained, and a few walked away, but she insists that the ones who remained are the ones worth keeping.

Another challenge is the lack of boundaries. Because she works at home, her friends assume that she is available at any time, and her mother regularly asks her to run errands during the day. Kamola now keeps strict hours, from nine until five, with a lunch break that she does not skip, and she answers clients' messages only within those hours. She says that this discipline has paid off in unexpected ways: her work is better, and clients seem to respect her more when she is not instantly available.

She also had to learn to price her services. At the beginning she charged very little, believing that low prices would attract customers. In fact they attracted the wrong kind: people who negotiated every comma and complained about every word. When she doubled her rate for technical documents, her workload fell by a third, but her income rose, and the clients were noticeably more courteous. Specialising in medical texts, which few translators in her city can handle, helped her justify the higher price.

Does she recommend freelancing? Cautiously. She believes it suits people who can tolerate uncertainty and who are disciplined without a supervisor, but she warns that the first year is financially dangerous. Her advice is to keep savings that would cover at least six months of expenses before leaving a regular job. She herself had only two months of savings, and she describes the decision to leave as courageous but careless. If she had waited a little longer, she would have avoided the worst of the stress.
options: An employee is paid for time, a freelancer for results
A freelancer is always paid in advance
items.explain: Employees are paid for time; freelancers for results.

items.prompt: At what time did Oliver arrive on his first Monday?
items.passage:
Oliver Grant arrived at the architecture studio in Leeds at ten to nine on his first Monday, which he thought was early, only to find that the lights were already on and three people were sitting at their desks. He was a third-year university student, nineteen weeks away from his final exams, and the eight-week summer internship had been arranged by his tutor, who had warned him that interns are often given the dullest tasks. Oliver nodded politely and privately decided that he would be the exception.

For the first fortnight, however, his tutor's prediction seemed accurate. He was asked to scan old drawings, to organise a cabinet of material samples that had not been touched for years, and to buy sandwiches for the Friday meeting. Nobody was unkind; they were simply busy, and nobody had planned what to do with him. Oliver found himself checking the clock and wondering whether he had wasted the summer. He considered complaining to his tutor, but decided that this would look immature.

The turning point came unexpectedly in the third week. Maureen, one of the senior architects, was preparing a presentation for a school that wanted a new library, and her assistant fell ill the day before the deadline. She hesitated, then asked Oliver whether he could build a simple three-dimensional model of the building in the software he had used at university. He had never worked on a real project, and his hands were shaking slightly, but he stayed until eleven that night. The next morning, Maureen examined the model for ten minutes, pointed out two errors in the staircase, and then, without any ceremony, told him to fix them and attend the presentation.

From that moment, the internship changed. He was invited to site visits, where he learned that drawings and reality rarely match exactly, and that a builder's opinion is often worth more than a manual. He also learned something about workplaces: that people rarely give opportunities to those who wait for them, but frequently give them to those who are visibly useful at a difficult moment. Oliver is careful, though, not to exaggerate. He was not paid beyond a small travel allowance of fifty pounds a week, and he knows that some of his classmates, whose families could not afford to support them, could never have accepted such an unpaid position.

On his last day, the studio director offered no job, since the firm was not hiring, but he promised a strong reference and invited Oliver to apply again once he had graduated. Oliver says that the best result of the internship was not the reference or the experience, but a more realistic picture of the profession. He still wants to be an architect, though he now expects the first few years to involve far more spreadsheets than sketches.
items.explain: He arrived at ten to nine.

Oliver Grant arrived at the architecture studio in Leeds at ten to nine on his first Monday, which he thought was early, only to find that the lights were already on and three people were sitting at their desks. He was a third-year university student, nineteen weeks away from his final exams, and the eight-week summer internship had been arranged by his tutor, who had warned him that interns are often given the dullest tasks. Oliver nodded politely and privately decided that he would be the exception.

For the first fortnight, however, his tutor's prediction seemed accurate. He was asked to scan old drawings, to organise a cabinet of material samples that had not been touched for years, and to buy sandwiches for the Friday meeting. Nobody was unkind; they were simply busy, and nobody had planned what to do with him. Oliver found himself checking the clock and wondering whether he had wasted the summer. He considered complaining to his tutor, but decided that this would look immature.

The turning point came unexpectedly in the third week. Maureen, one of the senior architects, was preparing a presentation for a school that wanted a new library, and her assistant fell ill the day before the deadline. She hesitated, then asked Oliver whether he could build a simple three-dimensional model of the building in the software he had used at university. He had never worked on a real project, and his hands were shaking slightly, but he stayed until eleven that night. The next morning, Maureen examined the model for ten minutes, pointed out two errors in the staircase, and then, without any ceremony, told him to fix them and attend the presentation.

From that moment, the internship changed. He was invited to site visits, where he learned that drawings and reality rarely match exactly, and that a builder's opinion is often worth more than a manual. He also learned something about workplaces: that people rarely give opportunities to those who wait for them, but frequently give them to those who are visibly useful at a difficult moment. Oliver is careful, though, not to exaggerate. He was not paid beyond a small travel allowance of fifty pounds a week, and he knows that some of his classmates, whose families could not afford to support them, could never have accepted such an unpaid position.

On his last day, the studio director offered no job, since the firm was not hiring, but he promised a strong reference and invited Oliver to apply again once he had graduated. Oliver says that the best result of the internship was not the reference or the experience, but a more realistic picture of the profession. He still wants to be an architect, though he now expects the first few years to involve far more spreadsheets than sketches.

items.explain: The model came in the third week.

items.prompt: At what time did the group reach the factory?
items.passage:
On the second Wednesday of October, twenty-eight students from School Number Forty-One in Namangan, accompanied by two teachers, spent a morning at the Arslan ceramics factory, a family-owned business on the edge of Rishton. The visit had been planned since the spring as part of the school's careers programme, and its organiser, a chemistry teacher named Mr. Alimov, hoped that it would persuade at least a few teenagers that manual and technical work could be a serious, well-paid option.

The coach left the school at seven fifteen, but because of roadworks it did not reach the factory until almost nine, which meant that the introductory talk had to be shortened. The manager, Mrs. Saidova, greeted the group at the gate and explained that, before entering any workshop, everyone had to wear a helmet and ear protection. Several students complained that the helmets made them look ridiculous, but the complaints stopped when they entered the first hall and found out how loud the machines were. Mrs. Saidova explained that the factory produces roughly twelve thousand plates and bowls per week, of which about sixty percent are exported to Kazakhstan and Russia.

The tour followed the path of the clay itself. In the first workshop, workers mixed raw clay with water in enormous tanks, then pressed it into sheets. In the second, a team of eleven painters, nearly all of them women, decorated the pieces by hand with the traditional blue patterns of Rishton. Students were surprised to learn that a skilled painter needs about six years before she is allowed to work on the most expensive designs, and that none of the painters had studied at a university. The third area, containing the kilns, was the hottest. Temperatures inside reach one thousand degrees, and a single mistake in timing can destroy an entire batch worth several thousand dollars.

The part that most interested the students was unexpectedly a modest one: the quality-control table. There, an elderly inspector named Mr. Karimov picked up each plate, tapped it with a wooden stick, and listened to the sound. A clear ring meant that the plate was sound, while a dull note revealed a hidden crack. He claimed that no machine had yet matched his ear. Asked how many pieces he rejected, he answered that it was about one in twenty, which sounded small until Mrs. Saidova calculated how many that was each month.

At the end, the students were given a short questionnaire. Eleven of the twenty-eight said that they would consider working in a factory, compared with only four before the visit. Mr. Alimov regarded that as a success, but he admitted that the number worth watching would be how many of them still felt the same in two years. The most common complaint was that the visit had been too short, and the school is already considering a second trip next spring, when the group could try to make a simple bowl under the guidance of the painters.
items.explain: The coach left at seven fifteen but arrived almost two hours later.

items.prompt: For how many people did Naomi become responsible?
items.passage:
When the regional manager called Naomi Okafor into his office on a Tuesday afternoon in May, she assumed that she was about to be criticised for the previous week's figures. Instead, he offered her the position of team leader in the customer support department, with a salary increase of twelve percent and responsibility for nine people, six of whom she had worked beside for over three years. She said that she needed a night to think. Walking home, she realised that she had hoped for this promotion for two years, yet she felt strangely anxious rather than delighted.

The anxiety had a clear cause. Naomi had always been popular, partly because she was relaxed about rules; she swapped shifts for colleagues without fuss, and she never reported a late arrival. Now she would be the person who decided who worked on Saturdays and who received a warning. She was also aware that Gareth, a colleague with more years of service, had applied for the same post and had been rejected. On her first day as leader, he greeted her politely but did not look her in the eye, and he did not join the team lunch.

The first month was difficult. Naomi tried to remain everyone's friend and gave way whenever somebody asked for a favour, which resulted in a rota that nobody liked and in a drop in the team's response time from four minutes to nearly seven. Her own manager pointed out, gently but clearly, that being liked and leading well are not the same thing. She later described that conversation as the most useful criticism she had ever received. It did not tell her to become harder; it told her to become consistent.

Over the following weeks, she changed her approach. She wrote down the rules for shift swaps and applied them to everybody, including her closest friend. She arranged a private conversation with Gareth, in which she did not pretend that the decision had been easy, and asked him to lead a training session on the new software, a subject in which he was clearly the best expert. At first he refused, but a week later he agreed, and the session was so successful that the director sent a message of thanks to the whole team. Relations did not become warm overnight, but they became respectful, which Naomi considers more important.

After six months, the team's average response time dropped to under three minutes, the lowest in the region, and two members were considered for promotion themselves. Naomi believes that the biggest change was inside her. She used to think that a leader needed to be confident at all times, but she now thinks that the real requirement is the willingness to make unpopular decisions and then explain them honestly. She does not claim to have become perfect; she still finds it uncomfortable to say no. But she says that the discomfort is a small price for a team that trusts her.
items.explain: Responsibility for nine people, six of whom she knew well.

items.prompt: How far from the labourer did the bracket land?
items.passage:
At a quarter past two on a Thursday in late June, a steel bracket slipped from the fourth floor of an apartment building under construction in Tashkent and struck the ground, three metres from where a young labourer was carrying cement. Nobody was injured. The labourer, nineteen-year-old Behruz, later said that he heard the noise before he understood what it was, and that his legs would not move for almost a minute. The company's safety officer, Rustam Haydarov, who happened to be standing nearby, wrote in his notebook that the day could have ended in a funeral, and that was the reason for what followed.

Many companies would have scolded the worker who dropped the bracket and carried on. Rustam argued for a different approach. He had worked on building sites for twenty years, and he had seen how often a near-miss is forgotten precisely because no one is hurt. Statistically, he explained to the directors, for every serious accident there are many near-misses, and each one carries the same warning. He persuaded the management to stop work for two hours on the following morning so that every employee could take part in an investigation.

The investigation produced uncomfortable findings. The bracket had not been dropped carelessly; it had slipped because the rope that held the lifting basket was worn, and the worn rope had been reported by a supervisor three weeks earlier. The report had simply been left in a drawer. Furthermore, the exclusion zone beneath the working floor, which should have been marked with tape, had not been marked at all, because the tape had run out and nobody had ordered more. None of these failures involved a single dramatic mistake. Each was a small neglect that, combined with the others, nearly cost a life.

The company introduced several changes. Every worn piece of equipment would now be replaced within forty-eight hours of being reported, and the person who reports a problem would receive a written reply. Workers who were not wearing helmets would be sent home without pay for the day, a rule that proved unpopular but effective: within a month, compliance rose from roughly seventy percent to almost complete. Rustam also introduced a weekly ten-minute meeting, held every Monday at seven thirty, in which workers describe hazards they have noticed. The first meetings were awkward, since men who had spent decades keeping quiet about danger were not used to being asked for their opinions, but participation has grown steadily.

Rustam insists that the most important change cannot be measured. People who once feared punishment for reporting hazards now treat reporting as normal. He often reminds new employees that a safe site is not one without accidents, but one where people speak up before they happen. Behruz, the labourer, still works there, and every June he brings a small cake to the site in memory of the day he was lucky.
items.explain: It struck the ground three metres away.

items.prompt: How many copies of her CV had Laylo printed?
items.passage:
The annual careers fair at a university in Tashkent opened its doors at ten o'clock on a rainy Saturday, and by half past ten the main hall was so crowded that Laylo Sodiqova, a final-year economics student, considered going home. She had spent the previous evening printing twenty copies of her CV and practising a thirty-second introduction in front of the mirror, but now, surrounded by students in their best suits, she felt as if her preparation had been pointless. A friend persuaded her to stay for at least one hour.

The fair featured forty-five companies, ranging from international banks to a start-up that designs mobile games. Laylo had made a list of five organisations that interested her, and she approached the first, a telecommunications company, with her carefully rehearsed speech. The recruiter listened politely, glanced at her CV for about five seconds, and handed her a leaflet directing her to the company's website. She felt deflated. Only later did she understand that recruiters at such events meet several hundred people in a day and form first impressions very quickly.

The second conversation went better, and the reason was almost accidental. At the stand of a medium-sized logistics firm, the recruiter, a man called Farhod, asked her not about her grades but about the topic of her final-year project, which concerned the cost of transporting vegetables from the Fergana Valley to the capital. Laylo forgot her rehearsed speech and began to talk with genuine enthusiasm. Farhod interrupted her twice with sharp questions, and at the end he said that his firm would be interested in an internship application, which she could submit before the end of the month.

By midday she had visited eight stands, collected a bag full of pens and notebooks, and discovered something she had not expected: the most useful moments were not the formal ones. While waiting in a queue, she overheard a graduate from a bank explaining to a younger student why she had rejected two job offers. She had chosen a position with a lower salary, because the manager seemed willing to teach her. Laylo wrote that idea in her notebook, since she realised that she had been thinking only about salary.

She left at two o'clock, exhausted but encouraged. In the days that followed, she sent personal emails to the three recruiters who had taken her details, mentioning something specific from each conversation. Only Farhod replied, but his reply led to an interview a fortnight later. Laylo does not claim that the fair gave her a job; she got the internship on the strength of the interview, not the fair itself. Still, she advises first-year students to attend, even if they are not yet looking for work, because the fair teaches how companies think. Her own checklist is short: bring fewer CVs, ask real questions, and write to the people you spoke to within two days.
items.explain: She printed twenty copies.

items.prompt: How many hours a week did Carlos usually work?
items.passage:
For nearly six years, Carlos Mendoza believed that exhaustion was simply the price of ambition. As marketing director of a rapidly growing furniture company in Madrid, he regularly worked seventy hours a week, answered messages at midnight, and cancelled holidays at the last minute with a casual remark that the business needed him. items.prompt: For about how long has the bakery produced bread?
items.passage:
The Bakirov family bakery stands in a narrow street inside the old walls of Khiva, and it has produced the same round loaves, baked against the wall of a clay oven, for almost sixty years. Mirzo Bakirov, who is now sixty-eight, inherited the business from his own father, and for four decades he arrived at the bakery every morning at half past three. His daughter Umida, thirty-four, grew up among flour sacks and promised herself that she would never work there. She studied tourism management, spent five years in a hotel in Dubai, and returned to Khiva only because her father had a minor heart operation and nobody else could run the shop.

What was meant to be a temporary arrangement lasted longer than anyone intended. Umida found that the bakery was in a more fragile condition than her father had admitted. Its income depended almost entirely on tourists in the summer months, and in winter the oven burned more wood than it earned in bread. Furthermore, the bakery kept no written accounts at all; Mirzo carried the prices and debts in his head. When Umida proposed to record every sale in a notebook, her father was offended, saying that his family had never needed paper to know its own business.

The disagreements that followed were typical of family firms. Umida wanted to sell the bread online, to hotels and restaurants in Tashkent, and to introduce a small range of sweet products aimed at tourists. Mirzo feared that the bread would lose its character if it were baked in larger quantities, and he refused to put a single sweet pastry on the counter. For three months they communicated mostly through Umida's mother, who carried messages between them with the patience of a diplomat. Eventually, the oven provided the compromise. Mirzo agreed that Umida could use the second, smaller oven at the back for new products, while the main oven would remain untouched, baking only the traditional loaves.

The experiment gave both of them something they had not anticipated. The sweet pastries, flavoured with local honey and walnuts, sold out each day in the tourist season. Orders from a hotel group in Bukhara, who had tasted the bread during a visit, increased the sales of traditional loaves by almost a third. Mirzo, who had predicted failure, said nothing for several weeks, and then one morning appeared at the counter and began to arrange the pastries himself, with a satisfied expression that he made no effort to hide.

Umida now runs the business officially, but she insists that she has not replaced her father. He still arrives at four, half an hour later than he once did, to light the main oven, and no loaf leaves the bakery without his inspection. She believes that the strongest family businesses are those in which the older generation protects the identity and the younger generation protects the future, and that neither can do the other's task. Her own daughter, who is six, has already announced that she intends to become a pilot, and Umida has decided, with some amusement, that she will not object.
items.explain: It has produced the same loaves for almost sixty years.

items.prompt: How many jobs had Henry applied for before the Norwich advertisement?
items.passage:
Henry Walsh had applied for forty-three jobs in eight months, and his folder of rejection emails had grown longer than his folder of qualifications. He was twenty-seven, held a degree in history, and wanted nothing more than to work in a museum, but every reply began with the same polite sentence: they had received many strong applications, and unfortunately his had not been selected. By the time he saw an advertisement for an assistant curator at a small regional museum in Norwich, he had almost stopped believing that he would ever be chosen.

The advertisement asked for a CV and a cover letter of no more than one page. Henry's previous letters, he realised with discomfort, had all been written in the same cautious style. They began with the words I am writing to apply for the position of, they listed his skills in order, and they ended with a sentence expressing his enthusiasm. A friend who worked in human resources had once told him that managers read such letters in under thirty seconds, and that most of them are almost identical. Henry decided that this time he would write something different.

He spent three evenings on the letter, producing nine drafts. In the end he abandoned the list of skills and told a short story. When he was fourteen, he wrote, he had found his grandfather's broken clock in the attic and, instead of throwing it away, spent a whole summer repairing it with the help of an old manual and a neighbour who was a retired watchmaker. The clock still did not keep perfect time, but he had learned that objects carry the patience of those who made them, and that the work of a museum is to protect this patience for strangers. He ended with a plain sentence saying that he would like the chance to learn from people who understood this better than he did.

It was a risk. Henry feared that the letter would seem sentimental, and he nearly deleted the story at midnight before submitting. Two weeks passed in silence, which he interpreted as a rejection. Then, on a Wednesday morning, the museum director telephoned him herself. She said that she had received sixty-two applications, and that she remembered his clock. Of the five candidates she invited to interview, he was the only one whose letter had been read aloud at the selection meeting.

Henry did not get the job. The director told him, honestly, that another candidate had three years of experience in cataloguing collections, which was exactly what the museum needed. But she offered him a six-month voluntary placement and, when a paid position became available the following spring, she encouraged him to apply. He applied, was successful, and is now an assistant curator at the same museum. He says that the cover letter did not replace qualifications; it gave an employer a reason to look at them. His advice is simple: before writing, ask what only you can say, and then say it in a way that the reader will remember.
items.explain: He had applied for forty-three jobs in eight months.

items.prompt: According to the study, what was most strongly linked with poor sleep?
items.passage:
Dr Malika Rahimova has spent eleven years studying why teenagers in Samarkand sleep so badly, and her latest findings, published last spring, have surprised even her colleagues. Her team monitored one hundred and fifty students aged fifteen to seventeen for six weeks. Contrary to what most parents assume, the students who slept least were not those who spent the most hours on their phones, but those who had the most irregular bedtimes. Going to bed at ten on Monday and at half past one on Saturday, she explained, confuses the body clock far more than a consistently late night does.

The study also challenged a popular belief about weekends. Many teenagers claim that sleeping until noon on Sunday repays the debt they built up during the week. Rahimova is sceptical. 'You can recover some alertness,' she says, 'but memory remains impaired for several days.' Students who tried to catch up at weekends performed no better in Monday tests than those who slept only six hours throughout, although they reported feeling more cheerful, which she believes is rather misleading.

The most practical result concerned light. Half of the participants were asked to avoid bright screens for the last hour before bed, while the other half carried on as usual. After three weeks, the first group fell asleep on average twenty minutes earlier, but they did not sleep longer overall, because most of them still woke at the same early hour for school. Rahimova therefore argues that the real obstacle is not the students' habits but the school timetable, which begins at a quarter to eight. She is campaigning for lessons to start at nine, a change that has worked in several European cities, though she admits it would be costly and unpopular with bus companies.

Critics point out that the study had limits. All participants came from the same city, and none of them worked part-time, so the findings may not apply to students who finish evening jobs at eleven. Rahimova accepts this and has already begun a second project involving three hundred students from rural districts. Until then, her advice is modest: keep bedtime within an hour of the same time every night, dim the lights early, and do not rely on weekend lie-ins. Several school directors have promised to read the report, but none has yet agreed to change the timetable.

items.prompt: What was Dilnoza's rule about weekly distance?
items.answer: Never increase it by more than ten per cent
items.passage:
Week 3, Sunday. Today I ran eighteen kilometres, my longest distance so far, and I am not sure whether to feel proud or terrified. Eight weeks ago I could hardly jog for twenty minutes without stopping, yet here I am, signed up for the Tashkent marathon in October. My coach, Dilnoza, insists that the first month is about patience, not speed. She has forbidden me from increasing my weekly distance by more than ten per cent, which frustrates me because I feel remarkably strong and slightly invincible.

Week 7, Thursday. I made the mistake of ignoring her rule. After a good run on Tuesday I added an extra eight kilometres on Wednesday, and by this morning my left knee was sore on the stairs. Dilnoza was not angry, only disappointed, which was worse. She told me that most injuries do not come from a single hard run but from the weeks of overconfidence that precede it. I have been ordered to swim instead for ten days, and I must admit that the pool is more relaxing than the road, although I would never say so to her.

Week 12, Saturday. The knee has healed, and I returned to running slowly. The surprising part has been food. I used to eat a huge meal the night before a long run, believing it would give me energy, but Dilnoza says the body stores fuel over several days, not from one dinner. Now I eat normal portions and take a small breakfast about two hours before starting. I also learned, painfully, that new shoes should never be worn for the first time on race day; I developed blisters during a twenty-two kilometre test and had to walk the last three.

Week 16, Monday. The marathon is in six days, not sixteen, as my sister keeps joking. I have stopped worrying about finishing in under four hours. Dilnoza believes four hours and twenty minutes is a realistic goal, and she would rather I finish smiling than collapse at the finish line. Whatever happens, these months have changed me. I sleep better, I argue less with my brother, and I have discovered that I enjoy getting up at half past five, something I would have called impossible in spring. If I fail, at least I will fail healthy.
options: Never run more than eight kilometres extra
Never increase it by more than ten per cent

items.prompt: Why does Ismoilova say colour labels are needed?
items.answer: Shoppers rarely have time to read small print
items.passage:
A heated argument over food labels has divided the town of Namangan after the city council proposed that every packaged product sold in local supermarkets should carry a coloured warning if it contains high levels of sugar, salt or fat. The proposal, put forward by nutritionist Gulnora Ismoilova, was discussed at a public meeting on Thursday evening attended by more than two hundred residents, shop owners and food manufacturers. Ismoilova argued that most customers spend less than ten seconds choosing a product and therefore cannot be expected to read the tiny numbers on the back of the packet.

Supporters of the scheme pointed to research from Chile, where similar labels were introduced in 2016. According to figures quoted at the meeting, sales of sugary drinks there fell by almost a quarter within two years. Opponents were quick to remind the audience that Chile also banned cartoon characters on cereal boxes at the same time, so it is impossible to say which measure produced the change. Farid Karimov, who owns a family bakery, complained that a red label on his traditional honey cake would be unfair. 'My grandmother's recipe has been eaten at weddings for a century,' he said. 'Nobody is harmed by a slice at a celebration; the danger is a bottle of cola every day.'

Ismoilova replied that the labels would not forbid anything, they would merely inform. She also conceded that a simple colour code can be misleading: olive oil, for example, would be marked red because of its fat content, even though many doctors consider it healthy. To deal with this problem, she suggested that the council should add a short explanatory note for natural products, although she admitted that such exceptions would make the system more complicated. A supermarket manager, Behzod Aliyev, warned that printing new packaging would raise prices by roughly three per cent, a cost he said would eventually be paid by customers rather than producers.

At the end of the evening no vote was taken. The chairwoman announced that the council would first ask a university team to test the idea in two shops for three months, beginning in January. Observers noted, with some irony, that almost everyone left the hall agreeing on one point: the current labels are nearly impossible to understand. Whether colours will solve the problem remains to be seen, but the debate has at least made the town's shoppers look more carefully at what they eat.
options: Shoppers rarely have time to read small print
The council wants to ban sugar

Ismoilova argued that most customers spend less than ten seconds choosing a product and therefore cannot be expected to read the tiny numbers on the back of the packet.

Supporters of the scheme pointed to research from Chile, where similar labels were introduced in 2016. According to figures quoted at the meeting, sales of sugary drinks there fell by almost a quarter within two years. Opponents were quick to remind the audience that Chile also banned cartoon characters on cereal boxes at the same time, so it is impossible to say which measure produced the change. Farid Karimov, who owns a family bakery, complained that a red label on his traditional honey cake would be unfair. 'My grandmother's recipe has been eaten at weddings for a century,' he said. 'Nobody is harmed by a slice at a celebration; the danger is a bottle of cola every day.'

Ismoilova replied that the labels would not forbid anything, they would merely inform. She also conceded that a simple colour code can be misleading: olive oil, for example, would be marked red because of its fat content, even though many doctors consider it healthy. To deal with this problem, she suggested that the council should add a short explanatory note for natural products, although she admitted that such exceptions would make the system more complicated. A supermarket manager, Behzod Aliyev, warned that printing new packaging would raise prices by roughly three per cent, a cost he said would eventually be paid by customers rather than producers.

At the end of the evening no vote was taken. The chairwoman announced that the council would first ask a university team to test the idea in two shops for three months, beginning in January. Observers noted, with some irony, that almost everyone left the hall agreeing on one point: the current labels are nearly impossible to understand. Whether colours will solve the problem remains to be seen, but the debate has at least made the town's shoppers look more carefully at what they eat.
options: His honey cake contains no sugar
Labels would be too expensive for his bakery
Occasional celebration food is less harmful than a daily soft drink

items.prompt: What has the speaker noticed about people who suffer longest?
items.answer: They wait a long time before telling anyone
items.passage:
Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming on such a cold night. When I was asked to speak about mental health, I nearly refused, because I knew that most people expect a list of tips: breathe deeply, exercise, drink less coffee. Those suggestions are not wrong, but I want to begin with something less comfortable. Having worked as a counsellor for nineteen years, I have noticed that the people who suffer longest are rarely those with the most serious problems; they are those who wait the longest before telling anyone.

Let me explain why we wait. First, there is shame. In many families, including mine, a sadness that lasts more than a week is described as laziness or lack of gratitude. Second, there is the belief that a problem must be dramatic to deserve attention. I once met a young engineer who had not slept properly for months, yet he apologised for taking up my time because, as he put it, 'nothing terrible has happened to me.' Third, and perhaps most surprising, there is the fear that help will be useless. Research suggests, however, that about seventy per cent of people who attend regular counselling report improvement within four months, which is far higher than most patients expect.

I should add a warning. Some influencers now present every mood as a medical condition, and that is unhelpful too. Feeling nervous before an interview is not an anxiety disorder, and mourning a friend for a few weeks is not depression. The difference lies in duration, intensity and effect on daily life. If you cannot work, eat or enjoy anything you used to like for two weeks or longer, that is a signal worth taking seriously. If you simply had a bad Tuesday, be kind to yourself, call a friend and perhaps go for a walk.

What can ordinary people do for each other? Almost nothing requires training. Ask a direct question, such as 'Are you coping?', and then be quiet long enough to hear the answer. Do not rush to repair the problem, and never say 'cheer up', because it suggests that the person is choosing to be sad. Finally, remember that I am not saying therapy is the answer for everyone. I am saying that silence is rarely the answer for anyone. Thank you; I think we have time for three questions, though I would be happy to stay afterwards.
options: They have the most serious problems
They wait a long time before telling anyone
They refuse all advice about exercise

items.prompt: What does the first paragraph suggest about why grandfather waited three weeks?
items.answer: He tried to persuade himself the problem was minor
items.passage:
On Tuesday morning my grandfather, Rustam, finally agreed to see a doctor about the pain in his chest, after pretending for three weeks that it was only indigestion. We arrived at the regional hospital at a quarter past eight, expecting to be home by lunch. That turned out to be wildly optimistic. The reception hall was crowded with people holding folders, and the single clerk behind the desk explained that appointments were only for patients who had registered the previous day. Fortunately, a passing nurse, who recognised grandfather from his years as a schoolteacher, led us to the correct queue.

We waited nearly two hours on a hard bench. During that time I noticed how differently people behaved. A young mother calmly fed her baby; a man in a leather jacket kept shouting at the clerk, which achieved nothing except making everyone nervous; and an elderly woman shared her bread with strangers. When our turn finally came, the cardiologist, Dr Karimova, was brisk but kind. She asked grandfather far more questions than I expected, including what he ate for breakfast and whether he still climbed the hill behind his house every evening. He admitted that he had stopped after the winter, which she clearly considered important.

The tests took the rest of the day. First came a blood sample, then a heart recording, and finally an ultrasound at the other end of the building, where the lift was out of order and we had to climb four floors. Grandfather insisted on carrying his own coat, as if the walk proved he was healthy. By half past three, I was exhausted, although he looked strangely cheerful. Dr Karimova examined the results and said there was no sign of a heart attack. The pain, she believed, came from a combination of high blood pressure and years of salty food, both of which could be controlled with tablets and a change in diet.

I expected relief to be the main emotion, yet on the way out I felt irritated. Nothing in the hospital was truly unkind; it was simply disorganised, and I could not help wondering how many people give up and go home before they are seen. Grandfather, on the other hand, had no complaints. 'Three weeks of worrying,' he said, 'and the cure is less salt and a walk. I should have come in January.' He has promised to climb the hill again on Sunday, and I have promised to go with him, although I suspect I will be the slower one.
options: He tried to persuade himself the problem was minor
He could not find a doctor

items.prompt: What was the bet?
items.answer: If Timur went thirty days without meat, Nilufar would pay for dinner
items.passage:
Last January I made a bet with my cousin Nilufar: I would give up meat for thirty days, and if I succeeded she would pay for dinner at the best restaurant in Bukhara. I was confident, even smug. In Uzbekistan, after all, plov, kebab and manti are practically a national religion, and I had never skipped meat for more than two days. My friends found the idea hilarious, and my father, a butcher's son, asked whether I was feeling ill.

The first week was harder than expected, though not for the reason I imagined. I did not crave the taste of meat so much as the convenience. Most cafes near my office offered only a sad salad as a vegetarian choice, and I discovered that some soups I had always considered harmless were cooked in beef stock. By day six I was so hungry in the afternoons that I ate an entire bag of biscuits, which rather defeated the purpose of a healthy experiment, and my colleagues enjoyed pointing that out. My cousin, who is a trained dietitian, explained that I was not eating enough protein and recommended lentils, eggs, cheese and chickpeas.

Once I began cooking at home, things improved dramatically. By week three I had learned to make a lentil stew with dried apricots that even my sceptical father admitted was delicious. I also noticed that I felt lighter in the mornings, although I am cautious about claiming too much. items.prompt: How did Akmal's injury happen?
items.answer: He landed badly while chasing a pass, with no one touching him
items.passage:
Akmal Yusupov had waited all season for the semi-final. At nineteen, he was the youngest player in his club's first team, and the coach had finally promised him a starting place. In the thirty-fourth minute, while chasing a long pass, he landed awkwardly, heard a sharp crack in his right knee and fell without being touched by anyone. 'I knew instantly that something was seriously wrong,' he recalls, 'because the pain was not sharp, it was strangely hot.' The match continued without him, and his team lost by a single goal.

The scan the next morning showed a torn ligament, and the surgeon advised an operation within two weeks. Akmal's first reaction was to refuse. He had read online stories of footballers who never recovered their speed, and he feared he would lose his place permanently. His physiotherapist, Madina Rashidova, spent nearly an hour persuading him. She explained that, contrary to popular belief, an operation is not always the end of a career; the real danger is returning too soon. 'The surgery takes ninety minutes,' she told him. 'The rehabilitation takes nine months, and that is the part which decides everything.'

The first month was the worst. Akmal could not bend his leg, depended on crutches and, by his own admission, became bad-tempered with his family. Then Rashidova introduced a routine of small goals: bending the knee to ninety degrees, then walking without limping, then cycling for ten minutes. Each target was modest, but crossing them off a list gave him a feeling of progress that the endless waiting had denied him, and slowly his bad temper began to fade. He also began watching recordings of his own matches with the coach, which taught him more about positioning than three years of playing had done.

He returned to training after eight months, one month ahead of schedule, and Rashidova insisted that he wait four extra weeks before playing a full match. Looking back, Akmal admits she was right. 'If I had returned at once, I would have been injured again,' he says. Today he plays as a midfielder rather than a striker, a change he first resisted but now prefers. The injury, he insists, was not a disaster but an unwelcome teacher; still, he adds that he would not recommend the lesson to anyone.
options: He landed badly while chasing a pass, with no one touching him

'I knew instantly that something was seriously wrong,' he recalls, 'because the pain was not sharp, it was strangely hot.' The match continued without him, and his team lost by a single goal.

The scan the next morning showed a torn ligament, and the surgeon advised an operation within two weeks. Akmal's first reaction was to refuse. He had read online stories of footballers who never recovered their speed, and he feared he would lose his place permanently. His physiotherapist, Madina Rashidova, spent nearly an hour persuading him. She explained that, contrary to popular belief, an operation is not always the end of a career; the real danger is returning too soon. 'The surgery takes ninety minutes,' she told him. 'The rehabilitation takes nine months, and that is the part which decides everything.'

The first month was the worst. Akmal could not bend his leg, depended on crutches and, by his own admission, became bad-tempered with his family. Then Rashidova introduced a routine of small goals: bending the knee to ninety degrees, then walking without limping, then cycling for ten minutes. Each target was modest, but crossing them off a list gave him a feeling of progress that the endless waiting had denied him, and slowly his bad temper began to fade. He also began watching recordings of his own matches with the coach, which taught him more about positioning than three years of playing had done.

He returned to training after eight months, one month ahead of schedule, and Rashidova insisted that he wait four extra weeks before playing a full match. Looking back, Akmal admits she was right. 'If I had returned at once, I would have been injured again,' he says. Today he plays as a midfielder rather than a striker, a change he first resisted but now prefers. The injury, he insists, was not a disaster but an unwelcome teacher; still, he adds that he would not recommend the lesson to anyone.

As something he would recommend to others

items.prompt: Why did Otabek join PowerZone?
items.answer: The salesman was charming and the first month was almost free
items.passage:
In September I signed a twelve-month contract at a new gym called PowerZone, mainly because the salesman was charming and the first month cost almost nothing. He promised me a personal programme, free towels and 'cancellation whenever you like'. I paid forty dollars a month, which seemed reasonable for a place with a swimming pool. For the first three weeks I went four times a week, posted photos online and felt magnificent. By November, I was going once a week, and by January I had not entered the building for six weeks.

What changed? Partly it was the crowds. Between six and eight in the evening, the machines are occupied, and people queue with towels as if for a bus. Partly it was the weather, since the walk from my flat takes twenty minutes, and nobody enjoys it in the snow. But if I am honest, the main problem was motivation. I had bought the membership the way some people buy exercise books at the start of the school year: as a promise to a better version of myself, who, unfortunately, never turned up to use it.

When I finally decided to cancel in February, I discovered that the salesman's promise had been somewhat creative. The contract required written notice at least thirty days in advance, and a fee of eighty dollars if I left before the end of the year. At the reception, a polite girl apologised and said she could not change the rules. I wrote to the manager, who replied that I could freeze the membership for up to two months for free. That seemed pointless, since I had no desire to return, but a friend, a lawyer, advised me to be patient and keep every email.

In the end, the matter was solved without a fight. After my friend's letter mentioned the consumer protection law, the manager reduced the fee to forty dollars and cancelled the contract from the end of March. I lost money, but I also learned something. Now I run in the park behind my building, which costs nothing, and I never sign anything before reading the final page. The salesman, incidentally, has left PowerZone; I hope it was for reasons unrelated to me. Anyone considering a gym, I would say: try a month-to-month plan first, and be honest about what kind of person you really are.
options: It was close to his flat
The salesman was charming and the first month was almost free

items.prompt: What happens to the number of students seeking help during the exams?
items.passage:
Every June, the corridors of the National University in Tashkent change character. The cheerful noise of the spring term gives way to whispered conversations, pale faces and an unusual amount of energy drinks. Counsellor Shirin Abdullayeva, who has worked at the university's advice centre for eight years, says that the number of students seeking help roughly triples during the exam period. 'Most of them are not failing,' she observes. 'In fact, many of the most anxious students are the ones with the best marks, because they set impossibly high standards for themselves.'

Abdullayeva identifies three habits that make exam stress worse. The first is studying through the night. Although it feels heroic, memory consolidates during sleep, so a student who revises until four and sleeps for three hours often remembers less than someone who stops at midnight. The second habit is comparing oneself with others. Social media is full of classmates announcing that they have 'already finished the whole syllabus', and it is rarely true. The third, perhaps the most damaging, is catastrophic thinking: the conviction that one poor result will ruin one's entire future.

The centre offers a surprisingly simple programme. Students learn to divide their revision into forty-minute blocks separated by ten-minute breaks, and to write down worries on paper rather than carrying them in their heads. There are also group sessions in which students describe their fears aloud. One participant, Jahongir, a third-year economics student, says that hearing others admit they felt equally lost was the biggest relief. 'I thought I was the only one who understood nothing,' he laughs. 'It turned out the whole room was pretending.' He now studies in the library with a timer and, to his surprise, scored higher in his statistics exam than the previous year.

Not everyone is convinced. Professor Anvarov, who teaches law, argues that some pressure is both normal and useful, and that universities risk raising a generation unable to cope with ordinary difficulty. Abdullayeva agrees up to a point. 'A little tension sharpens attention,' she says. 'The problem begins when it prevents sleep, appetite or concentration.' Her advice to parents is equally direct: ask your children how they are, not what marks they expect. The first question helps; the second often adds to the weight they already carry.

items.prompt: Why is Sarvak cut off for part of the year?
items.passage:
For thirty-one years, Dr Kamola Sodiqova has been the only doctor in the mountain village of Sarvak, a place that disappears from the road for four months each winter when the snow closes the pass. Her clinic consists of two rooms, a refrigerator for vaccines and, as she likes to remind visitors, a bicycle that she has not ridden since 2010 because the paths have become too steep for her knees. Instead, she borrows a neighbour's donkey whenever a house call is needed, a creature she describes as 'more reliable than most ambulances and considerably more stubborn than most patients'.

Her working day rarely resembles a city doctor's. At seven she opens the clinic, where perhaps a dozen people are already waiting, some of whom have walked for two hours through mud or dust, depending on the season. By ten she has usually delivered advice rather than medicine, because half of her patients suffer from problems that tablets cannot cure: back pain from carrying water, coughs from smoky stoves, loneliness after children have moved to the capital. 'I have noticed that three of my patients out of ten want to talk more than they want treatment,' she says. 'Listening is part of the prescription.'

Equipment is the great difficulty. The village has electricity only from six to eleven in the evening, which limits what she can do with the small ultrasound machine donated by a charity. Seriously ill patients must travel ninety kilometres to the district hospital, a journey that takes three hours in summer and is sometimes impossible in January. Two years ago, a boy with appendicitis was saved only because a shepherd carried him down the mountain on his back. Since then, the villagers have collected money for a second-hand jeep, although they still need a driver willing to take the risk.

Younger doctors often ask Sodiqova why she never moved to a city. She answers without hesitation. 'In a city, I would be one doctor among two thousand. Here, I know every child's birthday and every grandfather's temper.' She admits that she is tired and has begun training a nurse, Zarnigor, to take over in the long term. But when asked whether she will retire soon, she shrugs. 'Perhaps when the road is repaired,' she says, 'which, as people here say, will happen the same year the donkey learns to read.'
options: The road is repaired each winter

items.prompt: Which drinks are taxed?
items.answer: Those with more than five grams of sugar per hundred millilitres
items.passage:
When the government announced a sugar tax in the spring of 2021, soft-drink companies predicted disaster, health campaigners predicted miracles, and most ordinary shoppers simply shrugged. Two years later, the results are more complicated than either side promised. The tax, which adds the equivalent of fifteen cents to every litre of drink containing more than five grams of sugar per hundred millilitres, has raised about forty million dollars. Officials had hoped that much of the money would be spent on school meals and sports facilities, and, to be fair, roughly two thirds of it has been.

The most visible change, however, has not been in what people buy but in what companies sell. Faced with the tax, several manufacturers reduced the sugar in their recipes to just below the limit, so that their products escaped the charge altogether. A popular orange drink now contains nearly a third less sugar than before, and most customers have not noticed. Public-health economist Dr Laylo Mirzaeva calls this 'the quiet victory', since it improves diets without asking anyone to change habits. She estimates that the average child now consumes about six teaspoons less sugar a week than in 2020.

Critics, however, remain unconvinced. The Consumers' Union argues that the tax is unfair because poorer families spend a larger share of their income on cheap fizzy drinks and therefore pay proportionally more. Some shopkeepers near the border report that customers drive across to buy cola abroad, while others say that people have simply turned to fruit juice, which is often just as sweet and is not taxed at all. Dr Mirzaeva admits that this loophole is a genuine weakness, but she notes that extending the tax to juice would be politically difficult, since parents consider juice a healthy product.

Whether obesity rates will fall is still unknown, since it takes years to see such changes. For now, the evidence suggests that the tax has been neither a failure nor a triumph: a modest success, perhaps, in a field where modest success is rare. What seems clear is that the strongest effect came not from punishing consumers but from pressuring producers. Dr Mirzaeva's own conclusion is cautious. 'Taxes alone cannot teach people to eat well,' she says. 'But they can persuade companies to stop making it so difficult.'
options: Those with more than five grams of sugar per hundred millilitres

items.prompt: Why did Halima start swimming?
items.answer: Her doctor warned her about her blood pressure and bones
items.passage:
At eighty-two, Halima Qodirova swims a kilometre every Tuesday and Friday at the municipal pool in Urgench, and she is irritated when people call her 'remarkable'. 'I am not remarkable,' she says, towelling her hair. 'I am merely stubborn.' She began swimming only seven years ago, after her doctor warned her that her blood pressure and bones were deteriorating. Until then, she had not entered the water since childhood, and she was so nervous on the first day that she held the pool's edge for ten minutes before letting go.

Geriatric specialist Dr Sanjar Ibragimov, who has studied older residents of the region for two decades, says that Halima is a good example, though not an unusual one. His research suggests that the strongest predictor of healthy ageing is not diet, wealth or even genes, but regular movement combined with social contact. 'We found that people who walk daily and have at least three close friends live, on average, four years longer than those who are physically active but isolated,' he explains. 'Loneliness appears to be as harmful as smoking, which surprises almost everyone.' He is quick to add that the findings show a link, not a proof of cause.

Halima's own routine confirms this. After her swim, she meets four friends in the pool cafe for tea, and the conversation, she admits, is more tiring than the exercise. They discuss grandchildren, politics and the shocking price of apricots. She eats simply, with plenty of vegetables and little red meat, but refuses to give up sweets entirely. 'A life without halva is not a life,' she declares. Dr Ibragimov does not object. He says that rigid rules often fail among older people, who tend to abandon any plan that makes them miserable.

There are, however, obstacles. Many older residents cannot afford pool tickets, and public transport in the evening is unreliable. The city offers discounts for pensioners on Tuesday mornings, but only a handful of people use them, partly because they do not know about the scheme. Halima has therefore taken matters into her own hands: she posts notices in the market and walks neighbours to the pool herself. 'Nobody should wait until eighty to discover they like water,' she says. 'I wasted seventy-five years, but I intend to enjoy the rest.'
options: Her doctor warned her about her blood pressure and bones
She had loved swimming as a child
