items.prompt: Why did the writer sign up for the course?
items.answer: His doctor had advised him to eat less oil
items.passage:
I signed up for the Wednesday cooking class at the community centre in Chilonzor mainly because my doctor had suggested that I eat less oil, and I assumed that a course called 'Light Kitchen' would be full of retired women exchanging recipes. I was half right. Of the twelve participants, nine were indeed women over fifty, but there were also two university students and a taxi driver named Sherzod, who confessed that he had eaten in cars for eleven years and wanted to stop. Our teacher, a former hotel chef named Ravshan Oripov, welcomed us in a spotless apron and immediately banned the phrase 'I can't cook'.

'Nobody is born able to cook,' he said, 'but everybody is born able to taste.' The first lesson, therefore, had nothing to do with recipes. He gave us five bowls of almost identical tomato soup and asked us to say what was missing from each. The answers were salt, acid, sweetness, fat and heat, though I confidently guessed only two. The point, he explained, was that most people add salt whenever a dish tastes flat, when a squeeze of lemon or a pinch of cumin would often fix the problem without the health risks. I wrote this in my notebook and underlined it twice.

Over the following weeks we cooked a surprising range of dishes: baked fish with herbs, a carrot and chickpea stew, and a version of plov made with brown rice and only half the usual oil. The plov caused the loudest debate. Two of the older women declared it an insult to tradition, while Sherzod, who had been sceptical, asked for a second plate. Oripov refused to take sides. 'My job is not to defend plov or attack it,' he said, 'but to show you that you have choices.' By the fourth week, even the doubters had agreed that the dish, though different, was not bad at all.

On the final evening each of us cooked a three-course dinner for the others, and I made the mistake of choosing a dessert that required exact timing. It collapsed, naturally. Nobody minded; we ate it with spoons and called it a pudding. What I value most from the course is not any single recipe, but a change in attitude. I now read labels, taste before I season and, most importantly, enjoy standing in the kitchen. My doctor says my cholesterol has dropped slightly, although I suspect the greater improvement is in my mood. Sherzod, I should add, now brings his lunch to work.
options: He wanted to meet retired women
His doctor had advised him to eat less oil
He hoped to become a hotel chef

items.prompt: What did the survey show about children aged eight to eleven?
items.answer: They spend three and a half hours a day on screens, an hour more than before
items.passage:
At the parents' evening of School Number Twelve in Andijan, the usual complaints about homework and canteen food were set aside for a more urgent subject: children and screens. The head teacher, Mavjuda Nazarova, opened the meeting with a survey of her pupils' habits. Among children aged eight to eleven, the average daily screen time outside lessons had reached three and a half hours, which was an hour more than two years earlier. 'I am not here to blame anybody,' she said. 'I am here because teachers can see the effect every morning, in tired eyes and short tempers.'

The guest speaker, paediatrician Dr Otabek Raximov, tried to calm the room. He explained that research does not show screens to be uniformly harmful. A child who spends an hour video-calling a grandmother abroad or building a game with a friend is in a different situation from one who scrolls silently through short videos until midnight. 'The question is not only how long, but what and when,' he said. The strongest evidence, in his view, concerns sleep: children who use devices in the hour before bed take longer to fall asleep and wake up more often. He recommended a simple rule: no screens in bedrooms after eight.

Several parents objected. Dildora, a nurse who works night shifts, said that such rules are easy for people with regular jobs, whereas she depends on tablets to keep her son occupied while she sleeps in the daytime. Another father argued that banning devices would make his children look strange among classmates, who all use messaging groups for homework. Dr Raximov listened patiently and conceded that perfect solutions do not exist. He suggested that families should aim for 'good enough': one screen-free meal a day, outdoor play at weekends and, above all, adults who put their own phones down. 'Children copy what we do, not what we say,' he remarked, 'and at this moment half the audience is checking messages.' There was laughter, followed by several embarrassed hands retreating into pockets.

The meeting ended with a modest decision rather than a dramatic ban. The school will hold a screen-free reading hour each Thursday afternoon, and a working group of five parents will meet monthly to suggest further ideas. Nazarova admitted that the plan was small, but she hoped it would start a conversation inside homes as well as inside the school. 'If children see that we take the question seriously,' she said, 'they are more likely to take it seriously too.'
options: They spend three and a half hours a day on screens, an hour more than before
They spend an hour a day on screens, half as much as before
They spend three and a half hours on homework

The head teacher, Mavjuda Nazarova, opened the meeting with a survey of her pupils' habits. Among children aged eight to eleven, the average daily screen time outside lessons had reached three and a half hours, which was an hour more than two years earlier. 'I am not here to blame anybody,' she said. 'I am here because teachers can see the effect every morning, in tired eyes and short tempers.'

The guest speaker, paediatrician Dr Otabek Raximov, tried to calm the room. He explained that research does not show screens to be uniformly harmful. A child who spends an hour video-calling a grandmother abroad or building a game with a friend is in a different situation from one who scrolls silently through short videos until midnight. 'The question is not only how long, but what and when,' he said. The strongest evidence, in his view, concerns sleep: children who use devices in the hour before bed take longer to fall asleep and wake up more often. He recommended a simple rule: no screens in bedrooms after eight.

Several parents objected. Dildora, a nurse who works night shifts, said that such rules are easy for people with regular jobs, whereas she depends on tablets to keep her son occupied while she sleeps in the daytime. Another father argued that banning devices would make his children look strange among classmates, who all use messaging groups for homework. Dr Raximov listened patiently and conceded that perfect solutions do not exist. He suggested that families should aim for 'good enough': one screen-free meal a day, outdoor play at weekends and, above all, adults who put their own phones down. 'Children copy what we do, not what we say,' he remarked, 'and at this moment half the audience is checking messages.' There was laughter, followed by several embarrassed hands retreating into pockets.

The meeting ended with a modest decision rather than a dramatic ban. The school will hold a screen-free reading hour each Thursday afternoon, and a working group of five parents will meet monthly to suggest further ideas. Nazarova admitted that the plan was small, but she hoped it would start a conversation inside homes as well as inside the school. 'If children see that we take the question seriously,' she said, 'they are more likely to take it seriously too.'

items.prompt: What does Ulugbek call the 'real enemy'?
items.passage:
My company sent all of its employees on a compulsory first-aid course last month, and I attended with the reluctance of a man who expects an afternoon of slides. I could not have been more wrong. The instructor, a paramedic named Ulugbek who looked far too young to have seen so much, began by asking us to describe the worst emergency we had ever witnessed. The stories were sobering. One colleague had watched a stranger collapse in a bus queue while everyone stood still, each waiting for somebody else to act. 'That,' said Ulugbek, 'is the real enemy: not ignorance, but hesitation.'

He then taught us in the order that mattered. First, check that the scene is safe, because a second casualty helps no one. Second, call the emergency number, and preferably send another person to do so while you start helping. Third, begin the actual treatment. For an adult who is not breathing, this means pressing hard in the centre of the chest about one hundred times a minute, which is close to the rhythm of a well-known pop song. We practised on plastic dummies for forty minutes, and my arms were trembling by the end. Ulugbek warned that real chest compressions often break ribs, and that this is acceptable. 'A broken rib heals,' he said. 'A stopped heart does not.'

The second half of the course dealt with more ordinary accidents, and here our beliefs were corrected repeatedly. Burns should be cooled with running water for at least twenty minutes, not covered in butter or toothpaste, as several of us had learned from our grandmothers. Nosebleeds are treated by leaning forward, not backward, so that the blood does not run down the throat. And a person who is choking but can still cough should be encouraged to keep coughing; hitting their back is only for the case when they cannot make any sound at all. I was astonished how many of my confident assumptions were wrong.

At the end, each of us received a certificate valid for three years, though Ulugbek told us frankly that the paper matters less than the confidence. He urged us to repeat the practice every six months, because skills fade faster than people expect. I left tired but oddly cheerful. On the way home, I caught myself looking around the metro carriage, wondering who would act first if somebody fell. I decided, uncomfortably, that it might have to be me. Our manager has already announced that next year the course will be offered to our families, which I think is the best decision the company has made in a decade.

topic: A driverless shuttle trial, A coding bootcamp, A lab accident that led to a discovery, ...
title: O'qish 11
intro: Har bir matnni diqqat bilan o'qing va uning savollariga javob bering.

items.prompt: How autonomous was the shuttle during the trial?
items.answer: A safety operator could take control, but rarely did
items.passage:
When the city council of Samarkand announced that a driverless shuttle would carry passengers along a two-kilometre route near the Registan, most residents reacted with curiosity rather than alarm. The trial, which began on the fourteenth of March and was scheduled to last ninety days, was organised by an engineering firm led by Dilnoza Rakhimova, who had spent eleven years working on navigation software before moving back to Uzbekistan. Contrary to what many people assumed, the shuttle was not completely autonomous: a trained safety operator sat in the front seat and could take control with a single button, although in practice she touched the wheel only four times during the first month.

The vehicle was equipped with six cameras, three radar sensors and a roof-mounted laser scanner that measured distances to objects up to two hundred metres away. Rakhimova explained that no single sensor was reliable enough on its own. Cameras struggle in strong sunlight, radar cannot read road signs, and lasers are confused by heavy rain. items.prompt: How long had Zarina worked at the pharmacy?
items.passage:
Zarina Yusupova had worked as a pharmacy assistant in Namangan for six years when she decided, at the age of twenty-nine, to attend a coding bootcamp in Tashkent. The programme lasted twenty-six weeks, cost the equivalent of four thousand dollars, and promised that graduates would be ready for junior developer positions. Her friends were sceptical. Her cousin Jasur, who had studied computer science at university for four years, told her that bootcamps were only a clever way of selling hope to people in a hurry. Zarina listened politely, but she had already made up her mind.

The first month was harder than she had expected. Classes started at nine in the morning and finished at six, but the real work began in the evening, when students were supposed to complete exercises that often took until midnight. Of the thirty-two people who began the course, five dropped out before the end of the second week. Zarina nearly joined them. She later admitted that she cried twice in the first fortnight, not because the material was impossible, but because everybody around her seemed to understand it faster. Her instructor, a patient man named Timur, noticed her frustration and advised her to stop comparing herself with others. 'Programming is not a race,' he told the group. 'Nobody remembers who finished the exercise first, but everybody remembers who gave up.'

Gradually, things improved. By the tenth week Zarina could build a simple website, and by the twentieth she was working in a team of four on a booking application for a local dentist. This project taught her something that no textbook could: that most of a programmer's time is spent not writing new code but reading and fixing code written by other people. She also discovered that she was much better at testing software than her classmates, because years in the pharmacy had trained her to check details carefully.

Graduation took place in early June, and the results were mixed. Eighteen of the twenty-seven graduates found jobs within three months, but Zarina was not among the first. She sent out forty applications and received only six replies, mostly because employers wanted at least a year of experience. In the end it was her dentist project that changed everything. The dentist recommended her to his brother, who ran a small logistics company, and she was hired as a junior tester in September on a salary lower than she had earned at the pharmacy.

Looking back, Zarina has a balanced view. She does not believe that a bootcamp is a shortcut, and she would not recommend one to anyone unwilling to sacrifice evenings and weekends. Still, she considers it the best decision of her adult life. 'My cousin was partly right,' she says with a smile. 'Nobody sold me hope. They sold me a chance, and I had to do the rest myself.'

items.prompt: Why did Solheim leave the beaker on the hotplate?
items.answer: She was distracted by a phone call from her daughter's school
items.passage:
On a rainy Thursday in November 2014, Dr. Ingrid Solheim, a materials scientist at a small university laboratory in Bergen, made a mistake that she now describes as the most useful of her career. She was testing a new type of plastic film designed to protect fruit during transport, and she needed to heat a mixture of seaweed extract and a resin to exactly eighty degrees. Distracted by a phone call from her daughter's school, she forgot the beaker on the hotplate and left the building. When she returned, almost two hours later, the temperature had reached one hundred and forty degrees, and the mixture had turned into a dark, rubbery sheet that stuck to the glass.

Most researchers would have thrown it away. Solheim, however, noticed that the sheet had an unusual property: when she pulled it apart, it slowly joined together again, as if it were healing. Her assistant, a cautious young man named Eskil, suggested that the effect was probably caused by moisture in the air and would disappear by the next morning. It did not. Over the following weeks the team cut the material into pieces, left them under different conditions, and measured how quickly the cuts closed. At room temperature the repair took six hours, but when the material was warmed to forty degrees it took less than twenty minutes.

The discovery would have been of little interest, Solheim says, if the sheet had been weak. In fact, it was surprisingly strong, and it was made almost entirely from waste seaweed, which coastal factories normally pay to dispose of. Within a year the group had published a paper, and within two a company that makes protective cases for mobile phones had asked to buy a licence. Not everyone was enthusiastic. A senior colleague warned that the public might wrongly conclude that accidents are a reliable method of research, and that young scientists would stop being careful. Solheim partly agrees. 'Luck only helps people who are paying attention afterwards,' she says. 'Had Eskil and I ignored that sheet, the accident would have been just an expensive stain.'

The laboratory has since changed its safety rules, not because of the accident itself but because Solheim left a hotplate unattended. Every heating device now has an automatic timer that switches it off after ninety minutes. Ironically, she admits, the timer would have prevented the discovery. She has framed a photograph of the original dark sheet and hung it above her desk, next to a handwritten note that reads, in Norwegian, 'Look twice at what you wanted to throw away.' Her next project, she says, will be a version of the material that can be recycled completely, a goal that her department expects to take at least three more years.
options: She was distracted by a phone call from her daughter's school
A fire alarm forced her to leave
She was called to a meeting with a colleague

items.prompt: According to Karimova, why do people lose track of time on apps?
items.answer: Systems are designed to maximise the time users spend
items.passage:
Every evening, millions of people open an app 'just to check one thing' and look up forty minutes later, wondering where the time has gone. This is not an accident, nor is it a sign of weak character. According to Nodira Karimova, a data analyst who spent five years working for a social media company before resigning in 2021, it is the predictable result of systems designed to maximise one number: the time users spend on the platform.

The algorithms that decide what appears in your feed do not understand quality, truth or kindness. They understand behaviour. If you pause for three seconds on a video about cats, you will see more videos about cats; if you argue in the comments under a political post, you will see more political posts, usually the angriest ones, because anger keeps people engaged longer than agreement does. Karimova points out that companies rarely lie about this. What they avoid saying is that the system is not neutral, and that it quietly shapes opinions by deciding which voices are heard and which disappear.

Defenders of the platforms offer a different view. They argue that algorithms simply give people what they ask for, and that blaming a recommendation system for human curiosity is like blaming a library for the books it lends. There is some force in this argument, Karimova concedes, but it ignores a crucial difference: a librarian does not follow you home, rearrange the shelves every time you look away, and send notifications at midnight. Moreover, a library does not earn money from the number of hours you remain inside it.

The consequences are most serious for teenagers. A study of nine hundred students in four Uzbek regions found that those who spent more than three hours daily on short-video apps were twice as likely to report difficulty concentrating in class. The researchers were careful, however, to avoid claiming that the apps caused the problem; it is equally possible that students who already struggle with concentration are drawn to such content. Karimova considers this honesty typical of good science, and she regrets that headlines rarely show the same caution.

So what can be done? She does not recommend deleting every account, which she considers unrealistic. Instead, she suggests three habits: turning off notifications, choosing manually whom to follow rather than relying on suggestions, and setting a fixed time limit on the phone itself instead of trusting willpower. She also supports legislation that would force companies to offer a chronological feed as the default option. 'People should be able to choose,' she says, 'but at the moment the choice is made for them, and they do not even notice.' Whether governments will act soon remains uncertain, since regulators are often several years behind the technology they are trying to control.
options: Systems are designed to maximise the time users spend

items.prompt: Anger keeps people ___ longer than agreement does.
items.passage:
Every evening, millions of people open an app 'just to check one thing' and look up forty minutes later, wondering where the time has gone. This is not an accident, nor is it a sign of weak character. According to Nodira Karimova, a data analyst who spent five years working for a social media company before resigning in 2021, it is the predictable result of systems designed to maximise one number: the time users spend on the platform.

The algorithms that decide what appears in your feed do not understand quality, truth or kindness. They understand behaviour. If you pause for three seconds on a video about cats, you will see more videos about cats; if you argue in the comments under a political post, you will see more political posts, usually the angriest ones, because anger keeps people engaged longer than agreement does. Karimova points out that companies rarely lie about this. What they avoid saying is that the system is not neutral, and that it quietly shapes opinions by deciding which voices are heard and which disappear.

Defenders of the platforms offer a different view. They argue that algorithms simply give people what they ask for, and that blaming a recommendation system for human curiosity is like blaming a library for the books it lends. There is some force in this argument, Karimova concedes, but it ignores a crucial difference: a librarian does not follow you home, rearrange the shelves every time you look away, and send notifications at midnight. Moreover, a library does not earn money from the number of hours you remain inside it.

The consequences are most serious for teenagers. A study of nine hundred students in four Uzbek regions found that those who spent more than three hours daily on short-video apps were twice as likely to report difficulty concentrating in class. The researchers were careful, however, to avoid claiming that the apps caused the problem; it is equally possible that students who already struggle with concentration are drawn to such content. Karimova considers this honesty typical of good science, and she regrets that headlines rarely show the same caution.

So what can be done? She does not recommend deleting every account, which she considers unrealistic. Instead, she suggests three habits: turning off notifications, choosing manually whom to follow rather than relying on suggestions, and setting a fixed time limit on the phone itself instead of trusting willpower. She also supports legislation that would force companies to offer a chronological feed as the default option. 'People should be able to choose,' she says, 'but at the moment the choice is made for them, and they do not even notice.' Whether governments will act soon remains uncertain, since regulators are often several years behind the technology they are trying to control.

items.prompt: How long did the telescope take to reach its final position?
items.passage:
When the Meridian Space Telescope was launched in a rocket from French Guiana on the ninth of December, its designers held their breath for twenty-nine days. That was how long it took for the instrument to travel one and a half million kilometres to its final position, a point in space where the gravity of the Sun and Earth together keeps it in a stable place. Once there, it had to unfold a mirror made of eighteen separate hexagonal segments, a procedure that involved three hundred and forty points of potential failure. Engineers often joke that the mission's real name should have been 'Nothing Goes Wrong'.

Nothing did go wrong, but the telescope was not an instant success in the public imagination. Its first image, released in July, showed a tiny patch of sky no larger than a grain of sand held at arm's length, and many viewers expected something more dramatic. Dr. Aigerim Beisenova, an astrophysicist from Almaty who has worked on the project since 2012, understands that disappointment. 'People imagine planets and glowing clouds,' she says, 'but this picture contains thousands of galaxies, some of them more than twelve billion years old. The light we see left them long before the Earth existed.'

The telescope observes in infrared light, which means that it can see through dust clouds that block ordinary telescopes, but it also means that it must be kept extremely cold. A sunshield the size of a tennis court protects the instruments, keeping them below minus two hundred and twenty degrees. If the shield were damaged, the telescope's own heat would overwhelm the faint signals it is trying to detect.

The cost of the project has been a source of controversy. The original budget was one billion dollars and the planned launch date was 2007, but delays and redesigns pushed the final cost to almost ten billion and the launch fourteen years later than planned. Critics argue that the money could have funded dozens of smaller missions, which would have produced more varied results. Supporters respond that no smaller instrument could have detected the faintest galaxies, and that the technology developed along the way, such as new methods for polishing mirrors, has already been adopted by hospitals and manufacturers.

The most exciting work, according to Beisenova, concerns the atmospheres of distant planets. By studying starlight as it passes through a planet's air, scientists can identify gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide. Within the first year, the team detected clouds on a planet nearly two hundred light years away. This does not mean that life has been found, and Beisenova is quick to correct journalists who suggest it. 'Finding water is exciting, but it is only one ingredient,' she says. 'We would need several signs at once before anyone could responsibly claim a discovery.'

The telescope has enough fuel to operate for about twenty years, though its mirrors will probably remain useful much longer. Beisenova hopes that by then a successor will exist, and she tells her students that the person who designs it may be sitting in their classroom today.

items.prompt: Who did the caller claim to be from?
items.passage:
Last month my grandmother, Gulchehra, who is seventy-three and has never owned anything more complicated than a basic mobile phone, received a call from a stranger who knew her full name, her address and the name of her local clinic. The caller claimed to be from the health ministry and offered a free check-up if she would confirm her passport number. Fortunately, she hung up and rang my father. I tell this story not because it is unusual but because it is typical: the information used against her was not stolen in a dramatic hack, but gathered from dozens of small, legal sources.

Most of us believe that privacy means keeping secrets, and since we have 'nothing to hide', we shrug our shoulders when apps ask for permission to access our contacts, location or microphone. This is a misunderstanding. Privacy is not about hiding wrongdoing; it is about controlling who knows what about you, and for what purpose. You do not mind your doctor knowing your medical history, but you would certainly mind your employer or your insurance company knowing it.

The problem is that data rarely stays where it was collected. A free fitness app records your daily route, and sells the anonymised data to an advertising broker. The broker combines it with shopping records from a loyalty card and a map of your neighbourhood. 'Anonymised' sounds reassuring, yet researchers have shown that four locations visited at known times are enough to identify ninety-five percent of individuals in a large dataset. In other words, removing a name protects far less than companies imply.

Some experts insist that the solution lies in stronger legislation, and several countries have already introduced rules requiring companies to delete personal data upon request and to explain, in plain language, what they collect. Others are less optimistic. They point out that fines are often smaller than the profits made from the violation, so that breaking the law becomes simply a cost of doing business. My own view is that laws are necessary but insufficient; individuals must also learn to protect themselves.

Here are the habits I now teach my family. First, read the permission list before installing an app, and refuse anything that has no obvious connection to the app's purpose: a torch does not need your contacts. Second, use a different password for every important account, and keep them in a password manager rather than a notebook. Third, never confirm personal details to someone who has called you; instead, end the conversation and phone the organisation yourself using the number on its official website. My grandmother has now written that last rule on a card beside her telephone, and, she says, she is rather proud of it. Not every threat can be avoided, but most can be made much harder to carry out.

items.prompt: How long did it take Rustam to connect everything?
items.passage:
When Rustam Hasanov, a thirty-eight-year-old accountant in Bukhara, bought a smart home package for his new flat, he imagined that his life would become effortlessly comfortable. The kit, which cost about six hundred dollars, included a thermostat, four light bulbs, a door lock, two cameras and a voice assistant that sat on the kitchen shelf like a small black bowl. The salesman had promised that everything would be connected within an hour. In reality, it took Rustam an entire Saturday, three phone calls to customer support and one argument with his wife, Shahlo, who suspected that he cared more about the gadgets than about the weekend they had planned.

The first weeks were delightful. The lights turned on as he walked into the corridor, the heating lowered itself when the flat was empty, and the thermostat learned, after ten days, that the family liked the bedroom cooler at night. Their electricity bill fell by roughly eleven percent in the first quarter. Rustam could also check the cameras from his office, and he admits that he did so more often than necessary.

Problems began in the second month. One evening the internet connection failed, and the door lock, which depended on it, refused to open for Shahlo, who stood outside with two heavy bags and a crying toddler. Rustam, stuck in traffic across the city, could do nothing except advise her to knock on a neighbour's door. 'A machine that is supposed to simplify life must never become a reason for locking your own family out,' he says. The next day he bought a traditional key and installed it beside the electronic one.

There were more subtle issues too. The voice assistant sometimes started to answer when nobody had spoken to it, and Shahlo noticed that advertisements for baby clothes appeared on her phone shortly after she had mentioned the subject in the kitchen. Whether the device was actually listening to conversations or whether it was merely coincidence, nobody could say with certainty, but the feeling was uncomfortable enough that she asked Rustam to disconnect its microphone when guests visited.

Today the family uses about half of the original equipment. The thermostat and the bulbs remain, because they provide clear savings, whereas the cameras were moved to the front door only and the voice assistant is used mainly as a kitchen timer. Rustam does not regret the purchase, but he would give different advice to friends. 'Start with one device that solves a real problem,' he says. 'Buy others only after you have lived with the first one for a few months. And always keep a key in your pocket.'

items.prompt: How does Alimov describe vaccine development?
items.answer: A series of locked doors opened only by evidence
items.passage:
Many people believe that developing a vaccine is simply a matter of money and urgency, but Dr. Sardor Alimov, who leads a research team at a university institute in Tashkent, says the process is better described as a series of locked doors, each of which can be opened only by evidence. His group has spent nine years working on a vaccine against a bacterial infection that mainly affects children in rural areas, and they are still two doors away from the end.

The first stage, which lasted almost three years, took place entirely in the laboratory. Researchers identified a protein on the surface of the bacterium that the human immune system could recognise, and they tested dozens of ways of delivering it. Most failed. 'Failure is the normal state of the beginning,' Alimov says. 'If everything works at once, we suspect an error.' The second stage involved animals, and it is the part of the work that the team finds most uncomfortable, although the law requires it before any person can receive an experimental dose. Only after two independent committees approved the results was permission granted for human trials.

Human trials proceed in three phases. In the first, a small group of about forty volunteers receives the vaccine so that doctors can check safety and find a suitable dose. The second phase includes several hundred people and measures how strongly the body responds. The third and longest phase, involving thousands of participants, compares those who received the vaccine with those who received a harmless placebo, and it shows whether the vaccine really prevents illness. Neither the volunteers nor the doctors know who has received which, a method called a double-blind trial, designed to prevent hope from influencing the result.

Alimov's team is currently in the second phase, and the delays have been frustrating. In 2023 a batch of the vaccine had to be destroyed because the refrigerator at one clinic broke down overnight, and the team lost eight months repeating production. Some parents have written angry letters demanding faster progress, while others worry that rapid approval would mean cut corners. Alimov sympathises with both groups. He does not believe that safety should be sacrificed for speed, yet he accepts that every month of delay has a human cost.

When asked how he stays motivated, he mentions a village in the Surkhandarya region where he met a mother who had lost two children to the disease. 'She did not ask me for a miracle,' he recalls. 'She asked me to be honest about how long it would take. So I tell everybody the same thing: the vaccine will be ready when the evidence says it is ready, not one day sooner.'
options: A simple matter of money and urgency
A series of locked doors opened only by evidence

items.prompt: Why did Omarov install the robot?
items.answer: To deal with long queues on busy mornings
items.passage:
In the centre of Almaty, on the ground floor of an old office building, there is a café where the barista never says good morning, never takes a day off and never spills a drop. The barista is an industrial robot arm named Zhanna, installed in September by a young entrepreneur, Daniyar Omarov, after he spent a year watching how his own café, staffed by humans, wasted time and money. 'I did not build it to be fashionable,' he insists. 'I built it because on busy mornings I had a queue of forty people and only three workers on shift.'

Zhanna makes a cup of coffee in about forty seconds, which is slightly slower than a trained human, but she can do it two hundred times a day without any variation in quality. Customers order on a screen, pay by card, and watch through a glass wall as the arm selects a cup, grinds the beans, steams the milk and slides the drink onto a counter. Many take a photograph before drinking. The café attracted so much attention on social media in its first fortnight that sales rose by sixty percent, although Omarov admits that much of this was curiosity rather than loyalty. 'Novelty brings people once,' he says. 'Only good coffee brings them back.'

The robot has not replaced the staff, contrary to the fears of local residents. Omarov employs five people, the same number as before, but their work has changed. Instead of making drinks, they greet customers, clean tables, prepare sandwiches and help elderly visitors who find the screen confusing. One of them, Madina, a student who works weekends, says she was initially afraid of losing her job. 'Now I enjoy it more,' she says, 'because I talk to people instead of repeating the same movements all day. But I do not think every manager would be as generous as Daniyar.'

Her scepticism is shared by economists. Professor Kairat Seitov of the local university warns that a café with a robot is, in the short term, an expensive experiment: the machine cost the equivalent of forty-five thousand dollars and will need about three years to repay itself. Large chains, however, could save much more by installing hundreds of machines, and in that case employees might not be as fortunate as Omarov's. 'The technology itself is neither good nor bad,' Seitov says. 'The consequences depend on the decisions of owners, and on what governments require them to do for the workers they replace.'

Not everything works perfectly. During a power cut in November, Zhanna froze with a full cup of hot milk in her gripper, and the staff had to wait twenty minutes before they could safely remove it. A customer also discovered that the robot cannot draw patterns in the milk foam, something that most human baristas learn in their first month. Omarov is working with the manufacturer to correct this, and he hopes that by next spring his robot will produce a heart or a flower on request, although he knows that some customers will always prefer a smile to a pattern.
options: To deal with long queues on busy mornings
Because his workers asked for it

items.prompt: Why was so much of the family's fruit lost?
items.answer: Drying on rooftops depended on the weather and attracted flies
items.passage:
Abdulla Nazarov was born in 1921 in a village near Kokand, the fifth of nine children in a family of apricot growers. As a boy he noticed something that most adults overlooked: nearly a third of the fruit his family harvested rotted before it could be sold, because the traditional method of drying it on rooftops depended on the weather and attracted flies. He left school at fourteen to work in a repair workshop, but he continued to read whatever technical books he could borrow, including, to his surprise, an old textbook on physics that a teacher had thrown away.

His first invention, built in 1948 when he was twenty-seven, was a wooden box with a sloping glass lid and a black metal tray inside. Fruit placed on the tray dried in four days instead of eight, and, because the box was closed, insects could not reach it. Nazarov did not patent the design. He made forty copies by hand and gave most of them to neighbours, believing that an idea kept secret was a wasted idea. Some historians regard this generosity as admirable; others consider it naive, since a company in another country later sold a nearly identical dryer for profit and never mentioned him.

The turning point of his career came in 1957, when a visiting agricultural inspector, Valentina Orlova, saw the dryers in use and wrote a report recommending that the ministry support their production. Nazarov was invited to Tashkent, where he spent three years improving the design with a team of engineers. The new version could dry ten times as much fruit, and it included a small fan powered by a solar panel, a feature he had suggested but initially been told was impractical. Within a decade, more than eight thousand dryers were in use across Central Asia, and the proportion of fruit lost after harvest in some regions dropped from thirty percent to under ten.

Nazarov never became wealthy, and he seemed to care little about that. He lived in the same modest house for fifty years, and when he was offered a post as director of a research institute, he refused, explaining that he would be happier in a workshop than behind a desk. His students, however, remember that he was far from sentimental about his work. He insisted that every device be tested for at least a year before it was recommended to anyone, and he once destroyed a prototype in front of them because it broke twice during trials.

He died in 1996, aged seventy-five. Today a small museum in Kokand displays his first wooden box, which still works, and a quotation attributed to him is painted above the entrance: 'A good invention is one that a poor man can build and a rich man cannot improve.'
options: It was stolen before the harvest
Drying on rooftops depended on the weather and attracted flies
It was sold too late in the year

items.prompt: What did the message on the screen demand?
items.answer: Two thousand dollars within seventy-two hours
items.passage:
On a Monday morning in February, Gulnora Abdullaeva, the office manager of a small furniture company in Andijan, switched on her computer and found that every file on it had been renamed with a strange extension. A message on the screen demanded payment of two thousand dollars in cryptocurrency within seventy-two hours, otherwise, it threatened, all the company's data would be deleted. Within minutes, the same message appeared on seven other machines. The company, which employed twenty-three people and had been in business for fourteen years, had become the victim of ransomware.

How the criminals got in is a lesson in how ordinary cyberattacks are. Nobody had cracked a clever code. Three weeks earlier, an accountant had received an email that appeared to come from the company's bank, asking him to confirm his login details through a link. The email contained no spelling mistakes and used the bank's real logo. He clicked, typed his password, and thought no more about it. The attackers then waited quietly, exploring the network, until they found the backup drive, which, by an unfortunate decision, was permanently connected to the main server. They encrypted the backups first, and the live files afterwards.

The owner, Botir, faced a dilemma. Paying would probably bring the data back, but there was no guarantee, and it would encourage the criminals to attack again. Not paying meant, in the worst case, the loss of fourteen years of orders, designs and customer records. He consulted a security specialist, Sevara Ismoilova, who advised against paying and offered to try to recover older copies stored by the company's email provider. After four exhausting days, she recovered about eighty percent of the data. The remainder, mostly recent invoices, had to be reconstructed from paper records and customers' own copies.

The financial damage was considerable, though not what the criminals had demanded: lost production, specialist fees and legal advice cost the company roughly six times the ransom. What disturbed Botir most, however, was how cheaply the disaster could have been prevented. A thirty-minute training session on suspicious emails, two-step verification on important accounts, and a backup disconnected from the network would have cost a fraction of that sum.

Ismoilova believes that small businesses are especially vulnerable because owners assume that criminals only target large banks or governments. 'Attackers are practical,' she says. 'They do not choose the richest victim; they choose the easiest one.' The furniture company now conducts a phishing test every quarter, and the accountant who clicked the link, far from being dismissed, has become the staff member responsible for explaining the incident to new employees.
options: Two thousand dollars within twenty-seven hours

items.passage:
On a Monday morning in February, Gulnora Abdullaeva, the office manager of a small furniture company in Andijan, switched on her computer and found that every file on it had been renamed with a strange extension. A message on the screen demanded payment of two thousand dollars in cryptocurrency within seventy-two hours, otherwise, it threatened, all the company's data would be deleted. Within minutes, the same message appeared on seven other machines. The company, which employed twenty-three people and had been in business for fourteen years, had become the victim of ransomware.

How the criminals got in is a lesson in how ordinary cyberattacks are. Nobody had cracked a clever code. Three weeks earlier, an accountant had received an email that appeared to come from the company's bank, asking him to confirm his login details through a link. The email contained no spelling mistakes and used the bank's real logo. He clicked, typed his password, and thought no more about it. The attackers then waited quietly, exploring the network, until they found the backup drive, which, by an unfortunate decision, was permanently connected to the main server. They encrypted the backups first, and the live files afterwards.

The owner, Botir, faced a dilemma. Paying would probably bring the data back, but there was no guarantee, and it would encourage the criminals to attack again. Not paying meant, in the worst case, the loss of fourteen years of orders, designs and customer records. He consulted a security specialist, Sevara Ismoilova, who advised against paying and offered to try to recover older copies stored by the company's email provider. After four exhausting days, she recovered about eighty percent of the data. The remainder, mostly recent invoices, had to be reconstructed from paper records and customers' own copies.

The financial damage was considerable, though not what the criminals had demanded: lost production, specialist fees and legal advice cost the company roughly six times the ransom. A thirty-minute training session on suspicious emails, two-step verification on important accounts, and a backup disconnected from the network would have cost a fraction of that sum.

items.prompt: What hidden assumption does the writer mention?
items.answer: That storage must be lithium batteries
items.passage:
For more than a decade, advocates of renewable energy have repeated a simple argument: the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, so without large-scale storage, green electricity will never replace fossil fuels. It is a persuasive claim, but it contains a hidden assumption, namely that the storage must be the lithium batteries found in phones and electric cars. A research team in Navoi, led by Dr. Sanobar Mirzaeva, has been testing a different approach for the past six years, and the first results are more encouraging than she had dared to hope.

Lithium batteries are excellent for small, light devices, but they have two weaknesses when used for entire power grids. First, lithium is relatively scarce, and mining it consumes huge quantities of water, often in regions that have little to spare. Second, these batteries lose capacity gradually, and after about ten years the owners of large installations face the expensive task of replacing thousands of units. Mirzaeva's team has instead built batteries based on sodium, an element so abundant that it is the main ingredient of ordinary salt. A sodium battery stores roughly a third less energy than a lithium battery of the same weight, but for a stationary installation, where weight hardly matters, this drawback is minor.

The prototype installed last year beside a solar farm near Navoi contains forty-eight modules, each the size of a refrigerator, and can supply electricity to about four hundred homes for six hours. During the hot summer months, the farm now stores its surplus midday energy and releases it after sunset, when demand peaks. The engineers measured that the system lost only seven percent of the stored energy in the process, a result comparable with lithium systems. Better still, the batteries have so far shown no decline in capacity after two thousand charging cycles.

Nevertheless, Mirzaeva is cautious about publicity. She points out that two thousand cycles equal about five and a half years of daily use, which is not long enough to make claims about lifetimes of twenty years. Costs are another uncertainty: at present, her batteries are more expensive than lithium ones, because lithium factories enjoy decades of experience and enormous scale, while hers is a pilot workshop that produces twelve modules a month. She expects the price to fall sharply only if a manufacturer invests in mass production, and nobody has yet agreed to do so.

Critics wonder whether the world needs another battery type at all, since lithium prices have recently fallen. Mirzaeva responds that prices rise and fall, and that depending on a single material, mined in a few countries, is risky for any energy system. 'Diversity is a form of security,' she says. 'We would not build a city with only one kind of bridge.' Her group is now negotiating with two companies, and she hopes for a decision before the end of the year.
options: That storage must be lithium batteries

items.prompt: What surprised the writer at the museum?
items.answer: His nephew asked to stay beyond closing time
items.passage:
I had expected the new science museum in Samarkand to be a collection of dusty glass cases and labels in tiny print, which is why I was astonished when my twelve-year-old nephew, Oybek, who normally measures any outing by how soon he can return to his phone, asked to stay beyond the closing time. The museum opened in April in a converted cotton warehouse, and it deliberately breaks several traditions. There are almost no objects that visitors are forbidden to touch, and the director, Dr. Feruza Najmiddinova, a former physics teacher, told me that she measures success not by the number of tickets sold but by the number of questions children ask on the way out.

The building has four floors, each devoted to a different theme. The ground floor, called Motion, contains a tall tower where visitors can drop objects of different weights and watch them fall through a transparent tube from which the air has been pumped out; a feather and a metal ball reach the bottom at the same moment, a sight that Oybek made me watch six times. The second floor explores light and sound, and includes a dark room where voices are turned into coloured patterns on the wall. The third floor, on the human body, was the least popular with my nephew, though I found its model of a beating heart, big enough to walk through, quite moving. The fourth floor is a workshop where, on weekends, anyone can build and test small machines under the guidance of volunteer engineers.

Not everything impressed me. The queue at the entrance was nearly forty minutes long on Saturday, and the café offers only sandwiches that I would not recommend. More seriously, several of the explanations are written for adults with a university education rather than for the children for whom the museum seems to be designed. Standing in front of a display about electricity, I overheard a boy ask his father what 'resistance' meant, and the father, apparently an electrician, answered correctly but too quickly for the boy to follow.

A more subtle criticism concerns the museum's name for its approach, 'learning by doing'. While hands-on activities are certainly entertaining, there is a danger that visitors leave remembering the fun but not the principle behind it. Najmiddinova accepts this risk. She says that curiosity must come first and understanding later, and that a child who has dropped a feather and a ball will one day, perhaps in a school lesson, recall the experience and finally grasp why the feather fell more slowly outside the tube.

Tickets cost about three dollars for children and six for adults, and on the first Wednesday of each month entry is free for school groups. If you plan to go, arrive before ten in the morning, wear comfortable shoes and allow at least three hours. Oybek, for the record, is already asking when we can return.
options: His nephew refused to touch anything
His nephew asked to stay beyond closing time
His nephew left early to use his phone

There are almost no objects that visitors are forbidden to touch, and the director, Dr. Feruza Najmiddinova, a former physics teacher, told me that she measures success not by the number of tickets sold but by the number of questions children ask on the way out.

The ground floor, called Motion, contains a tall tower where visitors can drop objects of different weights and watch them fall through a transparent tube from which the air has been pumped out; a feather and a metal ball reach the bottom at the same moment, a sight that Oybek made me watch six times. The second floor explores light and sound, and includes a dark room where voices are turned into coloured patterns on the wall. The third floor, on the human body, was the least popular with my nephew, though I found its model of a beating heart, big enough to walk through, quite moving. The fourth floor is a workshop where, on weekends, anyone can build and test small machines under the guidance of volunteer engineers.

Not everything impressed me. The queue at the entrance was nearly forty minutes long on Saturday, and the café offers only sandwiches that I would not recommend. More seriously, several of the explanations are written for adults with a university education rather than for the children for whom the museum seems to be designed. Standing in front of a display about electricity, I overheard a boy ask his father what 'resistance' meant, and the father, apparently an electrician, answered correctly but too quickly for the boy to follow.

A more subtle criticism concerns the museum's name for its approach, 'learning by doing'. While hands-on activities are certainly entertaining, there is a danger that visitors leave remembering the fun but not the principle behind it. Najmiddinova accepts this risk. She says that curiosity must come first and understanding later, and that a child who has dropped a feather and a ball will one day, perhaps in a school lesson, recall the experience and finally grasp why the feather fell more slowly outside the tube.

Tickets cost about three dollars for children and six for adults, and on the first Wednesday of each month entry is free for school groups. If you plan to go, arrive before ten in the morning, wear comfortable shoes and allow at least three hours. Oybek, for the record, is already asking when we can return.

items.prompt: What does Yuldashev say is the club's aim?
items.answer: To produce students who can solve problems nobody has explained
items.passage:
When the robotics club at School Number Forty-Four in Urgench was founded four years ago, it had five members, one broken laptop and a teacher who admitted that he knew less about robots than most of his students. Today, it has twenty-two members, a proper workshop and a trophy cabinet with, by the teacher's own account, more dust than trophies. The club's coach, Mr. Otabek Yuldashev, a mathematics teacher, says that this modest record is exactly what he is proud of: 'Our aim has never been to win. Our aim is to produce students who can solve a problem that nobody has explained to them yet.'

In October the team travelled eleven hours by train to Tashkent for the national school competition, where teams had six weeks to build a robot that could collect plastic bottles from a floor and sort them by colour. The favourites were two schools from the capital with expensive equipment and sponsors. Urgench had a budget of about two hundred dollars and a design that used a camera taken from an old mobile phone. Captain Madina Sobirova, sixteen, explains that the cheapness forced them to be creative: 'We could not buy a good sensor, so we taught the software to recognise colours ourselves. In the end, that was the part that the judges liked most.'

The competition did not go smoothly. During the first round, the robot's left wheel came loose, and the team lost nine of its twenty allowed minutes while fixing it with a hairpin borrowed from a girl in the audience. The robot completed the task only partially, collecting seven bottles out of fifteen. Many teams would have been discouraged, but the Urgench students used the break between rounds to redesign the wheel mount, and in the second round they collected fourteen bottles, the second-highest score of the day.

They finished third overall, because the judges also awarded points for teamwork and for a presentation about the design process. Sobirova admits that she was disappointed for a few minutes, since she had hoped for first place, but she changed her mind when an engineer from a technology company approached the team and offered each member a place on a summer programme. 'I realised that nobody had offered us that because of a medal,' she says. 'They offered it because of how we behaved when the wheel fell off.'

Back in Urgench, the club is now planning a different kind of project. Instead of a competition robot, they intend to build a simple machine that waters plants in the school garden according to the moisture in the soil. Yuldashev supports the idea warmly, though he hesitates to call it a step down. 'A machine that is actually used every day teaches more than a machine that is used for twenty minutes on stage,' he says. 'And the younger students, who are only eleven or twelve, will be able to take part from the beginning.'
options: To win as many trophies as possible
To produce students who can solve problems nobody has explained
To beat the schools from the capital

items.prompt: Why did Sherzod and the Japanese visitors stand in silence?
items.answer: Neither side could find a word the other understood
items.passage:
Sherzod Tojiev, a tour guide in Khiva, still remembers the day a group of visitors from Japan stood in front of him in silence for almost a minute because neither side could find a word the other understood. Ten years later, the same scene would be unlikely, since most of his clients now hold phones that translate speech almost instantly. Yet Sherzod, who speaks four languages himself, is not convinced that the technology is as wonderful as its advertisements suggest.

Modern translation software works in a way that would surprise most users. Instead of looking up each word in a dictionary, as early programs did, it has studied billions of sentences in many languages and learned which patterns usually correspond to each other. This is why the results are often fluent, even elegant. However, fluency is not the same thing as accuracy. Because the program predicts what a sentence ought to look like, it occasionally produces a smooth sentence that says something different from the original. Linguist Dr. Gavhar Rahmonova gives an example from a hospital in Tashkent, where a program turned a doctor's note saying 'no known allergies' into a sentence suggesting that the patient was allergic to several medicines.

Idioms create further difficulties. When an Uzbek speaker says that something is 'as easy as eating plov', the software may translate it literally, leaving the foreigner confused, or it may replace it with an English phrase of its own, such as 'a piece of cake', which is accurate in meaning yet loses the cultural flavour. Rahmonova considers the second solution better for business, but the first more interesting for literature, and she says that no program can choose correctly between them without understanding the purpose of the text.

Supporters point out that the technology has transformed the lives of immigrants, refugees and small traders, who can now communicate in situations where a professional interpreter would be unaffordable. Sherzod grants this but warns about dependence. He has noticed that some young guides have stopped learning languages altogether, assuming that the phone will do the work. 'A translator can give you words,' he says, 'but not a relationship. When I tell a joke in a visitor's own language, even badly, they laugh because I made an effort. A phone cannot make an effort on my behalf.'

Rahmonova offers a practical compromise. Use the machine for everyday needs such as menus, timetables and directions, where a small error causes little harm, but turn to a human professional for contracts, medical advice and legal documents, where a single wrong word may have serious consequences. She adds that the best users of translation software are people who know something of the language, because they can notice when a sentence feels strange. Sherzod, for his part, has begun to learn Korean, in the expectation that Korean visitors will outnumber Japanese ones within five years. He does not rely on his phone for lessons. 'I use it,' he says, 'only to check that my teacher is not laughing at me.'
options: The visitors were angry with the price
Neither side could find a word the other understood
Sherzod did not speak any foreign language

items.prompt: How many times was the message forwarded within forty minutes?
items.passage:
Last March, a message spread across messaging groups in the town of Kokand claiming that the municipal reservoir had been poisoned, and that residents should stop drinking tap water immediately. Within forty minutes it had been forwarded more than three thousand times. Dilnoza Karimova, a chemistry teacher who lives near the reservoir, received it from four different relatives, each of whom assumed that someone else had already checked it.

Rather than panic, Dilnoza phoned the water company, which told her that the last sample had been tested only that morning and that nothing unusual had been found. Meanwhile, queues formed outside shops, and by noon the price of bottled water had risen by nearly a third, although the shopkeepers insisted they had not meant to take advantage of anyone. The original message, it later emerged, had been written by a teenager as a joke, and he never expected it to travel beyond his own class group. He had copied the style of an official announcement, including a logo borrowed from the city council, which is why so many people believed it.

The council responded by publishing a denial, but it appeared at six in the evening, nearly nine hours after the rumour began, and by then the correction was reaching far fewer people than the lie. "A correction never runs as fast as a scandal," Dilnoza said. She argues that the real problem is not stupidity but habit: people forward messages from friends precisely because they trust the friends, not the content. Hardly anyone, she points out, reads past the first line before pressing the button.

Since then, Dilnoza has started a small workshop in her school's library for parents and grandparents. She teaches three simple rules: check who published the message, look for the same news on at least two reliable sites, and wait ten minutes before sharing anything alarming. Not everyone is convinced; her neighbour Rustam says that waiting is a luxury when your children might be in danger. Dilnoza accepts the objection but replies that an unnecessary panic can also harm children, as three elderly residents who were taken to hospital with stress-related symptoms that afternoon discovered. The teenager, who was never punished by law, spent a month cleaning the library as agreed with the council, and he now helps to run the workshops.

items.prompt: In which year did the Echo start to be published?
items.passage:
The Marlow Echo, a weekly newspaper that had been published without interruption since 1911, printed its final edition last Friday. The decision, announced by the owners in early May, came after circulation fell from eleven thousand copies at its peak to barely fourteen hundred. The editor, Margaret Okafor, who joined as a trainee reporter in 1994, said the closure was less a surprise than a relief from months of uncertainty, although she admitted that she had cried in the car park after the meeting.

The owners blamed falling advertising revenue. Estate agents and car dealers, who once filled whole pages, moved online years ago, and the supermarket chain that had advertised weekly cancelled its contract in January. Readers, however, tell a more complicated story. Many say they stopped buying the paper not because they disliked it but because the news was already stale by Friday; by the time a council decision appeared in print, it had been discussed on social media for four days. Okafor does not entirely accept this. "People complain that the Echo was slow," she said, "yet the posts they read were mostly rumours, and we were the ones who checked the minutes of the meeting."

The consequences are already visible. At last month's planning committee, nobody from the press attended for the first time in living memory, and a proposal to build forty flats beside the river was approved in nineteen minutes. A local councillor, Hamid Rahimov, admitted that he found the silence uncomfortable. "When a reporter is in the room, you think twice," he said. "Now I worry that decisions will be made simply because nobody is watching." Researchers who study so-called news deserts have found that in towns without a local paper, voter turnout tends to fall and spending on public projects tends to rise, although they stress that the link is not proven.

There is a small hope. A group of former staff, led by the sports reporter Tom Brennan, plans to launch a free online newsletter in September, funded by donations from readers. They need at least six hundred paying supporters to cover one salary and have so far found two hundred and ten. Okafor will not be involved; she is moving to Leeds to care for her mother and says she wants to read a newspaper for once rather than write one. Still, she left the office keys on the editor's desk with a note that said, "Somebody has to keep an eye on them."

items.prompt: Why did Nilufar originally join the pantry?
items.answer: She needed to complete hours required by her university.
items.passage:
When Nilufar Yusupova signed up at the Riverside Food Pantry two years ago, her motives were not especially noble. Her university required sixty hours of community work before the end of the second year, and the pantry was the closest organisation to her flat. She expected to stack tins for a few Saturdays, collect a signature and never return. Instead she has now logged over four hundred hours and recently became the youngest shift coordinator in the pantry's history.

What changed her mind was a conversation in her third week. An elderly man, who had been coming for months, told her that the hardest part was not the hunger but the queue, because neighbours could see him standing in it. Nilufar suggested a simple change: instead of a single queue on the pavement, families would book a ten-minute slot by text message and wait inside. Her manager, Gerald Ashworth, was sceptical, pointing out that half of the clients did not own a smartphone. She therefore agreed to keep a paper booking sheet at the door as well. The pilot began in October, and within two months the number of families using the pantry had risen from about ninety to a hundred and thirty, which Gerald believes shows that many people had previously stayed away out of embarrassment.

Volunteering has not been entirely easy. Nilufar admits that she once lost her temper with a client who complained about the quality of the bread, and she was reprimanded afterwards. She also finds it difficult to balance her studies with the pantry, and her grades dropped slightly last spring, a trade-off her parents did not welcome. Her father, a taxi driver, thought the hours would be better spent on paid work; her mother, on the other hand, comes every other Saturday to help sort vegetables. "My father hasn't changed his mind," Nilufar says, "but he has stopped asking me how much I earn."

Researchers who study volunteering say that stories like hers are common, but they warn against romanticising them. Many organisations depend on young people who are motivated by qualifications and who leave as soon as the requirement is met. Gerald agrees, which is why the pantry now pays for first-aid training and gives every volunteer a written reference after six months. The next target, Nilufar says, is to open a weekday evening session for people who work during the day. It will start in January if the council approves the extra heating costs, a decision expected at the end of next month.

She needed to complete hours required by her university.
Her mother asked her to help.

items.prompt: For how long did the protesters block the road?
items.passage:
On Tuesday morning, about two hundred residents of the Willowbrook estate blocked the main road for twenty minutes to protest against the city's decision to reroute the number 27 bus. From next month the bus, which has connected the estate to the hospital and the town centre for nearly thirty years, will instead run along the new ring road, saving, according to the transport authority, six minutes on every journey. Protesters, many of them pensioners holding hand-painted signs, argued that six minutes saved for commuters means a twenty-minute walk added for people who can hardly climb the hill to the new stop.

The authority's spokeswoman, Priya Nair, defended the plan. The old route, she said, was the slowest in the network, with an average speed of eleven kilometres per hour, and nearly a quarter of the buses arrived late. She added that the new route would serve a technology park where three thousand people work, and which has no public transport at all. "We have to think about who is not yet using the bus as well as who is," she said. Critics replied that the authority's own survey, carried out last autumn, asked only passengers on the ring road, so Willowbrook residents were never consulted.

The protest was organised by Kamola Tursunova, a nurse who works night shifts at the hospital and uses the 27 every evening. She stressed that the demonstration was peaceful and that police, who had been informed in advance, only redirected traffic. Not everybody on the street was sympathetic, though. A van driver, stuck in the queue, shouted that people who chose to live on a hill should expect to walk, and a few commuters complained that the delay had made them miss trains. Kamola took the criticism calmly. "I understand their frustration," she said. "But if I cannot reach the hospital at night, the people who suffer are the patients, not me."

By the afternoon, the authority had agreed to a meeting on Thursday, though it refused to promise any change before then. Councillor Daniel Fischer, who represents the estate, proposed a compromise: a smaller minibus that would loop through Willowbrook twice an hour and connect with the main route at the old stop. The authority said it would study the cost, but warned that a minibus would probably require a subsidy of around fifty thousand pounds a year. Whether that is a price worth paying remains to be seen; what is clear is that, in the space of one morning, a quiet dispute about timetables became a question about who a city is built for.

items.prompt: How long does the film last?
items.passage:
Few documentaries have made me want to leave the cinema and call my grandmother, but The Last Salt Harvest, directed by Aigerim Sadykova, did precisely that. The film, which lasts ninety-four minutes, follows the Baimenov family through what is probably their final season of collecting salt from a shrinking lake in southern Kazakhstan. There is no narrator and almost no music. Instead, Sadykova, who spent fourteen months living in the nearest village, lets the camera linger on hands, boots and the white crust that covers everything, and she trusts the audience to understand what is at stake without being told.

Admittedly, this approach will frustrate some viewers. The first twenty minutes move at the pace of the workers themselves, and a friend who watched it with me whispered that nothing was happening. I disagree; I think a great deal is happening, but it happens in silence. The father, Nurlan, never complains about the lake's retreat, yet in one memorable scene he walks further each morning to reach the water, and the film simply counts his steps. The daughter, Dana, who is sixteen, wants to study engineering in the capital and is the only member of the family who speaks openly about leaving. Her mother's reaction, a long pause followed by a question about dinner, tells us more than any speech could.

The film is not without weaknesses. A subplot about a visiting mining company is introduced in the middle and dropped within minutes, which feels less like restraint than like a missing scene. Moreover, the director has admitted in interviews that two of the conversations were repeated for the camera because the sound had failed the first time. Purists may object, although I do not believe that a slightly rehearsed sentence betrays the truth of a family's situation. More troubling is the absence of any scientist or official, since viewers who know little about the region are left to guess why the lake is disappearing.

Even so, the final fifteen minutes are among the most moving I have seen this year. Without giving too much away, the harvest ends earlier than expected, and the family's decision is shown not through dialogue but through a closed door and an empty truck. The film opened at the Almaty festival in March, where it won the audience prize, and it will reach cinemas in the autumn, with a wider release planned for January. I would give it four stars out of five, and I would give a fifth to anyone who watches it with the patience it deserves.

items.prompt: How many branches does the council plan to close?
items.passage:
When the council announced last year that it would close seven of its fourteen public libraries to save two million pounds, the reaction was predictable: petitions, angry letters and a march of several hundred people carrying books. What was less predictable was the discovery that many of the people most upset had not borrowed a book in years. The head librarian, Sofia Marchetti, finds this contradiction revealing. "People value the idea of a library," she says, "much more than they use it as it exists now."

Indeed, the figures show that book lending has fallen by almost forty percent in a decade, which supporters of the closures cite as proof that libraries are obsolete. But Marchetti points out that visitor numbers tell a different story. The Eastgate branch, for example, recorded eighty-one thousand visits last year, nearly twice as many as ten years ago, even though fewer of those visitors left with a book. They came to use computers, to apply for jobs, to attend a baby-singing session on Wednesday mornings, to study quietly when seven people share a flat of two rooms, or simply to sit somewhere warm where nobody asked them to buy anything.

This broader role is exactly what worries opponents of the cuts. Nobody disputes that books are cheaper than ever, but access to the internet, a quiet room and a trained adult who can help fill in a benefits form is another matter. A retired engineer, Abdulla Nazarov, who has attended the Eastgate computer class every Thursday for three years, says that without it he would have been unable to renew his passport, since the application is now online only. Meanwhile, the council's leader, Councillor Eleanor Whitfield, argues that money spent on buildings used by a minority would be better spent on social care. She also insists that no staff will be dismissed and that a mobile library van will serve the neighbourhoods that lose their branch, although the van will visit each of them for only two hours a week.

There is, however, a more hopeful possibility. Three of the seven branches under threat have been taken over by local volunteer groups, who run them with a small grant and the help of two paid staff. Marchetti has mixed feelings. On one hand, she is delighted that the buildings remain open; on the other, she fears that a library run by volunteers is vulnerable the day they get tired. "A library is not charity," she says. "It is infrastructure, like a road, and we do not ask neighbours to keep the road in repair." The final vote on the closures will take place in March, and nobody, including the councillors, is willing to predict the result.

items.prompt: How many signatures does the petition have?
items.passage:
For eleven years, the oak tree at the end of Alder Lane was nothing more than a tree. Today it has its own lawyer, a hashtag and a petition with six hundred signatures. The dispute began last June, when Mr Gennady Volkov, who lives at number nine, asked the council for permission to cut down the tree, which he claimed was lifting his garden wall and dropping branches onto his car. His neighbour across the road, Ms Shirin Abdullaeva, a primary school teacher, objected immediately. The tree, she said, was planted by pupils in the school's garden project, and removing it would be like erasing a small piece of the street's memory.

At first, both sides behaved civilly. They exchanged letters, and Mr Volkov even invited Ms Abdullaeva for tea, though she later described the conversation as "polite but completely deaf". Things deteriorated in September, when a bough fell during a storm and damaged the roof of his garage. Mr Volkov sent her a bill for four hundred and twenty pounds, arguing that she had encouraged the council to keep the tree. Ms Abdullaeva refused to pay, pointing out that the tree belongs to the council, not to her. Since then, they have not spoken, and each has begun to document the other's behaviour: she with photographs of his car blocking the pavement, he with notes of the hours when her pupils' parents park outside.

The wider street has divided too. Some residents, such as the retired postman Idris Qodirov, side with Mr Volkov, saying that he is hardly a villain for protecting his property. Others believe the tree is worth some inconvenience. A professional arborist, hired by the council in October, concluded that the oak is healthy and that the wall problem could be solved by repairing the foundation and removing two dead branches, at a cost of about nine hundred pounds. Mr Volkov rejected this conclusion, saying that an expert who does not live beside a tree will always find it charming.

The council has now offered to arrange mediation, in which a neutral person helps both sides to find a compromise. Ms Abdullaeva has accepted; Mr Volkov has not yet replied, claiming that he is waiting for his lawyer's advice. Neighbourhood disputes of this kind are more common than people realise, according to a mediator who has handled more than two hundred of them. Most are not really about trees, noise or parking, she says, but about the feeling of not being listened to. If that is true here, the solution may be cheaper than anyone expects: the first meeting, scheduled for the second week of December, would cost each side nothing.
