The dispute began last June, when Mr Gennady Volkov, who lives at number nine, asked the council for permission to cut down the tree, which he claimed was lifting his garden wall and dropping branches onto his car. His neighbour across the road, Ms Shirin Abdullaeva, a primary school teacher, objected immediately. The tree, she said, was planted by pupils in the school's garden project, and removing it would be like erasing a small piece of the street's memory.

At first, both sides behaved civilly. They exchanged letters, and Mr Volkov even invited Ms Abdullaeva for tea, though she later described the conversation as "polite but completely deaf". Things deteriorated in September, when a bough fell during a storm and damaged the roof of his garage. Mr Volkov sent her a bill for four hundred and twenty pounds, arguing that she had encouraged the council to keep the tree. Ms Abdullaeva refused to pay, pointing out that the tree belongs to the council, not to her. Since then, they have not spoken, and each has begun to document the other's behaviour: she with photographs of his car blocking the pavement, he with notes of the hours when her pupils' parents park outside.

The wider street has divided too. Some residents, such as the retired postman Idris Qodirov, side with Mr Volkov, saying that he is hardly a villain for protecting his property. Others believe the tree is worth some inconvenience. A professional arborist, hired by the council in October, concluded that the oak is healthy and that the wall problem could be solved by repairing the foundation and removing two dead branches, at a cost of about nine hundred pounds. Mr Volkov rejected this conclusion, saying that an expert who does not live beside a tree will always find it charming.

The council has now offered to arrange mediation, in which a neutral person helps both sides to find a compromise. Ms Abdullaeva has accepted; Mr Volkov has not yet replied, claiming that he is waiting for his lawyer's advice. Neighbourhood disputes of this kind are more common than people realise, according to a mediator who has handled more than two hundred of them. Most are not really about trees, noise or parking, she says, but about the feeling of not being listened to. If that is true here, the solution may be cheaper than anyone expects: the first meeting, scheduled for the second week of December, would cost each side nothing.

items.prompt: How far did one photographer follow her car?
items.passage:
When the actress Camille Okonkwo walked out of a restaurant in Lyon last April, three photographers were waiting. They had not been invited, and they did not leave, even when she asked politely and then less politely. One followed her car for twelve kilometres. The next morning, a photograph of her crying outside her sister's house appeared on the front page of a tabloid under the headline "Camille's Secret Crisis". The truth, as she later explained, was that she was grieving for her grandmother; nobody at the paper had bothered to ask.

Okonkwo, thirty-four, has since become an unlikely campaigner. Last month she gave evidence to a parliamentary committee considering a new privacy law, arguing that fame is a job, not a surrender of rights. "I agreed to be watched when I am on a stage," she told the members. "I did not agree to be watched when I am in a hospital car park." Her critics are numerous. One columnist wrote that famous people cannot enjoy the money and attention that publicity brings and then complain about its price. Another pointed out that Okonkwo herself sold exclusive photographs of her wedding for a large sum, which, in his view, undermines her argument.

She does not deny the wedding deal. Indeed, she raises it herself, saying that the difference is choice: she decided what was shown, when, and to whom. The distinction matters in law as well. The proposed legislation would not forbid the publication of photographs of public figures in public places, nor would it protect politicians from scrutiny of their official conduct. It would, however, make it illegal to photograph someone in a medical facility or in the home of a relative without consent, unless the picture serves a clear public interest. Defining that phrase is the hardest part, since editors tend to believe that anything that sells copies is interesting to the public, which is not at all the same thing.

Opinion polls suggest the public is divided. In a survey of two thousand adults, just over half supported stronger privacy rules, but seventy percent also admitted that they had clicked on a celebrity story that they knew had been obtained intrusively. Okonkwo finds this unsurprising and not especially hypocritical. "Everyone is curious," she says. "But being curious is not the same as being owed something." The committee will publish its recommendations in the spring, and the earliest the law could take effect is next year, assuming the government decides to support it.

items.prompt: How long did Ravshan have between his promise and the race?
items.passage:
Ravshan Tolipov had never run more than three kilometres in his life when, on his fortieth birthday, he promised his colleagues that he would run a full marathon to raise money for a rural school roof in Karakalpakstan. He made the promise partly as a joke, partly because his doctor had just told him to lose weight. Nobody, including Ravshan, expected him to keep it. Yet fourteen months later he stood at the start of the Tashkent Marathon with a number pinned to his shirt, a pair of second-hand running shoes and a sponsorship total of nine thousand two hundred dollars.

Training had been harder than he imagined. In the first month he managed only twelve minutes of continuous running, and he injured his knee in March by increasing his distance too quickly, a mistake that every beginner seems to make once. His coach, a retired athlete called Svetlana Ivanova, insisted that he rest for three weeks, during which he cycled instead. "The body adapts slowly," she told him. "It is the enthusiasm that adapts fast, and that is the problem." By September he was running thirty kilometres on Sundays, usually at five in the morning to avoid the heat, accompanied by a neighbour's dog that was not officially invited.

On race day, the weather was cooler than forecast, which helped. Ravshan reached the halfway point in two hours and ten minutes, faster than planned, and was feeling confident. That, he later admitted, was the error. Around the thirty-first kilometre his legs began to cramp, and he had to walk for almost a mile. It was then that strangers began shouting his name, because the organisers had printed the names of charity runners on their shirts. A schoolgirl handed him half an orange; an elderly man offered him a seat on a folding chair, which he refused, fearing that he would never stand again. He crossed the finishing line in five hours and twelve minutes, much slower than the champion, who had finished more than three hours earlier.

The total raised eventually reached eleven thousand dollars, enough, according to the school's headmistress, to repair the roof and buy desks for forty pupils. Some people have questioned whether charity marathons are an efficient way of raising money, since the cost of the event itself is high and participants often donate less than they receive in attention. Ravshan has no strong view on this. What he knows is that the roof will be finished before the winter, that he lost eleven kilograms, and that he has already registered for a half marathon in April. "Next time," he says, "I will start slowly. Everybody says that, and nobody does it."

items.prompt: What was the site originally?
items.passage:
The Tosh Darvoza Bazaar in the old part of the city did not begin as a market at all. According to the historian Professor Bahodir Ismoilov, the earliest records from the sixteenth century describe the site as a caravanserai, a walled inn where merchants rested their camels before the last stage of a journey. Traders who arrived exhausted needed food, repairs and somewhere to sell a few goods to cover their costs, so a small market grew outside the gate, and the name 'stone gate' survived long after the stones themselves had been carried away to build a bridge.

By the nineteenth century the market had become specialised. Copper workers occupied one lane, silk dealers another, and the street of bakers was so busy that, according to a travel account of 1874, a visitor could find his way at night simply by following the smell. Each trade was governed by an elder who settled disputes and inspected weights. A cheating seller was not taken to court but was publicly named, and that, historians say, was usually punishment enough. Imperial rule brought railways and cotton merchants, but the bazaar's structure changed less than might be expected, since its rules were not written down and therefore could not easily be abolished.

The twentieth century was less kind. In nineteen sixty-three, a large part of the market was demolished to build a concrete hall, which sellers disliked because it was dark in winter and unbearably hot in summer. Many stalls moved onto pavements, and for decades the bazaar existed in an awkward partnership with the authorities, who tolerated it without admitting it was legal. Ismoilov argues that this ambiguity actually preserved the bazaar, because a market that nobody planned could not be redesigned by planners. The concrete hall has been renovated twice, in nineteen ninety-eight and again in two thousand and nineteen, though shoppers still say the old lanes are more pleasant.

Today the bazaar faces a new challenge: online shopping. Sellers report that younger customers browse in the lanes and then order the same goods on their phones, sometimes while standing at the stall. Some traders have responded by joining the competition; Gulchehra Rakhimova, who sells dried fruit, now photographs her products each morning and delivers across the city by motorbike. Others stress what cannot be delivered, such as the chance to taste, to bargain and to be advised by someone who has sold the same thing for thirty years. Ismoilov is cautiously optimistic. "The bazaar has outlived the caravans, the empire and the planners," he says. "I would not bet against it surviving the internet." The city council plans to publish a protection plan next year, although many sellers believe that the best protection is customers.

items.prompt: How long was the recording the judge heard?
items.passage:
In a courtroom in Birmingham last Thursday, a judge listened to a recording that lasted exactly forty seconds, and it may cost a family restaurant its licence. The recording, made by a flat owner named Priyanka Desai, captured the sound of live music from the Blue Lantern, a restaurant on the ground floor of her building. Measured at eleven forty at night, with all windows shut, the noise reached fifty-eight decibels, which is roughly the level of a loud conversation. The restaurant's owner, Marco Bellini, argued that this figure was not excessive, and that the council's own limit for that time of night is sixty-five.

Desai's lawyer replied that decibels were only half of the story. The council limit, he explained, applies to the street outside; inside a bedroom the rules are stricter, and, more important, the type of sound matters. A steady hum may be tolerable, but a drum beat, however quiet, is difficult to ignore because the brain keeps waiting for the next one. Desai herself testified that she had not had a full night's sleep since February, that she had begun to wear earplugs and that her doctor had prescribed medication for anxiety. Under cross-examination, however, she admitted that she had bought the flat knowing that the restaurant existed, and that she had complained only after the music started in January.

That detail was the centre of the defence. Bellini's lawyer reminded the court that the Blue Lantern had been open for twenty-six years, which was longer than the building had contained flats, and that a new resident cannot reasonably expect a long-established business to change simply because she dislikes the noise. The prosecution countered that the restaurant had only recently introduced live music, and that the licence, which dates from nineteen ninety-eight, allowed background music but not performances after ten o'clock. Bellini conceded that two musicians play on Fridays and Saturdays, though he insisted that they stop at half past eleven rather than at midnight, as one neighbour claimed.

The judge, who has promised a decision within three weeks, indicated that she was not inclined to close the restaurant. A more likely outcome, she suggested, is a compromise: live music on Friday only, finishing at eleven, and a thicker ceiling paid for by the restaurant. Bellini said that he could accept the first condition but not the second, because the repairs would cost about thirty thousand pounds, nearly a year's profit. Desai said that she would be satisfied with silence after eleven, adding that she had nothing against music and in fact plays the piano herself. "I just think," she said outside the court, "that everyone should be allowed to sleep in their own home."

items.prompt: The judge intends to close the restaurant.
items.passage:
In a courtroom in Birmingham last Thursday, a judge listened to a recording that lasted exactly forty seconds, and it may cost a family restaurant its licence. The recording, made by a flat owner named Priyanka Desai, captured the sound of live music from the Blue Lantern, a restaurant on the ground floor of her building. Measured at eleven forty at night, with all windows shut, the noise reached fifty-eight decibels, which is roughly the level of a loud conversation. The restaurant's owner, Marco Bellini, argued that this figure was not excessive, and that the council's own limit for that time of night is sixty-five.

Desai's lawyer replied that decibels were only half of the story. The council limit, he explained, applies to the street outside; inside a bedroom the rules are stricter, and, more important, the type of sound matters. A steady hum may be tolerable, but a drum beat, however quiet, is difficult to ignore because the brain keeps waiting for the next one. Desai herself testified that she had not had a full night's sleep since February, that she had begun to wear earplugs and that her doctor had prescribed medication for anxiety. Under cross-examination, however, she admitted that she had bought the flat knowing that the restaurant existed, and that she had complained only after the music started in January.

That detail was the centre of the defence. Bellini's lawyer reminded the court that the Blue Lantern had been open for twenty-six years, which was longer than the building had contained flats, and that a new resident cannot reasonably expect a long-established business to change simply because she dislikes the noise. The prosecution countered that the restaurant had only recently introduced live music, and that the licence, which dates from nineteen ninety-eight, allowed background music but not performances after ten o'clock. Bellini conceded that two musicians play on Fridays and Saturdays, though he insisted that they stop at half past eleven rather than at midnight, as one neighbour claimed.

items.prompt: What does the opening sentence suggest about the podcast?
items.answer: The author found it very absorbing.
items.passage:
I started listening to Between Two Homes, a weekly podcast about migration, on a long train journey, and I missed my stop. The host, Elena Voronina, moved from Tashkent to Warsaw at the age of twenty-three, and she brings to the microphone the patience of someone who remembers being a stranger. Each episode lasts forty minutes and follows one person for a year, returning at intervals to ask how things have changed, which gives the series a rare sense of time passing.

Episode nine, which I recommend most, features Tariq Mansoor, a Syrian-born dentist who now works as a hospital cleaner in Hamburg because his qualifications are not recognised. He had expected the process to take six months; it has taken three years, and he still has two exams to pass. What makes the episode remarkable is that he refuses to describe himself as a victim. He jokes that he is the only cleaner in the hospital who can diagnose a toothache from across the corridor. Yet the humour does not hide his frustration, particularly when he recalls a patient who, mistaking him for a doctor, asked for advice, and a colleague who then laughed at him.

The series is at its best when it complicates easy answers. A later episode interviews both a family who left a village because of drought and a farmer who stayed and now works their land. Instead of declaring who is right, Voronina asks each of them what they would say to the other, and the replies are surprisingly generous. Economists appear occasionally, but rarely to give an opinion; their role is to supply a number, such as the fact that the country in question receives three times as much money from emigrants' transfers as from foreign aid. I found myself wishing for more of these facts, since a few episodes lean heavily on emotion.

Not every listener will be satisfied. A reviewer for a national newspaper complained that the podcast avoids the political debate altogether, and that this is a kind of dishonesty. I see the point, but I disagree. Policy is discussed everywhere; what is rare is the chance to listen to a person describing an ordinary Tuesday in a country where he does not yet feel at home. The podcast has been downloaded more than four hundred thousand times since its launch two years ago, and a book based on the episodes is due in the spring. Season three begins on the fifth of January, with the first episode already recorded in Lisbon.

items.prompt: How long was the meeting originally supposed to last?
items.passage:
The town hall meeting that was supposed to last ninety minutes ended up lasting almost four hours, which surprised nobody who had read the agenda. Item six, a proposal to replace the car park behind the library with a skatepark and a small café, had been described by the mayor, Olga Smirnova, as "a modest improvement". By eight o'clock, a hundred and fifty people had crowded into a hall designed for a hundred, and the temperature had risen along with the tempers.

The first speaker, a shop owner named Farrukh Aliev, argued that the car park provides forty-two spaces that his customers rely on, and that no business can survive if people have to walk ten minutes with heavy bags. He was applauded loudly. A teenager, Maya Kowalski, then stood up and said that the town's young people have nowhere to go, apart from the shopping centre, where security guards ask them to leave after twenty minutes. Her answer was applauded even more loudly, which made the mayor laugh, though she was not sure whether that was wise.

What impressed several observers was how often speakers changed their minds. Mr Aliev, for instance, admitted in his second speech that he had never counted how many customers actually arrive by car, and the council's survey, presented at nine fifteen, showed that fewer than a third do. A retired councillor, Mr Hughes, proposed moving the skatepark to the field beside the river, but a planning officer replied that the ground floods every spring, which would make the site unusable for two months a year. Another speaker suggested building a multi-storey car park elsewhere; that was rejected immediately by the treasurer, who calculated that it would cost eight times the entire annual budget for parks.

In the end, no decision was taken. The mayor announced that the council would conduct a six-week consultation, including a vote in which anyone over twelve could take part, and that the results would be presented at the next meeting in January. Some residents left angry, feeling that the delay was a way of avoiding the issue. Others, including Maya, were cautiously pleased. "Honestly, I expected them to ignore us," she said. "Nobody ignored anyone tonight, even the people who disagreed." Whether that goodwill survives six weeks of leaflets, social media arguments and parked cars remains to be seen, but as one old man remarked on his way out, it was the first time in years that the hall had been full.

items.prompt: What was Maya's complaint about the shopping centre?
items.answer: Guards make young people leave after twenty minutes.
items.passage:
The town hall meeting that was supposed to last ninety minutes ended up lasting almost four hours, which surprised nobody who had read the agenda. Item six, a proposal to replace the car park behind the library with a skatepark and a small café, had been described by the mayor, Olga Smirnova, as "a modest improvement". By eight o'clock, a hundred and fifty people had crowded into a hall designed for a hundred, and the temperature had risen along with the tempers.

The first speaker, a shop owner named Farrukh Aliev, argued that the car park provides forty-two spaces that his customers rely on, and that no business can survive if people have to walk ten minutes with heavy bags. He was applauded loudly. A teenager, Maya Kowalski, then stood up and said that the town's young people have nowhere to go, apart from the shopping centre, where security guards ask them to leave after twenty minutes. Her answer was applauded even more loudly, which made the mayor laugh, though she was not sure whether that was wise.

What impressed several observers was how often speakers changed their minds. Mr Aliev, for instance, admitted in his second speech that he had never counted how many customers actually arrive by car, and the council's survey, presented at nine fifteen, showed that fewer than a third do. A retired councillor, Mr Hughes, proposed moving the skatepark to the field beside the river, but a planning officer replied that the ground floods every spring, which would make the site unusable for two months a year. Another speaker suggested building a multi-storey car park elsewhere; that was rejected immediately by the treasurer, who calculated that it would cost eight times the entire annual budget for parks.

In the end, no decision was taken. The mayor announced that the council would conduct a six-week consultation, including a vote in which anyone over twelve could take part, and that the results would be presented at the next meeting in January. Some residents left angry, feeling that the delay was a way of avoiding the issue. Others, including Maya, were cautiously pleased. "Honestly, I expected them to ignore us," she said. "Nobody ignored anyone tonight, even the people who disagreed." Whether that goodwill survives six weeks of leaflets, social media arguments and parked cars remains to be seen, but as one old man remarked on his way out, it was the first time in years that the hall had been full.
options: Guards make young people leave after twenty minutes.
It is closed in the evenings.

items.prompt: What time did Amir arrive on his first day?
items.passage:
Amir Rashidov had rehearsed his first day as a reporter so often that the real one felt like a disappointment. He arrived at the offices of the Daily Dispatch at a quarter to eight, fifteen minutes early, wearing a tie that his mother had ironed twice, and discovered that the newsroom was empty apart from a cleaner and a man asleep under a coat. The man turned out to be the night editor, Bill Harrington, who woke, looked at him without interest and said, "You're early. That's either very good or very bad."

The morning meeting began at nine, and Amir had expected a discussion of the great issues of the day. Instead, the editors argued for twenty minutes about whether a story about a lost parrot deserved the front page. It did not, Amir thought, but the editor-in-chief, a quiet woman called Grace Lindqvist, pointed out that the parrot's owner was a retired war veteran and that readers always want to know how such stories end. Amir noticed that she never raised her voice, yet everyone fell silent when she spoke. Afterwards, he was assigned to a senior reporter, Natalia Chernova, to "carry her bag and keep his mouth shut", as she put it, though she said it with a smile.

By noon they were standing outside a primary school, where parents were protesting about the closure of a crossing after a minor accident. Amir had prepared nine questions, but Natalia told him to ask only one: "What would you like the council to hear?" The answers were so honest that he stopped taking notes and simply listened, which Natalia later told him was his first mistake. She explained that he should have written down the exact words of a mother who said, "I will not let my son cross that road until somebody is held responsible." Fortunately, he remembered the sentence almost perfectly, and she let him write the first paragraph of the report.

That paragraph was changed four times before it appeared on the website at six thirty. Amir was upset until Natalia pointed out that the final version was shorter, clearer and, she admitted, better than hers would have been. On the way home he realised that he had not eaten since breakfast, nor had he used any of the grand sentences he had prepared. What he had learned was less glamorous: that journalism consists mostly of waiting, checking and listening, and that the skill lies in deciding what to leave out. The following morning he arrived at eight o'clock sharp, exactly on time, and Bill Harrington gave him a nod, which Amir decided to treat as a promotion.

items.prompt: Why was the festival first organised?
items.answer: To raise money to repair the church clock
items.passage:
The Tanner Street Festival began in 1987 as a single table of homemade cakes outside a hardware shop, organised by a woman who wanted to raise money to repair the church clock. Almost forty years later it occupies eleven streets, attracts around forty thousand visitors over a single weekend and requires a team of one hundred and twenty volunteers to run, most of whom return every year. The clock, incidentally, was repaired in the second year and has been wrong by about ten minutes ever since.

This year's festival, held on the second weekend of June, was meant to be the biggest yet, but the planning was troubled. In March, the council announced that it would charge organisers for road closures, a bill of nearly nine thousand pounds. The chairman, Jamshid Ergashev, who owns a bakery on the corner, said that he nearly cancelled the event. Instead, the committee persuaded twelve local businesses to sponsor a street each, and a group of students designed a map that earned money from advertisements. "We did not solve the problem," Jamshid says, "we just shared it out."

The programme, as usual, was a mixture of the traditional and the improbable: a brass band from the neighbouring village, a competition for the longest line of rubber ducks, cooking demonstrations by families from nineteen different countries, and a debate on whether the festival had become too commercial. This last item attracted the biggest crowd, and the verdict was divided. Older residents complained that food stalls now sell the same fried snacks as every other festival; younger ones replied that they had never tasted anything like the Ethiopian coffee served on Tanner Close, and that without outside sellers the event would be half the size.

Not everything went smoothly. A thunderstorm on Saturday afternoon emptied the streets within ten minutes, and about thirty stalls lost most of their stock. Sunday, however, was bright, and attendance on the second day was higher than on the first by roughly a third. The final accounts will not be known until August, but Jamshid is confident that the festival will break even for the first time in four years. Asked whether he would organise it again, he laughed. "Ask me in September," he said. "By then I will have forgotten how tired I am."
options: To raise money to repair the church clock
To celebrate the opening of a bakery

Almost forty years later it occupies eleven streets, attracts around forty thousand visitors over a single weekend and requires a team of one hundred and twenty volunteers to run, most of whom return every year. The clock, incidentally, was repaired in the second year and has been wrong by about ten minutes ever since.

This year's festival, held on the second weekend of June, was meant to be the biggest yet, but the planning was troubled. In March, the council announced that it would charge organisers for road closures, a bill of nearly nine thousand pounds. The chairman, Jamshid Ergashev, who owns a bakery on the corner, said that he nearly cancelled the event. Instead, the committee persuaded twelve local businesses to sponsor a street each, and a group of students designed a map that earned money from advertisements. "We did not solve the problem," Jamshid says, "we just shared it out."

The programme, as usual, was a mixture of the traditional and the improbable: a brass band from the neighbouring village, a competition for the longest line of rubber ducks, cooking demonstrations by families from nineteen different countries, and a debate on whether the festival had become too commercial. This last item attracted the biggest crowd, and the verdict was divided. Older residents complained that food stalls now sell the same fried snacks as every other festival; younger ones replied that they had never tasted anything like the Ethiopian coffee served on Tanner Close, and that without outside sellers the event would be half the size.

Not everything went smoothly. A thunderstorm on Saturday afternoon emptied the streets within ten minutes, and about thirty stalls lost most of their stock. Sunday, however, was bright, and attendance on the second day was higher than on the first by roughly a third. The final accounts will not be known until August, but Jamshid is confident that the festival will break even for the first time in four years. Asked whether he would organise it again, he laughed. "Ask me in September," he said. "By then I will have forgotten how tired I am."

items.prompt: What did Dilnoza assume about the rusting ships when she first saw them?
items.passage:
When Dilnoza Karimova first stood on the dried-up seabed near Moynaq in 2009, she assumed the rusting ships in front of her were a tourist gimmick. Her guide, a retired fisherman named Bakhtiyor, quickly corrected her. Until the early 1960s, he explained, the Aral Sea was the fourth largest lake in the world, and Moynaq was a busy port that canned around one sixth of the Soviet Union's fish. Then the rivers feeding the sea, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, were diverted to irrigate cotton fields, and the water began to retreat. By 1990 the shoreline had moved more than sixty kilometres away from the town, and the fishing industry had collapsed almost overnight.

Many visitors, Bakhtiyor said, assume that drought alone caused the disaster. He disagreed strongly. Weather played a minor role, he argued; the real culprit was a decision made in offices far from the sea, where officials valued cotton harvests more than a fragile ecosystem. The consequences were not limited to unemployment. Salt and chemical dust blown from the exposed seabed damaged crops, and local doctors reported unusually high rates of throat and kidney illness. Rainfall in the region actually became less predictable, since the sea no longer softened the climate.

Dilnoza had expected the trip to be thoroughly depressing, yet she left with mixed feelings. In the northern part of the sea, known as the Small Aral, a dam completed in Kazakhstan in 2005 has allowed the water level to recover, and fishermen there now catch species that had vanished for decades. The southern part, by contrast, has almost entirely dried out, and scientists hardly expect it to return in anyone's lifetime. A new forest of saxaul shrubs, planted across about two million hectares, is helping to hold the salty soil in place, although experts warn that it cannot replace the lost water.

Tourism now supplies a modest income for Moynaq. Guesthouses offer simple rooms for around twenty dollars a night, and a small museum displays old photographs of the harbour. Bakhtiyor admits he is torn: he is pleased that people finally listen to his story, but he worries that visitors treat the ships as a photo opportunity rather than a warning. 'Take as many pictures as you like,' he tells each group, 'but please do not leave without asking yourself who made the decision, and who paid for it.' Dilnoza, who now writes about environmental policy, says that sentence changed the direction of her career.

They were left behind after a war

items.prompt: How are the cabins heated?
items.answer: By wood stoves burning fallen branches
items.passage:
When my editor suggested that I spend a week at Sarvar Lodge, a small eco-lodge in the Fann Mountains of Tajikistan, I accepted mainly because the views looked spectacular. I confess I also expected to be uncomfortable. The lodge was built in 2016 by two sisters, Madina and Zarina Rahimova, using local stone and timber, and it has only fourteen cabins, each one heated by a wood stove fed with fallen branches rather than felled trees. Electricity comes mostly from solar panels, and a small turbine in the stream covers the winter months, when the sun is weak and the days are short.

The first surprise was the hot water. It is heated by the sun, so the showers are warm only in the late afternoon, and each guest is asked to keep to five minutes. I assumed I would resent the rule, but it made me far more aware of how carelessly I normally use water at home. The second surprise was the food. Around eighty percent of everything we ate, from the yoghurt at breakfast to the apricot jam, came from the lodge's own garden or from neighbouring families. Madina told me that she used to buy cheaper vegetables from the market in Dushanbe, but the transport costs, both financial and environmental, were absurd.

Not every guest is delighted. There is no wifi in the cabins, and a couple from Germany left a day early, complaining that they could not work. Madina was unapologetic. 'If we installed wifi,' she said, 'people would sit inside looking at screens, and the mountains would become wallpaper.' I sympathised, although I admit that on the second evening I walked up to a ridge, where one weak signal reaches, simply to check my messages. A night costs forty-five dollars per person, with all meals included, which strikes me as fair given the work involved.

The most interesting conversation was with Zarina, who handles the accounts. She told me that the lodge hardly makes a profit, because most of the income goes into the village school and into repairing footpaths damaged by spring floods. Requests for rooms arrive every week, and many people urge the sisters to expand. Zarina has refused so far. 'Twice as many cabins would mean twice as many visitors, and then we would stop being the place they came to find,' she said. She did mention one change: a greenhouse that will open next spring, so that the lodge can grow salad leaves in March, when the ground outside is still frozen.
options: By wood stoves burning fallen branches

items.prompt: How many hikers were in the group?
items.passage:
The alarm went off at a quarter to six, and by half past eight our group of thirteen hikers was standing at the foot of the Solheimajokull glacier in southern Iceland, adjusting the metal spikes, called crampons, that we had strapped to our boots. Our guide, a lean, softly spoken man named Gunnar Olafsson, checked every strap personally. 'Nobody walks on the ice without crampons,' he said, 'and nobody walks ahead of me, not even for a photograph.' I had expected a rather gentle stroll, but within ten minutes I understood why he was so strict: the surface was uneven, slippery and cut by narrow cracks that were hard to see.

The walk lasted about three hours, with a break for sandwiches beside a pool of astonishingly blue meltwater. Gunnar used the pause to explain what he has watched happen over fifteen years of guiding. When he started in 2011, the starting point for tours was a short walk from the car park; today it takes twenty minutes to reach the ice, because the glacier has retreated by roughly one kilometre. In some years it has shrunk by thirty metres in a single summer. He pointed to a pole on the hillside marking where the tongue of ice ended in 2005. It was now almost invisible against the grey rock far below us.

What interested me most was Gunnar's attitude. I had assumed that a guide who earns his living from glacier tourists would play down the problem, or at least avoid depressing his customers. Quite the opposite. He told us bluntly that the glacier would probably be too small for safe tours within a few decades, and that he sometimes feels like a doctor taking visitors to say goodbye to a patient. A Canadian woman in our group argued that this kind of 'last chance tourism' is hypocritical, since flying to Iceland adds to the very warming that melts the ice. Gunnar did not disagree. 'The flight is the biggest part of the problem,' he admitted, 'but I have noticed that people who touch the ice tend to become more careful about their choices than people who only read about it.'

I am still not sure who is right. Standing on the glacier, I felt something that statistics have never given me, and the following week I cancelled a planned weekend trip by plane. Yet I also know that one honest gesture does not offset a long-haul flight. On the walk back, Gunnar handed each of us a small bag and asked us to pick up any rubbish we saw; we collected almost nothing, which he said was the best result of the season so far.

items.prompt: What did the author do after the trip?
items.passage:
The alarm went off at a quarter to six, and by half past eight our group of thirteen hikers was standing at the foot of the Solheimajokull glacier in southern Iceland, adjusting the metal spikes, called crampons, that we had strapped to our boots. Our guide, a lean, softly spoken man named Gunnar Olafsson, checked every strap personally. 'Nobody walks on the ice without crampons,' he said, 'and nobody walks ahead of me, not even for a photograph.' I had expected a rather gentle stroll, but within ten minutes I understood why he was so strict: the surface was uneven, slippery and cut by narrow cracks that were hard to see.

The walk lasted about three hours, with a break for sandwiches beside a pool of astonishingly blue meltwater. Gunnar used the pause to explain what he has watched happen over fifteen years of guiding. When he started in 2011, the starting point for tours was a short walk from the car park; today it takes twenty minutes to reach the ice, because the glacier has retreated by roughly one kilometre. In some years it has shrunk by thirty metres in a single summer. He pointed to a pole on the hillside marking where the tongue of ice ended in 2005. items.prompt: How many plastic items did the author count in her flat on the first evening?
items.passage:
Last July, my friend Aziz bet me that I could not survive one month without buying anything wrapped in plastic. I accepted, mostly out of stubbornness, and I assumed the hardest part would be the kitchen. On the first evening I counted the plastic items in my flat and stopped at fifty-three, which included things I had never noticed: the lining of my coffee cups, the seals on tea bags, the tiny pieces of plastic in my chewing gum. I had always considered myself reasonably green because I recycled, but a little research showed that only a small fraction of the plastic collected in my city is actually turned into something new.

The first week was frustrating. The supermarket near my flat sells almost every vegetable in a plastic bag or tray, so I walked twenty minutes to the Chorsu bazaar, where I could buy tomatoes and cucumbers loose and put them in the cotton bags my grandmother had sewn years ago. Prices were lower there, which surprised me, although the shopping took roughly twice as long. Bread was easy, but cheese and yoghurt were nearly impossible, and I eventually learned to make yoghurt myself in a glass jar. The bathroom was a different story: I replaced shampoo with a solid bar and toothpaste with a tin of tablets, and I have to say that the tablets were awful.

By the third week I had a rhythm, yet an unexpected problem appeared. Friends began to treat my challenge as a performance. At a birthday dinner, a colleague named Kamola whispered that I was being a little extreme, and later that evening I found myself defending a plastic straw I had not even used. My brother Jasur was more direct. He argued that individual choices are almost meaningless when factories produce millions of tonnes of packaging each year, and that governments, not shoppers, should ban single-use plastic. I do not think he is entirely wrong, but I disagree that personal effort is pointless. When two neighbours asked where I bought my loose rice, I realised habits spread more quietly than laws do.

At the end of the month my household bin was lighter, though not empty: I had produced one small bag of plastic waste, mostly from medicine packaging, which I could not avoid. Aziz admitted I had won, and he paid for dinner. I will not keep every rule, because the tablets are going straight back to the shop. But I will continue buying vegetables at the bazaar, and I have promised to repeat the challenge next March, this time with Jasur as my partner, reluctant though he sounds.

I had always considered myself reasonably green because I recycled, but a little research showed that only a small fraction of the plastic collected in my city is actually turned into something new.

The first week was frustrating. The supermarket near my flat sells almost every vegetable in a plastic bag or tray, so I walked twenty minutes to the Chorsu bazaar, where I could buy tomatoes and cucumbers loose and put them in the cotton bags my grandmother had sewn years ago. Prices were lower there, which surprised me, although the shopping took roughly twice as long. Bread was easy, but cheese and yoghurt were nearly impossible, and I eventually learned to make yoghurt myself in a glass jar. The bathroom was a different story: I replaced shampoo with a solid bar and toothpaste with a tin of tablets, and I have to say that the tablets were awful.

By the third week I had a rhythm, yet an unexpected problem appeared. Friends began to treat my challenge as a performance. At a birthday dinner, a colleague named Kamola whispered that I was being a little extreme, and later that evening I found myself defending a plastic straw I had not even used. My brother Jasur was more direct. He argued that individual choices are almost meaningless when factories produce millions of tonnes of packaging each year, and that governments, not shoppers, should ban single-use plastic. I do not think he is entirely wrong, but I disagree that personal effort is pointless. When two neighbours asked where I bought my loose rice, I realised habits spread more quietly than laws do.

At the end of the month my household bin was lighter, though not empty: I had produced one small bag of plastic waste, mostly from medicine packaging, which I could not avoid. Aziz admitted I had won, and he paid for dinner. I will not keep every rule, because the tablets are going straight back to the shop. But I will continue buying vegetables at the bazaar, and I have promised to repeat the challenge next March, this time with Jasur as my partner, reluctant though he sounds.

items.prompt: When does Rustam recommend visiting Khiva?
items.passage:
If you ask Rustam Madrahimov what the best time to visit Khiva is, he will say early March or late October, and then he will give you a lecture on why July is a terrible idea. Rustam has guided visitors through the old walled town, Ichan Kala, for twenty-two years, and he speaks about its streets with the affection of someone describing a stubborn but loved relative. The walls, which are about two and a half kilometres long and in places ten metres high, were rebuilt many times in clay, which is why they appear to glow orange at sunset. In 1990 the inner town became one of the first sites in Central Asia to be recognised by UNESCO.

His tour begins at the western gate at eight o'clock, before the tour buses arrive, and he insists that guests walk in silence for the first few minutes. 'Look at the doors first,' he says. 'Each carved door tells you who lived behind it.' The visitors usually laugh, then notice that the patterns differ. He points to the unfinished Kalta Minor minaret, covered in turquoise tiles, and tells the story that it was meant to rise to about seventy metres before its patron died, leaving it only twenty-nine metres tall. Rustam finds the incomplete tower more moving than any finished one, because it shows how fragile ambition can be.

Yet he is not uncritical. He admits that the restoration of the nineteenth century buildings has been uneven, and he dislikes the way several former madrasas have been turned into souvenir shops, where guests can buy sheepskin hats before they have understood what the building was for. He accepts that the shops bring income to families who would otherwise leave for work in Russia or Korea, so he refuses to call them a disaster. 'I would not close them,' he says, 'but I would ask them to sell fewer cheap imports and more local silk and ceramics.' Only about two thousand people still live inside the walls, down from several times that number in the Soviet period, and he worries the town may become a beautiful stage set rather than a living neighbourhood.

At the end of the tour Rustam takes guests to a tea house on the roof of a family home, where they sit for as long as they wish. Hardly anyone leaves quickly. From there, he says, you can see the difference between a monument and a place: laundry hangs between the minarets, a boy practises football in an alley, and an old woman shouts across the roof at her neighbour. Next year, he plans to start a second route outside the walls, so that tourists spread out and the inner town can breathe.

items.prompt: How did Sardor feel during his first two weeks in Helsinki?
items.passage:
When Sardor Ismoilov landed in Helsinki in August 2024 to begin a master's degree, he felt confident. He had studied English for ten years, read about Finnish education for months and even learned to say good morning in Finnish. For the first fortnight everything delighted him: the clean air, the punctual trams, the university library that stayed open until midnight. He later described this stage as the honeymoon period, a phase that almost every expatriate experiences and few expect to end.

It ended around the third month. By November the daylight lasted barely six hours, and Sardor began to notice small things that irritated him out of proportion. In his home city of Namangan, a neighbour would knock on the door with a plate of food at least once a week; in Helsinki he lived for ten weeks next to a man whose name he never learned. People in the lift stared at the floor, and a classmate who had seemed friendly on Monday walked past him on Wednesday without a greeting. Sardor concluded that Finns were cold and uninterested in foreigners, and he phoned his mother twice a day, which he now describes as a mistake.

The turning point came from a Finnish tutor, Elina, who explained that silence in her culture is not rudeness but respect. 'If I leave you alone, I am saying that I trust you to manage,' she told him. Sardor admits he did not believe this at first. Yet when he joined a volleyball club that met on Thursday evenings, he noticed that team-mates who spoke little during the day shouted encouragement during matches and invited him to the sauna afterwards. 'It was a shock to be so naked among people I hardly knew,' he laughs, 'and it was also the day I understood them.'

Researchers who study the subject often point out that culture shock is rarely caused by dramatic differences such as food or religion, which people prepare for. It is the invisible habits, such as how close to stand, when to speak, or whether to make small talk, that cause the most stress, because nobody explains them. Sardor agrees, though he adds one qualification: he thinks the effort must come from both sides. Three months ago he began organising a monthly dinner where new students cook dishes from home and invite Finnish classmates. The first dinner attracted nine people, last month's attracted twenty-six, and Elina arrived early with a bag of rye bread.

items.prompt: How are the Maasai families paid?
items.answer: A monthly payment, if they limit cattle and tourist beds
items.passage:
At five-thirty on a cold July morning, ranger Wanjiru Kamau was already scanning the grass near the Mara River with binoculars, listening to the radio for news of the lions. Wanjiru works in a private conservancy next to the Maasai Mara National Reserve in Kenya, and she is quick to point out that the difference between the two is more than a fence. In the national reserve, visitors pay a fee to the government and minibuses often crowd around a single animal. In the conservancy, the land is leased from around eight hundred Maasai families, who receive a monthly payment as long as they limit the number of cattle and tourist beds on their land.

The rules sound strict. No more than five vehicles may approach an animal at once, nobody may leave the car except at designated spots, and night drives are allowed only for guests staying inside the conservancy. A visit costs about three times as much as in the national reserve, which Wanjiru defends without embarrassment. 'You can pay a smaller price and see fifty cars around a leopard,' she says, 'or you can pay more and see the leopard.' Not every guest agrees. A Spanish family I met at breakfast complained that the price seemed unreasonable, though they admitted that their children had watched a lioness teach her cubs to hunt for forty minutes without a single other vehicle in sight.

The results are visible. According to the conservancy's records, the number of lions has risen from nine to fourteen over the past decade, and cheetah sightings, once rare, now happen weekly. Wanjiru credits the improvement to something other than tourism alone. Because families are paid to share land, young Maasai men have stopped hunting lions in revenge for lost cattle, and instead several of them train as trackers who warn herders when predators approach. She herself grew up three villages away and spent her childhood being told to fear lions; now she earns a salary studying them.

Still, she refuses to describe the model as perfect. Droughts push cattle toward the protected grass, and during the last dry season, nearly four hundred animals were found grazing illegally inside the boundary. Elephants occasionally destroy crops, and compensation can take months to arrive. 'A conservancy works only while people believe they are winning,' she says, 'and belief is easier to lose than lions.' As we drove back at dusk, a cheetah crossed the track ahead of us, and the guide switched off the engine. For a minute, nobody spoke.

A monthly payment, if they limit cattle and tourist beds
A share of the government's fee

items.prompt: Why did the narrator join the tour?
items.passage:
I am normally suspicious of organised food tours, so when my cousin Farrukh insisted I join one during my week in Mexico City, I agreed only because he had already paid. The tour began at six in the evening outside a metro station in the Roma district, and our guide, a cheerful university lecturer named Lucia Herrera, announced that we would be eating at six stalls over four hours. 'Nobody should leave hungry,' she said, 'and nobody should leave without learning something.' The price was thirty-five dollars, which seemed expensive until I realised how much food it included.

Our first stop was a woman selling tamales from a steaming metal pot on the pavement. Lucia explained that tamales, parcels of corn dough cooked in leaves, are older than the Spanish arrival, and that the dish changes completely every few streets depending on the filling. I chose one with green sauce and chicken, and my cousin chose sweet pineapple. Both were better than anything I had eaten in the restaurants where I had spent the previous three evenings. Our second stop was a taco stand, where a man sliced pork from a spinning cone of meat with the speed of a surgeon. Lucia reminded us that Mexicans do not eat hard, crunchy shells; those are an invention of restaurants abroad.

Many of the guests, including me, had arrived afraid of getting ill. A nervous Australian man asked whether street food was safe, and Lucia answered with a surprising argument. In her experience, stomachs suffer more from buffets, where food sits for hours at an unsafe temperature, than from stalls where meat is cooked in front of the customer. 'Watch for a queue of local people,' she advised. 'A long queue means fresh food and a cook who cannot afford to disappoint.' I noticed that the busiest stalls were indeed the cleanest, and none of our group of eleven was ill the following day, although one vegetarian, Madina, found that most of the stops offered her little more than beans and cheese.

The final stop was the most memorable: a tiny cart selling churros dipped in thick chocolate, which we ate sitting on a kerb at ten o'clock while a street musician played accordion. I had begun the evening as a sceptic. By the end, I was convinced that the best way to understand a city is not through its monuments but through what its people eat standing up. Farrukh smiled and said he had been right all along. I conceded the point, on the condition that he pay for tomorrow's lunch as well.

items.passage:
In the town of Rishtan, in the Fergana Valley, the family workshop of master potter Abdulaziz Yusupov stands behind a plain blue gate that visitors often walk past. Inside, six people sit among shelves of drying plates, each decorated with the deep turquoise and cobalt patterns for which the region has been famous for roughly eight hundred years. Abdulaziz belongs to the seventh generation of his family to work with clay, and he is quick to say that the secret of Rishtan ceramics is not a technique but a combination of ingredients. The local red clay is unusually fine, and the glaze is made from ishkor, a plant ash gathered from desert shrubs, which produces the characteristic glossy blue when fired.

A large ceremonial plate takes about three weeks to make, because the clay must dry slowly, then be fired twice, with a pause for painting in between. Rushing any stage, Abdulaziz says, produces cracks that appear only when a customer takes the plate home. He once threw away an entire kiln load of forty pieces because the temperature rose too quickly. 'Money is not the only thing you lose,' he told me. 'You lose a week of other people's trust.' Customers come from as far as Japan and Germany, and a few ask him to explain each pattern. A pomegranate means abundance, he says, while a moon shape represents the passing of time.

The business, however, has not been easy. During the 1970s, factories supplied cheap, uniform plates to every household, and demand for handmade work almost disappeared. Abdulaziz's grandfather kept the workshop alive by repairing broken dishes. Today the opposite problem exists: tourists want souvenirs, but many look for the lowest price, and machine-made copies imported from other countries now sell in the capital for a quarter of what a handmade piece costs. Abdulaziz does not blame buyers entirely. He argues that most people cannot tell the difference unless someone shows them, which is why he insists that every visitor tries throwing a bowl on the wheel for ten minutes. 'After that,' he laughs, 'they stop asking why it costs so much.'

The future of the craft depends on young people, and the master is cautiously hopeful. Four years ago, only his own son was learning the trade; now there are five apprentices, including a fourteen-year-old girl named Sevara, who arrives after school each afternoon. The workshop does not pay high wages, but it offers something many jobs cannot: skill that cannot be replaced by a machine. Abdulaziz hopes to build a small school next to the workshop within three years, funded partly by visitors. Whether tradition survives, he suggests, will depend less on pride than on whether a young person can earn a decent living from it.
options: A glaze made from plant ash

topic: Overtourism in a historic city, A desert expedition, Climate and farming in the Fergana Valley, ...
title: O'qish 24
intro: Har bir matnni diqqat bilan o'qing va uning savollariga javob bering.

items.prompt: How many permanent residents live inside the walls?
items.passage:
Few cities illustrate the problem of overtourism as clearly as Dubrovnik. Inside its medieval walls live barely one thousand five hundred permanent residents, yet on the busiest summer days the narrow streets can receive eight thousand cruise passengers within a few hours. A resident I spoke to, a retired teacher named Ivana, described walking to the bakery as swimming against a river of selfie sticks. When her neighbours sold their apartments to investors who rented them to visitors, the building lost its grocery shop, then its pharmacy, and finally its sense of being a community.

Defenders of mass tourism make a reasonable argument. Tourism supplies roughly a quarter of the country's income, and thousands of families depend on guesthouses, restaurants and taxis. Ivana's own nephew, who drives a boat to the nearby islands, earns three times what he would in a factory. It is easy for commentators in wealthy countries to criticise crowds, she says, but harder to ask a young person to refuse a job. The question, she believes, is not whether tourists should come, but how many, when, and who benefits.

Dubrovnik has already tried several measures. In 2019 the city introduced cameras to count visitors on the main street, and in 2023 it banned souvenir stalls from the old town. Neither measure changed much. A more ambitious rule, limiting cruise ships to two per day, was approved by the council last year and will take effect only in 2028, after lengthy negotiations with the port authority. Critics doubt it will work, pointing out that a cruise passenger spends on average far less in the city than someone who stays three nights, so reducing the number of ships might actually raise the income per visitor. Supporters respond that fewer ships would also reduce pollution in the harbour.

Having spent a week there, I am convinced that no single policy can solve the problem. A tourist tax would raise money, but it would not reduce the crowds at noon. A strict cap would protect the old town but might push prices up and exclude ordinary families. The most promising idea may be the least dramatic: spreading visitors across the day and across the region, so that guests arrive at seven in the morning or at six in the evening, and so that smaller towns share the benefits. Ivana was sceptical when I mentioned this. 'Everyone agrees with that,' she said, 'until the day it costs them money.' I think she is right to be cautious, but I would still rather attempt a flawed solution than keep repeating the same photograph.

items.prompt: Why did they choose April for the expedition?
items.passage:
The Kyzylkum Desert looks flat and empty on a map, which is precisely why my friend Olimjon, a geography teacher, and I decided to cross a section of it on foot in April. We were joined by a guide called Bobur and two camels that carried our water. The plan was to walk for five days, covering about twenty-two kilometres each day, from a dried well near Nurota to a village on the edge of the dunes. We chose April because the daytime temperature is tolerable, around thirty degrees, whereas in July it regularly passes forty-five. What we did not take into account was how cold the nights would be.

On the first evening the temperature fell to four degrees, and I discovered that my sleeping bag, which I had bought for a summer festival, was totally inadequate. Bobur, who had said little all day, handed me a thick wool blanket without comment. That was typical of him. He woke us at four every morning so that we could walk through the cool hours, rest from eleven until around three, and walk again until sunset. Each of us carried six litres of water, and the camels carried forty more for emergencies. Bobur forbade us to drink more than two sips at a time, arguing that drinking small amounts often keeps the body cooler than occasional gulps.

The landscape surprised me more than the hardship. I had expected sand everywhere, but the desert was mainly hard clay covered with low shrubs, and on the third day we crossed a field of tiny yellow flowers that had appeared after the spring rain and would be gone within ten days. Bobur read the ground as other people read books. He identified a fox's tracks, a beetle's path and, to our amazement, a distant well that was invisible to us, simply by watching where birds flew at dawn. Olimjon, who had studied maps for years, was humbled. 'I know where everything is,' he admitted, 'but Bobur knows what everything means.'

Not everything went smoothly. On the fourth day I made a mistake that almost ruined the trip: I assumed the water was sufficient and refused to refill my bottle at a well, thinking we would soon reach the village. We did not; the shortcut took two additional hours, and by the time we arrived I was dizzy and silent. Bobur said nothing, but he poured water into my hands and watched me drink. I have rarely felt so foolish, or so grateful. The experience taught me that confidence is dangerous in a desert, where an estimate that is wrong by an hour can become a serious problem. Olimjon now keeps a photograph of those yellow flowers on his classroom wall, and tells his students that the desert is not empty, only quiet.

items.prompt: How has spring changed on Gulnora's farm?
items.answer: It arrives about three weeks earlier
items.passage:
Gulnora Tursunova has farmed eight hectares near Margilan for twenty-six years, and she claims she can predict the weather by smelling the air before dawn. Lately, her predictions have failed. Spring now arrives three weeks earlier than it did when her father ran the farm, and the glaciers in the mountains that feed the region's rivers are shrinking, which means that irrigation water arrives in a rush in early summer and then thins out just when the crops need it most. 'The sky is not lying,' she says, 'but it has changed its language.'

Two years ago, a dry July destroyed almost a third of her tomato crop. Rather than blame the weather, Gulnora decided to change her methods. She replaced flood irrigation, in which water simply runs between the rows, with drip lines that deliver water directly to the roots. The system cost about four thousand dollars, a sum she borrowed from a cooperative at low interest, and several neighbours told her she was wasting money. The results were difficult to argue with: she now uses roughly half as much water, and her yield per hectare rose by almost a fifth. She has also begun planting a variety of wheat bred to withstand heat, and she keeps a small field of cotton only because her family has always grown it, not because it is profitable.

Experts caution that such success stories are not simple to repeat. Drip irrigation requires clean water, because the narrow tubes block easily, and farmers must buy spare parts that are not always available locally. Dr. Nodira Alimova, an agricultural economist at Tashkent University, argues that technology alone is insufficient. In her opinion, the larger problem is the price of water, which in many regions is almost free; as long as it costs nothing, there is little reason to save it. She suggests that governments should charge for water use but compensate small farmers, so that those who save the most benefit the most. Gulnora, who is wary of officials, agrees with the principle but doubts the compensation would ever reach her.

Interestingly, Gulnora's neighbours have begun to change their minds. Last autumn, five of them asked for a tour of her fields, and three have since ordered their own drip lines. She is delighted, though she admits a certain pride she does not try to hide. She now teaches a short course for local women every Saturday, in which she explains how to check the soil with a handful of earth rather than a gadget. 'Farming has always been about guessing correctly,' she says. 'Now we have to guess faster, and share what we learn.'
options: It arrives about three weeks later
It arrives about three weeks earlier

Gulnora Tursunova has farmed eight hectares near Margilan for twenty-six years, and she claims she can predict the weather by smelling the air before dawn. Lately, her predictions have failed. Spring now arrives three weeks earlier than it did when her father ran the farm, and the glaciers in the mountains that feed the region's rivers are shrinking, which means that irrigation water arrives in a rush in early summer and then thins out just when the crops need it most. 'The sky is not lying,' she says, 'but it has changed its language.'

Two years ago, a dry July destroyed almost a third of her tomato crop. Rather than blame the weather, Gulnora decided to change her methods. She replaced flood irrigation, in which water simply runs between the rows, with drip lines that deliver water directly to the roots. The system cost about four thousand dollars, a sum she borrowed from a cooperative at low interest, and several neighbours told her she was wasting money. items.prompt: How did the festival begin?
items.answer: As a prayer to end an epidemic
items.passage:
I had read about the Gion Matsuri, Kyoto's month-long festival in July, long before I booked my flight, but nothing prepared me for the sheer scale of it. The festival, which has been held for more than eleven hundred years, began as a prayer to end an epidemic, and its most famous moments are two processions of enormous wooden floats, a grand one on the seventeenth of July and a smaller one on the twenty-fourth. I arrived on the fifteenth, on the evening known as Yoiyama, when traffic is banned from the central streets and thousands of people wander between the floats under paper lanterns.

My host, a retired schoolteacher named Haruko, warned me not to behave like a typical tourist. 'Do not touch the floats,' she said, 'and above all, do not walk away from a conversation just to take a picture.' I soon saw why. The floats, some of which weigh as much as twelve tonnes and stand taller than a two-storey house, are built without a single nail; the beams are tied together with rope, using knots that are taught from father to son. Each float belongs to a neighbourhood, and the families who own them treat visitors as guests rather than customers. On the second evening, a man invited me inside a merchant's house to see a screen painted two hundred years ago, and refused to accept any payment.

On the day of the main procession, I made a mistake that I will remember for a long time. I assumed that the best place to watch was the front row, so I arrived at six in the morning and stood in the hot sun for four hours. Haruko laughed when I told her. Local people, she explained, never stand at the corners; they watch from the shaded side streets, where the floats pause and turn, and where the men pulling them shout at each other to coordinate. I moved to such a street the following week and saw the smaller procession properly, with a cold barley tea in my hand.

I left Kyoto with mixed feelings. The festival is undeniably beautiful, yet I could not ignore how crowded it has become. According to Haruko, more than a million visitors come during the main days, and some residents now leave the city to avoid them. She is not bitter; she believes that a festival that stops being shared would soon be forgotten. Still, she hopes visitors will behave better. 'We do not want a quieter festival,' she said when I thanked her. 'We want a more thoughtful one.' I think of those words whenever I visit a place whose traditions are older than my country's borders.
options: As a prayer to end an epidemic

items.prompt: Why did the narrator choose the train?
items.answer: He wanted to see the distance
items.passage:
The train from Tashkent to Almaty is not fast, and I chose it for exactly that reason. After years of flying between Central Asian capitals in ninety minutes and arriving with no sense of having travelled, I wanted to see the distance. The journey takes about twenty hours, though the timetable promises nineteen, and my second-class compartment held four berths, two of which were occupied by a retired engineer, Mr Sultanbekov, and his granddaughter Aigerim, a nine-year-old with an extraordinary appetite for questions.

The first four hours were spent crossing the irrigated plains south of the Syr Darya, a landscape of cotton fields and straight canals that, from the window, resembled a green and brown chessboard. Mr Sultanbekov spread a cloth across the table and unpacked boiled eggs, flatbread, cucumbers and a jar of apricot jam, insisting that I join them. I had brought sandwiches, but it would have been rude to refuse. The tea, served by the carriage attendant from a huge samovar, cost the equivalent of one dollar for five glasses, and she refilled them whenever the conversation grew lively.

The border crossing was less romantic. At about two in the morning, the train stopped for almost three hours, officials in uniform entered every compartment, and Aigerim, who had been asleep, woke up and announced that she was not afraid of anything. Mr Sultanbekov smiled and said that he had made this journey in 1985 and again in 2004; the first time, he recalled, the border did not exist, and the second time it took six hours. Whether the delay is shorter or longer now depends, he said, on the mood of the officers and the age of the paperwork. I found his patience contagious.

By morning we were crossing the steppe of southern Kazakhstan, a vast, flat landscape of grass and distant mountains whose snow glowed pink. I realised that I had hardly looked at my phone since leaving Tashkent. Some travellers, I know, regard the train as a waste of time, and I understand their position: a flight would have cost less than a hundred dollars and saved a full day. Yet I would argue that the day was not lost. I had spoken to two strangers, read half a novel, and watched the continent change colour. When we arrived in Almaty two hours behind schedule, Aigerim hugged me and gave me her drawing of the train, which now hangs above my desk. I do not expect to travel this way every year, but I know I shall do it again.
options: He wanted to see the distance

items.prompt: Why did Marta want to learn Russian?
items.answer: She had an internship in Warsaw
items.passage:
When Nigora Yusupova, a twenty-three-year-old economics graduate from Samarkand, booked a six-week language exchange trip to Salamanca last summer, she expected to improve her Spanish. She did not expect to discover how much she did not know about her own language. The programme paired each foreign student with a local volunteer, and Nigora's partner was Marta, a bright, impatient law student who wanted to learn Russian before an internship in Warsaw. They agreed on a simple rule: thirty minutes in Spanish, thirty minutes in Russian, and no switching to English, even when the conversation became difficult.

The first week was exhausting. Nigora's school Spanish was grammatically accurate but painfully slow, and she often searched for words while Marta waited with polite silence. She was also startled by how fast people spoke in the bars and markets. 'They do not pronounce the ends of words,' she complained, 'and nobody warned me.' Yet she found that Marta's correction style helped more than any textbook. Instead of stopping her at every error, Marta noted the mistakes in a small notebook and discussed only the three most important ones at the end. On the fourth day, Nigora announced proudly to a room of amused strangers that she was embarazada, meaning embarrassed. In Spanish, the word means pregnant.

The most valuable lessons, however, were cultural. Nigora had assumed that being direct was impolite, as it often is at home, and she softened every request with long apologies. Marta found this endearing but confusing. In Spain, she explained, a short question is not rude; it is efficient. Meanwhile, teaching Russian forced Marta to ask Nigora why verbs behave as they do, and Nigora, who had never studied grammar formally, struggled to explain. By the fifth week, she was buying a Russian grammar book for herself, laughing that she had come to Spain to study Russian.

Nigora is convinced that immersion works faster than classroom study, but only under one condition: that learners avoid spending time with compatriots. Five of the nine students in her group, she noticed, ate every meal together and spoke Russian or Uzbek all evening. Their progress, she says, was visibly slower. When she left in August, she and Marta promised to continue their weekly calls, and Marta sent her a tiny notebook, identical to her own, with a single sentence on the first page: 'Your mistakes are my favourite part of your Spanish.' Nigora plans to return next year, and this time she hopes to bring a friend who will agree to sit at a different table.
options: She had an internship in Warsaw

When Nigora Yusupova, a twenty-three-year-old economics graduate from Samarkand, booked a six-week language exchange trip to Salamanca last summer, she expected to improve her Spanish. She did not expect to discover how much she did not know about her own language. The programme paired each foreign student with a local volunteer, and Nigora's partner was Marta, a bright, impatient law student who wanted to learn Russian before an internship in Warsaw. They agreed on a simple rule: thirty minutes in Spanish, thirty minutes in Russian, and no switching to English, even when the conversation became difficult.

The first week was exhausting. Nigora's school Spanish was grammatically accurate but painfully slow, and she often searched for words while Marta waited with polite silence. She was also startled by how fast people spoke in the bars and markets. 'They do not pronounce the ends of words,' she complained, 'and nobody warned me.' Yet she found that Marta's correction style helped more than any textbook. Instead of stopping her at every error, Marta noted the mistakes in a small notebook and discussed only the three most important ones at the end. On the fourth day, Nigora announced proudly to a room of amused strangers that she was embarazada, meaning embarrassed. In Spanish, the word means pregnant.

The most valuable lessons, however, were cultural. Nigora had assumed that being direct was impolite, as it often is at home, and she softened every request with long apologies. Marta found this endearing but confusing. In Spain, she explained, a short question is not rude; it is efficient. Meanwhile, teaching Russian forced Marta to ask Nigora why verbs behave as they do, and Nigora, who had never studied grammar formally, struggled to explain. By the fifth week, she was buying a Russian grammar book for herself, laughing that she had come to Spain to study Russian.

Nigora is convinced that immersion works faster than classroom study, but only under one condition: that learners avoid spending time with compatriots. Five of the nine students in her group, she noticed, ate every meal together and spoke Russian or Uzbek all evening. Their progress, she says, was visibly slower. When she left in August, she and Marta promised to continue their weekly calls, and Marta sent her a tiny notebook, identical to her own, with a single sentence on the first page: 'Your mistakes are my favourite part of your Spanish.' Nigora plans to return next year, and this time she hopes to bring a friend who will agree to sit at a different table.

Requests should always include an apology

items.prompt: What surprised Dilnoza most about her first term?
items.passage:
Dilnoza Karimova left Samarkand for Manchester in September, expecting that three years of studying civil engineering abroad would be the hardest challenge of her life. Looking back after her first term, she admits that the academic work was not the problem at all. Her English had been good enough to pass the entrance test with a comfortable score of 6.5, and she had always been the kind of student who finished assignments well before the deadline. What really surprised her was how lonely the first weeks felt, even though she was surrounded by thousands of people.

The university had arranged a welcome week, but Dilnoza found the crowded parties exhausting and left early on the second night. Her flatmates, a Nigerian medical student and two British first-years, were friendly but spent most evenings out. It was only when she joined the university's cycling club, almost by accident, that things began to change. She had never owned a bicycle in Uzbekistan, and she describes her first ride, which lasted only forty minutes, as the most embarrassing experience of the term. Nevertheless, the other members were patient, and by November she was joining the Saturday trips of around thirty kilometres.

Money was another worry. Her parents pay the tuition fees, which amount to nearly fifteen thousand pounds a year, but she is responsible for her own rent and food. A friend advised her to look for a part-time job, yet her student visa allows her to work no more than twenty hours a week during term, so she chose a modest eight hours in the library. The wages are low, but she says the real benefit is that colleagues correct her pronunciation without making her feel foolish.

Although she misses her family terribly, Dilnoza does not regret her decision. She phones her mother every Sunday, and they usually talk for an hour, mostly about food. Her younger brother has recently announced that he wants to study in Germany, which she finds both flattering and slightly worrying, since she knows how many difficulties he will face. Her advice to him is simple: do not expect the country to adapt to you. Learn the small habits, such as queueing politely and saying thank you to the bus driver, and the big problems will become much easier to solve.

If she could change one thing, she says, it would be her arrival date. She came only two days before lectures began, so she had no time to recover from the journey, find the shops or understand the bus system. Next year, she plans to arrive at least a fortnight early, and she is already encouraging new students from Samarkand to do the same.
options: How difficult the engineering course was
How low her English test score was
