items.prompt: Why had Harriet avoided looking at her loan figure for years?
items.answer: Her father's warnings made it unpleasant to think about
items.passage:
When Harriet Bellamy graduated from a university in Leeds, she owed the government a little over twenty-seven thousand pounds. For years she had avoided looking at the figure, partly because her father, who had paid for his own degree with a summer job in a factory, kept describing student loans as a mortgage on your future. Harriet now thinks that description is misleading, though she admits she did not understand the system when she signed the forms at eighteen.

The first surprise was that repayments do not begin immediately after graduation. They start in the April following the course, and only if the graduate earns more than twenty-five thousand pounds a year. Anyone earning less pays nothing, however large the original loan was. Above that threshold, the borrower pays nine per cent of the extra income, so Harriet, who earns thirty-one thousand pounds as a marketing assistant, hands over only about forty-five pounds a month. She points out that this amount is deducted automatically from her salary, so she never feels it as a separate bill.

The second surprise concerned interest. Harriet had assumed that the balance would shrink slowly each month. In reality, interest is added so quickly that someone on her salary will probably never reduce the original sum. Whatever remains is cancelled after thirty years. Critics call this unfair because it means most graduates will be paying for three decades, and Harriet partly agrees. Nevertheless, she argues that the system behaves more like a graduate tax than like a normal debt, because the payments rise and fall with income and disappear if she loses her job.

Her brother Tom is less relaxed. He is studying medicine, a course that lasts five years, so his loan will be considerably larger than hers, and he fears that it will make it harder to obtain a mortgage. Harriet has tried to reassure him by explaining that lenders only look at the monthly deduction, not at the total, but he remains unconvinced. Their father, meanwhile, has offered to pay off part of Tom's loan from his retirement savings, an idea both children have firmly rejected. Harriet believes it would be a waste, because the extra money would simply be cancelled anyway if Tom never earns enough to clear the balance.

Looking ahead, Harriet's main concern is not the loan itself but the choice between saving and repaying early. A colleague recently suggested she should make voluntary payments, but she decided against it. She would rather put the same money into a savings account for a deposit on a flat, which she hopes to buy before she turns thirty.
options: She had already repaid most of it
Her father's warnings made it unpleasant to think about
The government had never sent her a statement

items.prompt: How long did Kamila's search for a flat take?
items.passage:
Kamila Yusupova was twenty-four when she finally decided to leave her parents' house in Tashkent and rent a flat of her own, and she is now the first to say that she underestimated almost everything. She had imagined a pleasant weekend of looking at bright rooms, shaking hands with friendly landlords and signing a contract by Monday. Instead, the search took nearly six weeks, and she viewed nine flats before choosing one.

The first flat she saw looked perfect in the photographs. In reality, there was a dark patch of damp above the bed, which the owner described as just a little condensation. Kamila, who had been warned by an older cousin to trust her nose rather than the advertisement, said no politely and left. The fourth flat was cheap but so far from her office that the journey would have taken ninety minutes each way. The seventh was close to the metro, yet the landlord insisted on a contract of three years, which she considered far too long for someone who might change jobs.

The flat she eventually chose belongs to a retired engineer called Mr Okafor, who lives abroad and manages everything through his sister. The rent is four hundred and fifty dollars a month, and utilities are not included, something she only noticed after reading the contract twice. She also paid a deposit equal to one month's rent, which the owner promised to return at the end of the year if nothing was damaged. Her friend Jonas, who works as a nurse, shares the flat and pays half.

Looking back, Kamila believes her biggest mistake was not photographing the flat on the day she moved in. A month later, she noticed a long scratch on the kitchen table and a loose door handle in the bathroom, and she spent an anxious evening wondering whether she would be blamed. Fortunately, Mr Okafor's sister was understanding, but Kamila has since learned that many tenants lose a large part of their deposit for exactly this reason. She now advises friends to write a detailed list of every defect and send it to the owner by message so that there is a record.

The other lesson was about money. Her salary of nine hundred dollars a month seemed generous until she added rent, electricity, internet and food. After the first month, she had only forty dollars left for everything else. She has therefore started to cook at home rather than eating out, and she has cancelled a gym membership she hardly ever used. Despite the stress, she would not return to her parents' house. She says the feeling of unlocking her own door every evening is worth every complicated negotiation.

items.prompt: Why was the wedding postponed?
items.answer: The real cost was far higher than expected
items.passage:
Rustam Tursunov and Malika Hamidova had originally planned to get married last spring, but the date has now been moved to the second Saturday of next June. The reason was not a quarrel or a change of heart, as some relatives rather eagerly suggested, but a spreadsheet. When the couple finally wrote down every expected expense, the total came to just over twelve thousand dollars, almost double what they had imagined, and they realised that their savings were nowhere near enough.

At the beginning, both families wanted a traditional celebration with three hundred guests. Malika's grandmother, in particular, insisted that leaving out a distant cousin would cause lasting offence. Rustam, who works as a software tester, preferred a smaller gathering, arguing that he would rather spend money on the first year of their marriage than on a single evening. After several tense dinners, they agreed on a guest list of one hundred and fifty, which saved them roughly three thousand dollars in food alone.

They have so far saved five thousand dollars, mostly by transferring a fixed amount on the day they are paid. Malika, who teaches primary school, also gives private lessons on Saturday mornings, and every cent of that income goes into the wedding account. Rustam sold his motorbike, something he describes as painful, but not as painful as borrowing from a bank. Both of them are firmly against taking a loan for a party, although they admit it would have been the easiest way to keep the original date.

Their biggest disagreement concerned a generous offer from Rustam's uncle, who said he would pay for the whole venue. Malika was tempted, but Rustam eventually persuaded her to refuse. His reasoning was that gifts of that size often come with expectations, such as choosing the uncle's favourite restaurant or inviting his business friends. In the end, they accepted a smaller present, a photographer, from Malika's aunt, which seemed harmless.

The couple have also cut several items that once seemed essential. They will not hire a live band, and the flowers will come from the garden of Malika's parents rather than a florist. Rustam admits that he was disappointed at first, yet he now thinks the changes have made the project feel more personal. The only luxury they have kept is a two-night stay in a mountain hotel after the ceremony, which they booked early at a discount.

Asked what advice they would give other couples, Malika laughs and says that nobody should ever believe the first estimate. Rustam is more serious: talk about money before the invitations are printed, not after.
options: The couple quarrelled with their families
The real cost was far higher than expected

When the couple finally wrote down every expected expense, the total came to just over twelve thousand dollars, almost double what they had imagined, and they realised that their savings were nowhere near enough.

At the beginning, both families wanted a traditional celebration with three hundred guests. Malika's grandmother, in particular, insisted that leaving out a distant cousin would cause lasting offence. Rustam, who works as a software tester, preferred a smaller gathering, arguing that he would rather spend money on the first year of their marriage than on a single evening. After several tense dinners, they agreed on a guest list of one hundred and fifty, which saved them roughly three thousand dollars in food alone.

They have so far saved five thousand dollars, mostly by transferring a fixed amount on the day they are paid. Malika, who teaches primary school, also gives private lessons on Saturday mornings, and every cent of that income goes into the wedding account. Rustam sold his motorbike, something he describes as painful, but not as painful as borrowing from a bank. Both of them are firmly against taking a loan for a party, although they admit it would have been the easiest way to keep the original date.

Their biggest disagreement concerned a generous offer from Rustam's uncle, who said he would pay for the whole venue. Malika was tempted, but Rustam eventually persuaded her to refuse. His reasoning was that gifts of that size often come with expectations, such as choosing the uncle's favourite restaurant or inviting his business friends. In the end, they accepted a smaller present, a photographer, from Malika's aunt, which seemed harmless.

The couple have also cut several items that once seemed essential. They will not hire a live band, and the flowers will come from the garden of Malika's parents rather than a florist. Rustam admits that he was disappointed at first, yet he now thinks the changes have made the project feel more personal. The only luxury they have kept is a two-night stay in a mountain hotel after the ceremony, which they booked early at a discount.

Asked what advice they would give other couples, Malika laughs and says that nobody should ever believe the first estimate. Rustam is more serious: talk about money before the invitations are printed, not after.

items.prompt: What was Joanna's attitude to the mentoring scheme at first?
items.passage:
Joanna Reyes was twenty-six, three years into her first job at an architecture firm in Manchester, when her manager suggested that she should be paired with a mentor. She was suspicious. In her experience, mentoring schemes consisted of awkward lunches and vague promises, and she had a great deal of real work waiting on her desk. Nevertheless, she agreed, and she now regards that decision as one of the most important of her career.

Her mentor was Mr Hassan, a senior partner who had been designing hospitals for almost thirty years. They met on the first Thursday of every month, always for exactly one hour, and always in his small office rather than in a restaurant. At first, Joanna was frustrated, because Mr Hassan almost never gave a direct answer. When she asked whether she should apply for a promotion, he replied by asking what she hoped to learn in the new role. When she complained that a colleague was taking credit for her ideas, he asked what she had already done about it. She left the early meetings feeling that she had learned nothing.

The turning point came about eighteen months later, when Joanna nearly resigned. A major project had been taken away from her after a disagreement with a client, and she felt humiliated. She arrived at the Thursday meeting with her letter of resignation in her bag, expecting sympathy. Instead, Mr Hassan listened without interrupting for twenty minutes and then asked a single question: what would she advise a younger colleague in exactly her position? Joanna says that she sat in silence for almost a minute before admitting that she would tell the colleague to stay and learn from the mistake. She never handed in the letter.

Over time, she came to understand his method. By refusing to give instructions, he forced her to examine her own reasoning, and the solutions she found herself were far easier to carry out than any advice he could have offered. She also noticed that he never criticised other people in front of her, a habit she has deliberately copied. Hardly anyone in the firm knew that he had been rejected by three universities before he was finally accepted onto an architecture course.

Three years after they first met, Mr Hassan retired, and Joanna was promoted to project leader. She now mentors two junior architects, and she is trying to resist the temptation to hand out quick answers. Her first mentee, a talkative young man called Ilyas, complained after two meetings that she was being unhelpful. Joanna smiled and asked him what he thought a good mentor should do. She admits it was the most satisfying moment of her week.
options: Indifferent because she had no work

items.prompt: What did the twins do at eighteen?
items.passage:
Callum and Ethan Pritchard are identical twins, and for most of their childhood they were treated as a single unit. At eighteen, however, they made opposite decisions. Callum went to university to study business, while Ethan, to the surprise of his teachers, chose a four-year apprenticeship at an engineering company near Sheffield. Now, five years later, they sometimes argue about whose choice was wiser, and the truth is that neither of them can answer that question with any confidence.

On paper, Ethan was ahead from the start. His employer paid him around eighteen thousand pounds a year from the first month, and the company covered the cost of his training. By twenty-one, he had a recognised qualification, a driving licence funded partly by his salary and no debt at all. Callum, meanwhile, was living in a shared house in Bristol and eating an enormous quantity of pasta. His course fees were financed by a loan, and the part-time job in a bar earned him only enough to pay the rent.

Yet the picture is not as simple as it appears. Callum's degree opened doors that were firmly closed to his brother, at least at first. He was offered a graduate position in a consultancy, with a starting salary of thirty thousand pounds, and within two years he had been promoted. Ethan, though skilled, discovered that many senior roles in his sector asked for a degree, which he now has to complete in the evenings, at his own expense. He describes this as the hidden cost of the apprenticeship route, a cost nobody had mentioned at the careers fair.

The twins also disagree about the less measurable benefits. Callum insists that university taught him to argue, to question assumptions and to work with people he would never have met otherwise. Ethan counters that his workplace gave him the same things, together with something university could not: the discipline of being responsible for expensive equipment from the age of eighteen. He also points out that several of Callum's friends have graduated without finding any job in their field.

Their mother, who has listened patiently to this debate for years, believes that both of them are exaggerating. In her view, the quality of the particular course or employer matters far more than the type of path. She has seen a talented nephew waste three years on a poor degree, and a careless neighbour's son fail to finish an excellent apprenticeship. What counts, she says, is the willingness to learn, not the name of the institution.

The twins have at least agreed on one point. If either of them has children, they will encourage them to visit at least five workplaces and five universities before deciding anything.

items.prompt: Where did the argument begin?
items.passage:
It began over a Sunday lunch in Bukhara, when Gulnara Ismoilova's younger brother Sardor announced that he needed twenty thousand dollars to open a small furniture workshop. Their parents, who had been quietly saving for almost twenty years, immediately said they would help. Gulnara, who works as an accountant in Tashkent and had come home for the weekend, put down her fork and said, rather too sharply, that she thought it was a bad idea. The meal ended in silence, and the family has not fully recovered even now.

Her objections were practical rather than personal. Their father retired two years ago, and his pension is barely enough to cover the monthly bills. The savings, in her view, are not a business fund but a safety net for medical emergencies. She also remembered that Sardor had already started two other ventures, a bicycle repair shop and a coffee stall, and abandoned both within a year. She reminded him of this, which, as she now admits, was the wrong thing to say at the wrong moment.

Sardor felt humiliated. He argued that carpentry was the one thing he had always been good at, and that a workshop was an entirely different project from the previous attempts. He also pointed out that Gulnara had received money from their parents at the time of her wedding, a fact she had somewhat conveniently forgotten. This was true, though the sum had been smaller, around four thousand dollars, and she had repaid half of it within three years.

Their mother tried to calm both sides, but the most useful intervention came from an unexpected person: their uncle Bahodir, who has run a successful business for decades. He suggested a compromise that nobody had considered. The parents would lend Sardor ten thousand dollars, not twenty, and Sardor would sign a written agreement promising to repay it in monthly instalments over four years. He would also have to find the remaining half himself, either from a bank or from a partner.

Neither child was entirely satisfied. Gulnara still felt that her parents were taking an unnecessary risk, while Sardor complained that a written contract with his own father felt cold. However, after a week of reflection, both accepted. Gulnara even offered to review the business plan, free of charge, which Sardor took as an olive branch.

Looking back, Gulnara says the real lesson was how rarely money disagreements are really about money. Underneath the figures, she believes, were old questions about fairness, trust and who was the favourite child. She is trying, she says, to listen more and give her opinion less often, at least until lunch is over.

items.prompt: Why did Peter decide to study?
items.answer: He feared the automation of his workplace
items.passage:
At forty-one, Peter Lindqvist had never imagined that he would be sitting at the kitchen table at ten o'clock at night, struggling with a programming exercise. He had worked in a warehouse in Gothenburg for sixteen years, and when the company announced that part of the site would be automated, he decided that waiting to be told what to do would be a mistake. A friend recommended an online data analysis course lasting twelve weeks, and Peter signed up the same evening.

The first month was harder than he expected. The lectures were short and well made, but nobody was there to answer questions in real time, and his earlier education had been entirely in classrooms. On several occasions he watched the same ten-minute video four times before it made sense. He also discovered that studying alone was surprisingly easy to postpone. By week five, he had completed only a third of the material, and the figure on the progress bar, which he found strangely personal, made him feel guilty.

Things improved when he found a study group through the course forum. It consisted of six people from different countries, including a retired teacher in Kenya and a nurse from Portugal, and they agreed to meet online every Wednesday for an hour. Peter says that explaining a problem to someone else was the most effective way to understand it. The group also introduced a modest rule: anyone who missed two meetings in a row had to bring a cake to the next one, which, since the meetings were virtual, usually meant a photograph.

He finished the course in sixteen weeks rather than twelve, a delay he now considers perfectly normal. Statistics suggest that fewer than one in ten learners who start a free online course complete it, but Peter believes the figure is less shocking than it sounds, because many people sign up out of curiosity and never intended to finish. In his case, the cost, about two hundred euros, gave him a strong reason not to give up.

The certificate itself, he admits, did not impress his employer very much. What mattered was a small project that he built using the company's own delivery data. It revealed that a certain route was losing time every Tuesday, and his manager, to his surprise, asked him to present the findings to the directors. Six months later, Peter moved from the warehouse floor to a junior position in the logistics office, with a salary about fifteen per cent higher.

His conclusion is not that online learning is always better than classroom teaching. It is that the course matters less than the habit of applying what you learn to a real problem.
options: He had always wanted to study programming
He feared the automation of his workplace
His company paid for the course

At forty-one, Peter Lindqvist had never imagined that he would be sitting at the kitchen table at ten o'clock at night, struggling with a programming exercise. He had worked in a warehouse in Gothenburg for sixteen years, and when the company announced that part of the site would be automated, he decided that waiting to be told what to do would be a mistake. A friend recommended an online data analysis course lasting twelve weeks, and Peter signed up the same evening.

The first month was harder than he expected. The lectures were short and well made, but nobody was there to answer questions in real time, and his earlier education had been entirely in classrooms. On several occasions he watched the same ten-minute video four times before it made sense. He also discovered that studying alone was surprisingly easy to postpone. By week five, he had completed only a third of the material, and the figure on the progress bar, which he found strangely personal, made him feel guilty.

Things improved when he found a study group through the course forum. It consisted of six people from different countries, including a retired teacher in Kenya and a nurse from Portugal, and they agreed to meet online every Wednesday for an hour. Peter says that explaining a problem to someone else was the most effective way to understand it. The group also introduced a modest rule: anyone who missed two meetings in a row had to bring a cake to the next one, which, since the meetings were virtual, usually meant a photograph.

items.prompt: When did Nodira's interview take place?
items.passage:
Nodira Abdullayeva still remembers the date of her scholarship interview exactly: the fourteenth of March, a cold and rainy Thursday. She had applied for a full master's scholarship at a university in Edinburgh, and out of almost four hundred applicants, only fifteen had been invited to the final stage. She spent the night before reading her application again and again, convinced that she would be asked about every sentence.

The interview took place in a large room with a long table. Five people sat behind it: three professors, a representative of the funding organisation and a former scholar who had graduated the previous year. The chairwoman explained that the conversation would last twenty minutes, and Nodira, whose hands were shaking, noticed that a glass of water had been placed in front of her. She later learned that this small detail was deliberate. The panel wanted candidates to feel comfortable enough to think.

The first questions were easy, concerning her studies and her work as a translator. Then a professor asked her to describe a time when she had failed. Nodira had prepared an answer about a missed deadline, but she suddenly felt that it sounded artificial, so she told a different story instead: how she had lost an important translation contract because she had overestimated her ability to work at night. She explained what she had changed since, and she saw one panel member smile. Looking back, she believes that moment decided the outcome.

The most unexpected question came from the former scholar, who asked what Nodira would do if she did not receive the scholarship. She said that she would apply again the following year, working in the meantime to improve her research proposal. Several people nodded. She was careful, however, not to sound as though she needed the money desperately, since a friend had warned her that panels prefer candidates who are determined but not desperate.

The results were announced three weeks later, by email, at seven in the morning. Nodira was so nervous that she asked her sister to read it first. The scholarship covered eighty per cent of her tuition fees, but not her living costs, which meant that she still had to find about nine thousand pounds from other sources. She accepted without hesitation and spent the following summer working as an interpreter and giving evening classes.

If she could give one piece of advice to future applicants, it would be to avoid memorising answers. The panel, she says, can easily tell the difference between a prepared speech and a thoughtful person.

She spent the night before reading her application again and again, convinced that she would be asked about every sentence.

The interview took place in a large room with a long table. Five people sat behind it: three professors, a representative of the funding organisation and a former scholar who had graduated the previous year. The chairwoman explained that the conversation would last twenty minutes, and Nodira, whose hands were shaking, noticed that a glass of water had been placed in front of her. She later learned that this small detail was deliberate. The panel wanted candidates to feel comfortable enough to think.

The first questions were easy, concerning her studies and her work as a translator. Then a professor asked her to describe a time when she had failed. Nodira had prepared an answer about a missed deadline, but she suddenly felt that it sounded artificial, so she told a different story instead: how she had lost an important translation contract because she had overestimated her ability to work at night. She explained what she had changed since, and she saw one panel member smile. Looking back, she believes that moment decided the outcome.

The most unexpected question came from the former scholar, who asked what Nodira would do if she did not receive the scholarship. She said that she would apply again the following year, working in the meantime to improve her research proposal. Several people nodded. She was careful, however, not to sound as though she needed the money desperately, since a friend had warned her that panels prefer candidates who are determined but not desperate.

The results were announced three weeks later, by email, at seven in the morning. Nodira was so nervous that she asked her sister to read it first. The scholarship covered eighty per cent of her tuition fees, but not her living costs, which meant that she still had to find about nine thousand pounds from other sources. She accepted without hesitation and spent the following summer working as an interpreter and giving evening classes.

If she could give one piece of advice to future applicants, it would be to avoid memorising answers. The panel, she says, can easily tell the difference between a prepared speech and a thoughtful person.

items.prompt: How are Sven and Bobur described when they first met?
items.answer: Sven was reserved and Bobur was talkative
items.passage:
Bobur Nazarov and Sven Eriksson met eleven years ago, when a school exchange programme placed a fifteen-year-old from Tashkent in the home of a family near Stockholm. They had almost nothing in common. Sven spent his weekends sailing, while Bobur had never seen the sea. Sven spoke quietly and carefully, while Bobur talked constantly, mostly about football. Yet within a fortnight they were inseparable, and when the exchange ended after three months, both boys cried at the airport in a way that neither of them now likes to remember.

Since then, they have kept in touch by every method available. As teenagers they exchanged long emails, later they sent endless messages, and today they speak by video every other Sunday. The time difference is four hours, which means that Sven, in Stockholm, is usually cooking dinner while Bobur, in Tashkent, is already thinking about bed. In between the calls, they send each other voice messages, which Bobur prefers because they feel like a real conversation rather than a report. Sven, who is more private, admits that he would rather write.

Meeting in person has proved far more difficult than either of them expected. Sven has visited Tashkent only once, four years ago, and he still talks about the plov, the bazaar and the hospitality of Bobur's grandmother, who fed him until he could barely stand. Bobur, however, has never returned to Sweden. His first visa application was refused for reasons that were never properly explained, and a second attempt took so long that the invitation expired. He insists that he is not bitter, though his voice changes whenever the subject comes up.

The friendship has not been without crises. When Bobur's father died, Sven did not know what to say, and he waited nearly a week before writing a short, clumsy message. Bobur, who was grieving, felt abandoned, and for almost eight months they spoke only a few times. It was Sven who finally flew to Tashkent to repair the damage, and he says that the long talk they had on the roof of Bobur's building was the most honest conversation of his life. Both of them now agree that silence, not disagreement, is the real danger to a long-distance friendship.

They do not agree about everything. Bobur believes their friendship would be even closer if they lived in the same city. Sven doubts it, suggesting that two such different personalities might have drifted apart after school, and that distance forces them to make an effort that neighbours would never bother with. Next August, Sven is getting married in a small village near the coast, and Bobur, who has been asked to be best man, has already started his third visa application. Both men are quietly confident that this time, it will work.
options: Sven was reserved and Bobur was talkative
Bobur was a sailor and Sven loved football

items.prompt: What was Laura's feeling before she tried budgeting apps?
items.answer: Her salary seemed to vanish too quickly
items.passage:
Laura Whitfield, a twenty-nine-year-old nurse from Glasgow, does not consider herself careless with money. She pays her bills on time, she has never been in an overdraft and she can usually tell you roughly how much is in her account. Yet for several years she had a nagging feeling that her salary disappeared faster than it should, and last January she decided to try a budgeting app. Over the following twelve months, she tested three of them, and her experience has made her cautious about the claims such products make.

The first app was a disaster. It asked her to enter every purchase manually and to classify it using more than forty categories, including some that seemed to have been invented by an accountant with too much free time. She lasted nine days. The second app was far better. It connected directly to her bank account, sorted her spending automatically and sent a weekly summary. Within a month, it had told her something she did not want to hear: she was spending sixty-two pounds a month on coffee and one hundred and forty on takeaway meals. Laura cut the takeaways almost immediately, but she refused to give up the coffee, which she describes as the only thing that gets her through a night shift.

The third app charged a subscription of three pounds a month, which she cancelled after eight weeks when she realised that it offered nothing the second one had not. She also began to worry about privacy. Several of the free apps, she discovered, earn money by selling anonymous data about their users' habits, and although the information is supposedly impossible to trace, she found the idea unpleasant.

The most important discovery was about her own behaviour. For about four months, she checked the second app every day and felt more in control. Then, gradually, she stopped looking, and her spending drifted back to its old level. Her partner Kofi, by contrast, used exactly the same app and saved eighteen hundred pounds in a year without apparently making any effort. Laura thinks the difference is simple: Kofi is naturally cautious, whereas she needs a physical reminder.

Her present system is surprisingly old-fashioned. On the day she is paid, she withdraws a fixed amount in cash and divides it into four envelopes marked food, transport, leisure and emergencies. When an envelope is empty, she stops spending in that category until the next month. She admits that it sounds like something from her grandmother's time, but it works. In her view, an app can show you what you have done, though it cannot change what you will do. Awareness, she concludes, is only the first step; discipline has to come from somewhere else.
options: Her salary seemed to vanish too quickly
She never knew her account balance

items.prompt: What did Farhod find most difficult about organising the reunion?
items.passage:
When Farhod Qodirov agreed to organise the twenty-fifth reunion of his class in Bukhara, he thought that the hardest part would be finding people. In fact, social media made that surprisingly easy. Of the thirty-four students who had left the school together, he located thirty-one within a fortnight. The hardest part, he now says, was persuading them to actually come. Some replied immediately with enthusiasm, others promised vaguely to think about it, and a few simply read his message and never answered.

In the end, twenty-two people attended. The party was held in the old school hall on a Saturday evening, and each guest paid fifteen dollars towards food and decorations, a sum that was much criticised in the group chat until the bill arrived and turned out to be lower than anyone had predicted. Their former literature teacher, Mrs Ismoilova, who is now seventy-eight, came with her grandson and was greeted with a standing ovation. She had taught the class for four years, and she remembered almost every name without a single mistake, which impressed her former pupils far more than any of their own achievements.

Farhod had expected the evening to be a competition. He had imagined people comparing cars, salaries and holidays, and he was dreading it. To his relief, almost nobody mentioned money. Instead, they talked about the school cook who used to sing, the broken clock in the corridor and the day a goat wandered into the geography lesson. The only awkward moment came when one classmate, Anvar, who had been voted most likely to succeed, arrived late and rather quiet. He had run a successful construction firm for ten years, but it had collapsed during the recession, and he was now working as a driver. Nobody mentioned this at the party, though Farhod noticed that several people stayed beside Anvar all evening.

The real surprise was Shahlo, who in school had hardly spoken a word. She is now a surgeon in Samarkand, and she told the group that she had decided to become a doctor after Mrs Ismoilova praised one of her essays in front of the whole class. The teacher, who had completely forgotten the incident, sat in silence for a moment and then wiped her eyes. It was, Farhod says, the most memorable moment of the night.

He has since been asked whether he would organise another reunion in five years. His answer is cautious. He enjoyed the evening, but he found the planning exhausting, and he believes that the next organiser should be somebody else. What he learned is that people rarely remember what you achieved; they remember how you made them feel. After all, a school reunion is less about the past than about being seen once more by those who knew you before you had learned to hide your feelings.

items.prompt: How did Emily's father react to her plan?
items.answer: He was worried she would never come back to study
items.passage:
Emily Brandt was eighteen, with offers from three universities to study law, when she shocked her family by announcing that she would defer for a year. Her father, a solicitor, took it badly. He had always believed that a year away from education was a luxury for people who had not yet decided what to do, and he feared that his daughter, once she had tasted freedom, would never return to her studies. Her mother was more diplomatic, but even she asked several times whether this was really necessary.

Emily's plan had two stages. First, she worked in a café in Bristol for five months, six days a week, in order to earn enough money. The work was tiring, and the customers were not always polite, but she saved three thousand two hundred pounds, which she considers the real beginning of her education. Second, in March, she flew to Nepal to volunteer at a small village school, where she stayed with a local family for six weeks. The programme cost four thousand pounds in total, including flights, and she ended up spending roughly three thousand six hundred and fifty, since she cooked her own meals and walked rather than taking taxis.

The experience was far from the romantic adventure advertised in brochures. The first week was exciting, but the third was almost unbearable. She was homesick, the bed was hard, and she was frustrated that the children, who were mostly between seven and ten years old, spoke so little English. She admits that she nearly bought a ticket home. What changed her mind was a girl called Pema, who walked an hour each morning to attend lessons and who, when asked what she wanted to be, answered without hesitation that she wanted to be a doctor. Emily says she felt both inspired and ashamed.

The most unexpected result was a change of direction. During her stay, she noticed how much the village depended on a single stream for its water, and when the stream dried up in April, the family had to carry water for two kilometres. She returned to England convinced that she wanted to work on environmental problems, and instead of law she now studies environmental science at Edinburgh. Her father, to his credit, has accepted the decision, although he still describes it as an expensive way to change your mind.

Asked whether she recommends a gap year, Emily is careful. She believes that it is valuable only when it is planned, and that a year spent sleeping late or travelling without purpose would have been wasted. For her, the key was to earn the money herself, set a goal and accept that some days would be difficult. She remains grateful for the months in the café, which taught her patience, and for the weeks in Nepal, which taught her what she did not know.
options: He was worried she would never come back to study
He offered to pay for the trip

items.prompt: How long had Dani and Zafar been together before moving in?
items.passage:
After two years together, Dani Ortega and Zafar Mirzaev decided to move into a flat in Madrid, and everyone they knew assured them that it was the moment when the real relationship began. Friends warned about dirty dishes, relatives about money, and Zafar's grandmother, rather mysteriously, about the dangers of sharing a bathroom. Dani smiled politely at all of them, secretly convinced that two sensible adults who had never quarrelled seriously would manage without any help.

They were wrong, though not in the way they had expected. The first argument was not about dishes at all. It was about a sofa. Dani wanted a large grey one that she had seen in a shop, while Zafar, who had been living in a rented room with almost no furniture, insisted that they should not spend six hundred euros on something they could find second-hand. Neither of them was being unreasonable, and that was precisely what made the discussion so difficult. In the end, they bought a used leather sofa for one hundred and eighty euros, which both now agree is rather uncomfortable.

Money proved to be a more serious subject. Dani earns about two thousand euros a month as a graphic designer, whereas Zafar, who is a junior teacher, earns around twelve hundred. Dividing the rent equally would have left him with almost nothing, yet Dani felt uneasy about paying more simply because she earned more. After several evenings with a calculator, they agreed to split shared costs in proportion to their incomes, which meant that she pays sixty per cent and he pays forty. They keep their personal accounts separate and have opened a joint account only for rent, bills and food.

The habit that made the biggest difference was an unexpected one. Every Sunday evening, they sit down for a short conversation, about twenty minutes, in which each person may raise one complaint and one thing they appreciated during the week. At first, Zafar thought it was childish. Now he admits that it prevents small irritations from growing into major quarrels, such as the matter of the bathroom light, which he leaves on and which she turns off, sometimes with him inside.

Looking back, Dani says that the best preparation would have been to stay for a month at each other's places before signing a contract. She also thinks that couples underestimate how much they need time alone, so she has deliberately arranged a small desk in the bedroom where she can work in peace. Zafar, for his part, has started to enjoy the evening cooking, though he insists that this does not mean he will ever wash up willingly. Their conclusion is modest: living together is not a test of love, but it is certainly a test of habits.

items.prompt: What was Aziza's mark in the algebra test?
items.passage:
Aziza Rahimova is thirty-five and teaches mathematics at a secondary school in Namangan, and she knows exactly when she decided to become a teacher. She was fourteen, sitting at the back of Mr Tohirov's classroom, and she had just received a mark of 31 out of 100 in an algebra test. She remembers the number clearly, partly because she tried to hide the paper from her neighbour and partly because the mark was the lowest she had ever received in any subject.

At that time, Aziza had decided that she was simply bad at mathematics. Her older sister, who was good at it, had told her so, and the opinion had been quietly confirmed by other relatives. She had stopped doing homework, and she spent lessons drawing in the margins of her notebook. Mr Tohirov, a tall man in his fifties with a habit of talking to the blackboard, did not appear to notice. Aziza was quite certain that he had given up on her like everyone else.

The day after the test, however, he asked her to stay behind. She expected a lecture, but instead he asked her to explain how she had solved the first problem. She was embarrassed, but she explained, and he nodded and said that her method was nearly correct and that she had made an arithmetical slip on the third line. He proposed that she come to his room on Tuesdays and Thursdays for forty minutes after school. He would not charge anything, and he would not tell her parents. Aziza agreed mostly because she was too surprised to refuse.

What she remembers most clearly is that he never told her she was clever. He avoided praise altogether, and when she completed a difficult exercise, he simply wrote the next one on the board. Once, when she complained that she would never be good enough, he replied that she was not finished yet, which, she realised years later, was the kindest sentence anyone had said to her. By the end of the year, her marks had risen to about seventy, and by the end of school she was the best mathematician in her class.

She studied mathematics at university, became a teacher, and thought of him often. When she heard that he was retiring at sixty-seven, she wrote him a long letter thanking him. His answer came after two weeks, in careful handwriting. He wrote that he did not remember her test mark, nor the lessons on Tuesdays and Thursdays, but that he did remember the day she explained the first problem, because it was the first time in the whole year that anyone in the class had looked at him while he was talking.

Aziza has kept the letter in her desk drawer. When her own students lose heart, she tells them what Mr Tohirov told her, and she watches the look on their faces change.
